chapters.title: Letter 1
paragraphs: _To Mrs. Saville, England._
St. Petersburg, December 11th, 17—.

You'll be glad to hear that nothing has gone wrong at the start of this expedition you were so worried about. I arrived here yesterday. My first task is to reassure my dear sister that I'm well and more confident than ever in the success of my venture.

I'm already far north of London. As I walk through the streets of Petersburg, I feel a cold northern breeze on my cheeks that braces my nerves and fills me with delight. Do you understand this feeling? This wind has traveled from the very regions I'm heading toward, giving me a taste of those icy lands. Inspired by it, my daydreams grow more vivid and intense. I try to convince myself that the pole is nothing but frost and emptiness, but my imagination keeps painting it as a place of beauty and wonder. There, Margaret, the sun never sets. Its wide disk skims the horizon, spreading endless light. There — and forgive me, sister, if I trust the navigators who came before me — snow and frost are banished. We may sail over calm seas to a land more wondrous than any yet discovered. Its features may be unlike anything known, just as the heavenly bodies behave strangely in those unexplored regions. What might we find in a country of eternal light? I may discover the mysterious force that draws the compass needle. I may make a thousand astronomical observations that only this voyage can confirm. I'll see parts of the world no one has ever visited. I may walk on land no human foot has ever touched. These are my enticements. They're enough to conquer any fear of danger or death. They make me begin this difficult voyage with the joy a child feels setting out in a little boat on his first adventure up the river. And even if all my theories prove wrong, you can't deny the enormous benefit I'll bring to all of humanity by discovering a passage near the pole, or by unlocking the secret of magnetism — something that can only be achieved by an expedition like mine.

These thoughts have calmed the anxiety I felt when I started this letter. My heart glows with an enthusiasm that lifts me up, because nothing calms the mind like having a steady purpose — a fixed point on which the soul can focus. This expedition has been my dream since childhood. I devoured every account of voyages toward the North Pacific through the polar seas. You may remember that our good Uncle Thomas's entire library consisted of such travel books. My education was neglected, but I was passionately fond of reading. Those books were my constant study, day and night. They deepened the regret I'd felt as a child when I learned that my father's dying wish had forbidden my uncle from letting me go to sea.

Those dreams faded when I first read the great poets, whose words entranced my soul and lifted it to heaven. I became a poet myself and lived for a year in a paradise of my own making. I imagined I might earn a place in the temple where Homer and Shakespeare are honored. You know well how I failed and how heavily I bore the disappointment. But just at that time I inherited my cousin's fortune, and my thoughts turned back to their earlier direction.

Six years have passed since I committed myself to this great enterprise. I can still remember the exact hour when I dedicated myself to it. I began by toughening my body against hardship. I joined whale-fishers on several expeditions to the North Sea. I voluntarily endured cold, hunger, thirst, and sleeplessness. I often worked harder than the common sailors during the day and spent my nights studying mathematics, medicine, and the branches of science most useful to a naval adventurer. Twice I actually hired myself out as an under-mate on a Greenland whaler and performed admirably. I must admit I felt proud when my captain offered me the second-highest position on the vessel and begged me to stay, so valuable did he find my services.

And now, dear Margaret, don't I deserve to accomplish something great? I could have lived in ease and luxury, but I chose glory over every comfort that wealth offered me. Oh, if only some encouraging voice would say yes! My courage and resolution are firm, but my hopes waver, and my spirits often sink. I'm about to set out on a long and difficult voyage that will demand all my strength. I must not only lift the spirits of others but sometimes sustain my own when theirs are failing.

This is the best time to travel in Russia. The sledges fly quickly over the snow. The motion is pleasant — far more comfortable than an English stagecoach, in my opinion. The cold isn't unbearable if you wrap yourself in furs, a habit I've already adopted. There's a huge difference between walking on deck and sitting motionless for hours, when lack of exercise lets the blood practically freeze in your veins. I have no desire to die on the road between St. Petersburg and Archangel.

I'll leave for Archangel in two or three weeks. I plan to hire a ship there — easily done by paying the owner's insurance — and to recruit as many experienced whale-fishermen as I need. I don't intend to sail until June. And when shall I return? Ah, dear sister, how can I answer that? If I succeed, many months, perhaps years, will pass before we meet again. If I fail, you'll see me again soon, or never.
Farewell, my dear, excellent Margaret. May heaven shower blessings on you and keep me safe, so that I may again show my gratitude for all your love and kindness.
Your affectionate brother,
R. Walton

chapters.title: Letter 2
paragraphs: _To Mrs. Saville, England._
Archangel, March 28th, 17—.

How slowly time passes here, surrounded by frost and snow! Yet I've taken a second step toward my goal. I've hired a vessel and I'm now gathering my crew. The men I've already signed on seem dependable and certainly possess fearless courage.

But there's one thing I've never been able to find, and its absence now weighs on me as a terrible emptiness. I have no friend, Margaret. When I'm glowing with the thrill of success, there will be no one to share my joy. When disappointment strikes, no one will try to lift my spirits. I'll write my thoughts down, yes, but paper is a poor substitute for real human connection. I long for a companion who could understand me, whose eyes would meet mine with recognition. You may call me romantic, dear sister, but I feel the lack of a friend bitterly. I have no one near me who is both gentle and brave, whose mind is both cultivated and expansive, whose tastes match my own — someone who could improve or refine my plans. How such a friend would correct my faults! I'm too eager in action and too impatient with obstacles. But it's an even greater problem that I'm self-educated. For my first fourteen years I ran wild on the common and read nothing but Uncle Thomas's voyage books. I discovered the great English poets only at that age, and only when it was too late to benefit fully from such studies did I realize I needed to learn other languages. Now I'm twenty-eight and in reality less educated than many fifteen-year-old schoolboys. It's true that I've thought more deeply and that my daydreams are grander, but they lack — as painters say — "keeping." I desperately need a friend who has the sense not to dismiss me as a romantic and enough affection to help discipline my mind.

Well, these are useless complaints. I'll certainly find no friend on the open ocean or even here in Archangel, among merchants and seamen. Yet some feelings nobler than common human nature beat even in these rough hearts. My lieutenant, for instance, is a man of remarkable courage and drive. He's madly ambitious for advancement in his profession. He's an Englishman who, despite national and professional prejudices and a lack of refinement, retains some of humanity's noblest qualities. I first met him on a whale vessel. Finding him unemployed in this city, I easily recruited him for my expedition.

The ship's master is a man of excellent character, known among the crew for his gentleness and mild discipline. This quality, combined with his well-known integrity and fearless courage, made me eager to hire him. A youth spent in solitude, my best years passed under your gentle care — these have refined my character so deeply that I can't bear the usual brutality practiced aboard ships. I've never believed it was necessary. When I heard of a captain equally noted for his kindness and for the respect and obedience his crew showed him, I felt incredibly fortunate to secure his services. I first heard of him rather romantically, from a woman who owes her happiness to him. Briefly, here is his story. Some years ago he loved a young Russian woman of modest fortune. Having saved a considerable sum in prize money, the girl's father agreed to the match. He saw his sweetheart once before the wedding, but she was bathed in tears. Throwing herself at his feet, she begged him to release her, confessing that she loved another man who was too poor for her father to approve. My generous friend reassured her. When he learned her lover's name, he immediately gave up his pursuit. He had already bought a farm where he planned to spend the rest of his life, but he gave it all to his rival, along with the rest of his prize money so they could buy livestock. Then he went to the young woman's father himself and asked him to consent to her marriage with her true love. But the old man firmly refused, feeling honor-bound to my friend. When my friend found the father immovable, he left the country and didn't return until he heard that his former sweetheart had married the man she loved. "What a noble fellow!" you'll exclaim. He is. But he's entirely uneducated. He's as silent as a stone, and there's a kind of careless ignorance about him. It makes his conduct all the more astonishing, but it diminishes the interest and sympathy he would otherwise command.

But don't think that just because I complain a little, or because I can imagine a comfort I may never know, that I'm wavering in my resolve. My purpose is as fixed as fate. My voyage is delayed only until the weather allows me to set sail. The winter has been brutally severe, but spring looks promising. It may be a remarkably early season, so perhaps I'll sail sooner than expected. I'll do nothing rash. You know me well enough to trust my caution and care whenever others' safety is in my hands.

I can't describe what I feel at the prospect of my expedition. It's impossible to convey the trembling sensation, half pleasure and half fear, that fills me as I prepare to depart. I'm going to unexplored regions, to "the land of mist and snow," but I won't kill any albatross — so don't worry about my safety, or fear I'll come back as worn and woeful as the "Ancient Mariner." You'll smile at the reference, but I'll share a secret. I've often attributed my passion for the dangerous mysteries of the ocean to that poem by the most imaginative of modern poets. Something is at work in my soul that I don't understand. I'm practically industrious — diligent, hardworking, persistent — but alongside this there's a love of the marvelous, a belief in the marvelous, woven into all my plans. It drives me beyond the common paths of men, out to the wild sea and unvisited regions I'm about to explore.

But let me return to more personal matters. Will I see you again after crossing immense seas and returning by the southern cape of Africa or America? I dare not expect such success, yet I can't bear to imagine the alternative. Keep writing to me whenever you can. I may receive your letters when I need them most. I love you very tenderly. Remember me with affection, should you never hear from me again.
Your affectionate brother, Robert Walton

chapters.title: Letter 3
paragraphs: _To Mrs. Saville, England._
July 7th, 17—.
My dear Sister,

I'm writing quickly to say I'm safe and making good progress. This letter will reach England on a merchant ship now heading home from Archangel — luckier than me, who may not see my homeland for many years. But I'm in good spirits. My men are bold and seem resolute. The sheets of floating ice that drift past us constantly, warning of the dangers ahead, don't seem to frighten them. We've already reached a very high latitude. It's the height of summer, and though not as warm as England, the southern winds that blow us toward my destination carry a reviving warmth I hadn't expected.

Nothing noteworthy has happened so far. A couple of strong gales and a sprung leak are the kind of incidents experienced sailors barely bother to record. I'll be grateful if nothing worse happens during our voyage.
Goodbye, dear Margaret. Rest assured that for my own sake as well as yours, I won't recklessly seek out danger. I'll be cool, persistent, and careful.

But success _shall_ crown my efforts. Why not? I've come this far, tracing a safe course over pathless seas, with the very stars as witnesses to my progress. Why not continue over this untamed yet obedient element? What can stop the determined heart and resolved will of man?
My swelling heart pours itself out like this involuntarily. But I must stop. Heaven bless my beloved sister!
R.W.

chapters.title: Letter 4
paragraphs: _To Mrs. Saville, England._
August 5th, 17—.
Something so strange has happened that I must record it, even though you'll probably see me before these papers reach you.

Last Monday, July 31st, we were nearly surrounded by ice. It closed in on all sides, barely leaving the ship room to float. Our situation was dangerous, especially with a thick fog surrounding us. We stopped and waited, hoping for a change in the weather.

Around two o'clock the fog cleared, and we saw vast, irregular plains of ice stretching endlessly in every direction. Some of my companions groaned. My own mind grew tense with worry. Then a strange sight suddenly caught our attention and distracted us from our own predicament. We spotted a low carriage mounted on a sledge, pulled by dogs, heading north about half a mile away. Sitting in it was a figure shaped like a man but apparently of enormous size, guiding the dogs. We watched through our telescopes as the traveler disappeared among the distant ridges of ice.

This sight astonished us completely. We believed we were many hundred miles from any land. Yet this figure seemed to prove that land wasn't as far away as we'd thought. Trapped by ice, however, we couldn't follow the track, which we'd watched with the closest attention.

About two hours later we heard the sea shift beneath us, and before nightfall the ice broke apart and freed our ship. We stayed put until morning, though, not wanting to encounter in the dark those large loose masses of ice that float around after a breakup. I used the time to rest for a few hours.

In the morning, as soon as it was light, I went up on deck and found all the sailors gathered on one side of the vessel, apparently speaking to someone in the sea. It turned out to be a sledge, like the one we'd seen before, that had drifted toward us overnight on a large piece of ice. Only one dog was still alive, but there was a human being inside. The sailors were trying to persuade him to board our ship. Unlike the other traveler, he wasn't some savage from an undiscovered island — he was a European. When I appeared on deck, the master said, "Here is our captain. He won't let you die out on the open sea."
When the stranger saw me, he spoke in English, though with a foreign accent. "Before I come aboard your vessel," he said, "would you be kind enough to tell me where you're headed?"

You can imagine my amazement at hearing such a question from a man on the brink of death — someone for whom my ship should have been the most precious refuge on earth. I told him we were on a voyage of discovery toward the North Pole.

Hearing this, he seemed satisfied and agreed to come aboard. Good God, Margaret! If you'd seen the man who bargained for his safety like that, your shock would have been immense. His limbs were nearly frozen, and his body was terribly wasted from exhaustion and suffering. I'd never seen anyone in such wretched condition. We tried to carry him to the cabin, but as soon as he left the fresh air he fainted. We brought him back on deck and revived him by rubbing him with brandy and forcing him to swallow a little. As soon as he showed signs of life, we wrapped him in blankets and placed him near the kitchen stove chimney. Gradually he recovered and ate a little soup, which restored him wonderfully.

Two days passed before he was able to speak. I often feared his suffering had damaged his mind. When he'd recovered somewhat, I moved him to my own cabin and attended to him as much as my duties allowed. I've never met a more fascinating person. His eyes usually have a wild, even mad expression. But when someone shows him kindness or does him the smallest service, his whole face lights up with such warmth and sweetness that I've never seen its equal. Yet he's generally melancholy and despairing. Sometimes he grinds his teeth, as if crushed by the weight of his misery.

When my guest had improved a little, I had great difficulty keeping the men away. They wanted to ask him a thousand questions. But I wouldn't let them torment him with idle curiosity while his recovery clearly depended on complete rest. Once, however, the lieutenant asked why he'd come so far across the ice in such a strange vehicle.
His expression instantly turned to the deepest gloom. "To find someone who fled from me," he replied.
"And did the man you were chasing travel the same way?"
"Yes."
"Then I think we saw him. The day before we found you, we saw dogs pulling a sledge with a man in it across the ice."

This roused the stranger's interest. He asked many questions about the route the demon — as he called him — had taken. Soon after, when he was alone with me, he said, "I've no doubt stirred your curiosity, as well as these good people's. But you're too considerate to press me with questions."
"Of course. It would be deeply wrong of me to trouble you with my own curiosity."
"And yet you rescued me from a strange and dangerous situation. You kindly restored me to life."

Soon after, he asked whether I thought the breaking ice had destroyed the other sledge. I said I couldn't be certain. The ice hadn't broken until near midnight, and the traveler might have reached safety before then. But I couldn't say for sure.

From that moment, new life seemed to animate the stranger's failing body. He was desperate to go on deck and watch for the sledge that had appeared before. But I've persuaded him to stay in the cabin — he's far too weak to endure the raw air. I promised that someone would keep watch and notify him instantly if anything new appeared.

That's my account of this strange event up to now. The stranger has gradually improved in health but remains very silent and uneasy when anyone but me enters his cabin. Yet his manner is so gentle and agreeable that all the sailors are interested in him, despite having little contact with him. For my own part, I've begun to love him like a brother. His constant, deep grief fills me with sympathy and compassion. He must have been a noble person in better days, for even now, in his ruined state, he's remarkably attractive and kind.
I said in an earlier letter, dear Margaret, that I'd find no friend on the open ocean. Yet I've found a man who, before misery broke his spirit, I would have been proud to call a brother of my heart.
I'll continue writing about the stranger whenever something new happens.
August 13th, 17—.

My affection for my guest grows every day. He stirs both my admiration and my pity to an astonishing degree. How can I watch such a noble person destroyed by misery without feeling the sharpest grief? He's so gentle, yet so wise. His mind is so refined. When he speaks, though he chooses his words with the greatest art, they flow with remarkable speed and unmatched eloquence.

He's now much recovered from his illness and spends most of his time on deck, apparently watching for the sledge that came before his own. Yet despite his unhappiness, he's not so consumed by his own misery that he can't take a deep interest in others' projects. He's talked with me many times about mine, which I've shared with him openly. He listened closely to all my arguments for eventual success and to every detail of the measures I'd taken to ensure it. His sympathy easily led me to speak from the heart — to express the burning passion of my soul and to declare, with all the fervor that drives me, how gladly I would sacrifice my fortune, my existence, my every hope to further my enterprise. One man's life or death seemed a small price for the knowledge I sought, for the power I would gain over the forces of nature. As I spoke, a dark shadow spread over my listener's face. At first I saw him try to suppress his emotion. He put his hands over his eyes. My voice faltered as I watched tears streaming between his fingers. A groan burst from his heaving chest. I paused. Finally, in a broken voice, he said: "Unhappy man! Do you share my madness? Have you also drunk the intoxicating draught? Listen to me — let me tell you my story, and you'll dash the cup from your lips!"

Such words, as you can imagine, intensely stirred my curiosity. But the wave of grief that had seized him overwhelmed his weakened body. Many hours of rest and quiet conversation were needed before he regained his composure.

Having mastered his emotions, he seemed to despise himself for being a slave to passion. Pushing aside the dark grip of despair, he led the conversation back to me. He asked about my earlier years. My story was quickly told, but it sparked many reflections. I spoke of my longing for a friend, my thirst for a deeper connection with a kindred mind than I'd ever found. I expressed my conviction that a man who didn't enjoy this blessing could claim little real happiness.

"I agree with you," the stranger replied. "We are incomplete creatures, only half-formed, if someone wiser, better, dearer than ourselves — the kind of person a friend should be — doesn't lend their help to perfect our weak and flawed natures. I once had a friend, the noblest of human beings, and so I'm qualified to judge. You have hope. The world lies before you. You have no cause for despair. But I — I've lost everything and cannot begin life again."
As he said this, his face settled into a calm, profound grief that pierced my heart. But he fell silent and soon retreated to his cabin.

Even broken in spirit as he is, no one feels the beauties of nature more deeply. The starry sky, the sea, every sight these wonderful regions offer — they still have the power to lift his soul above the earth. Such a person lives a double life. He may suffer misery and be crushed by disappointments, but when he retreats into himself, he becomes like a celestial spirit surrounded by a halo, within whose circle no grief or foolishness can enter.

Will you smile at my enthusiasm for this extraordinary wanderer? You wouldn't, if you saw him. You've been refined by books and sheltered from the world, which makes you somewhat fastidious. But that only makes you better suited to appreciate this remarkable man's extraordinary qualities. I've tried to figure out what elevates him so far above every other person I've ever known. I believe it's an intuitive insight — a quick but unfailing power of judgment, a penetration into the causes of things unmatched in clarity and precision. Add to this an effortless way with words and a voice whose varied tones are music to the soul.
August 19th, 17—.

Yesterday the stranger said to me, "Captain Walton, you can clearly see that I've suffered great and unparalleled misfortunes. I once decided that the memory of these horrors should die with me. But you've changed my mind. You seek knowledge and wisdom, as I once did. I sincerely hope that fulfilling your wishes doesn't become a serpent that stings you, as mine did. I don't know if my story will be useful to you. But when I consider that you're following the same path, exposing yourself to the same dangers that made me what I am, I think you might draw a useful lesson from my tale — one that may guide you if you succeed, or console you if you fail. Prepare to hear of events usually considered extraordinary. If we were in tamer surroundings, I might fear your disbelief or ridicule. But many things will seem possible in these wild, mysterious regions that would provoke laughter elsewhere. And I'm confident my tale carries within it the evidence of its own truth."

You can imagine how eager I was to hear him, yet I couldn't bear for him to reopen his grief by recounting his misfortunes. I felt a burning desire to hear the promised story, partly from curiosity and partly from a strong wish to help him if I could. I expressed these feelings in my reply.

"Thank you," he answered, "for your sympathy, but it's useless. My fate is nearly sealed. I wait for one final event, and then I'll rest in peace. I understand your feelings," he continued, sensing I wished to interrupt, "but you're mistaken, my friend, if you'll allow me to call you that. Nothing can change my destiny. Listen to my story, and you'll see how unalterably it's been determined."

He told me he'd begin his tale the next day, when I'd be free. This promise drew from me the warmest thanks. I've resolved to record it every night, as closely as possible in his own words, whenever I'm not occupied by my duties. If I'm busy, I'll at least take notes. This manuscript will no doubt give you great pleasure. But to me, who knows him and hears it from his own lips — with what interest I'll reread it someday! Even now, as I begin my task, his rich voice fills my ears. His luminous eyes rest on me with all their melancholy sweetness. I see his thin hand raised with feeling, while the lines of his face are lit from within by his soul. His story must be strange and harrowing — terrible the storm that struck the gallant vessel on its course and wrecked it — thus!

chapters.title: Chapter 1
paragraphs: I'm Genevan by birth, and my family is one of the most prominent in the republic. My ancestors had been counselors and syndics for many years. My father held several public positions with honor and integrity. Everyone who knew him respected his dedication to public service. He spent his younger days constantly occupied by the affairs of his country. Various circumstances prevented him from marrying early, and it wasn't until late in life that he became a husband and father.

The story of his marriage says a great deal about his character, so I can't help telling it. One of his closest friends was a merchant named Beaufort who had fallen from prosperity into poverty through a series of misfortunes. Beaufort was a proud, unbending man who couldn't bear to live in poverty and obscurity in the same country where he'd once been distinguished for his wealth and status. After paying his debts honorably, he retreated with his daughter to the town of Lucerne, where he lived in hiding and wretchedness. My father loved Beaufort deeply and was devastated by his friend's retreat. He bitterly regretted the false pride that led his friend to behave so unworthily of their bond. He immediately set out to find him, hoping to persuade him to start over with his help and support.

Beaufort had hidden himself well. It took ten months before my father discovered where he was living. Overjoyed, he hurried to the house, which was on a poor street near the river Reuss. But when he entered, only misery and despair greeted him. Beaufort had saved only a tiny sum from his ruined fortune — enough to sustain him for a few months while he hoped to find respectable employment. But the waiting was spent in idleness. His grief only deepened when he had time to think. Within three months, it had taken such a hold on his mind that he lay bedridden, unable to do anything.

His daughter cared for him with the greatest tenderness, but she watched in despair as their small fund shrank rapidly with no other source of income. But Caroline Beaufort had an uncommon spirit. Her courage rose to meet her adversity. She took on plain needlework. She braided straw. By various means, she managed to earn a pittance barely enough to keep them alive.

Several months passed this way. Her father grew worse. Her time was consumed entirely by nursing him. Her means of support dwindled. In the tenth month, her father died in her arms, leaving her an orphan and penniless. This final blow overwhelmed her. She was kneeling by Beaufort's coffin, weeping bitterly, when my father entered the room. He came like a guardian angel to the poor girl. She entrusted herself to his care. After burying his friend, he brought her to Geneva and placed her under the protection of a relative. Two years later, Caroline became his wife.

There was a considerable age difference between my parents, but this seemed only to draw them closer together. My father's strong sense of justice meant he had to deeply admire someone before he could deeply love them. Perhaps in earlier years he'd been hurt by the unworthiness of someone he'd loved, which made him value proven character all the more. There was gratitude and devotion in his attachment to my mother, quite different from the doting fondness of old age. It was inspired by reverence for her virtues and a desire to somehow make up for the sorrows she'd endured. This gave a beautiful grace to his behavior toward her. Everything was arranged for her comfort and wishes. He sheltered her as a gardener shelters a delicate flower, protecting her from every harsh wind and surrounding her with everything that could bring pleasure to her gentle, generous heart. Her health, and even her once-steady spirit, had been shaken by what she'd been through. During the two years before their marriage, my father had gradually given up all his public duties. Immediately after their wedding, they traveled to Italy, seeking the pleasant climate and new experiences of that wonderful land to restore her weakened health.

From Italy they visited Germany and France. I, their eldest child, was born in Naples and traveled with them as an infant. For several years I was their only child. Deeply attached to each other, they seemed to draw inexhaustible stores of affection to pour upon me. My mother's tender embraces and my father's warm, pleased smile are my earliest memories. I was their plaything and their idol — and something better: their child, the innocent, helpless creature given to them by heaven, whose future happiness or misery lay in their hands. With this deep awareness of what they owed to the life they'd created, combined with the active tenderness that drove them both, every hour of my infancy was a lesson in patience, charity, and self-control. Yet I was guided so gently that it all felt like one continuous stream of happiness.

For a long time I was their only care. My mother had longed for a daughter, but I remained their only child. When I was about five, while traveling beyond the Italian border, they spent a week on the shores of Lake Como. Their generous natures often led them into the cottages of the poor. For my mother, this was more than a duty — it was a necessity, a passion. Remembering her own suffering and how she'd been helped, she felt compelled to be a guardian angel to the afflicted. During one of their walks, a poor cottage in a valley caught their attention. It looked especially wretched. Half-clothed children gathered around it, speaking of extreme poverty. One day, when my father had gone to Milan alone, my mother visited this cottage with me. She found a peasant and his wife, bent with care and labor, sharing a meager meal among five hungry children. Among them was one who stood out from the rest. She seemed to be of different stock. The other four were dark-eyed, hardy little urchins. This child was thin and very fair. Her hair was the brightest living gold. Despite her poor clothing, it seemed to crown her with distinction. Her brow was clear and broad, her blue eyes cloudless, and her lips and features so expressive of warmth and sweetness that no one could look at her without seeing her as a being apart — heaven-sent, bearing a celestial mark in every feature.

The peasant woman, noticing my mother's wonder and admiration for this lovely girl, eagerly told her story. The child wasn't hers but the daughter of a Milanese nobleman. Her mother was German and had died giving birth to her. The baby had been placed with these good people as a nurse. They'd been better off then. They hadn't been long married, and their eldest child was just born. The girl's father was one of those Italians raised on memories of Italy's ancient glory — one of the rebels who fought for his country's freedom. He became a victim of its weakness. Whether he'd died or still languished in an Austrian dungeon, no one knew. His property was seized. His child became an orphan and a beggar. She continued living with her foster parents and bloomed in their rough home, fairer than a garden rose among dark brambles.

When my father returned from Milan, he found a child playing with me in the hall of our villa — a child fairer than any painted angel, a creature who seemed to radiate light, whose movements were lighter than a mountain deer's. The mystery was soon explained. With his permission, my mother persuaded the foster parents to give the child to her. They were fond of the sweet orphan. Her presence had been a blessing to them. But it would be unfair to keep her in poverty when God had provided such powerful protection. They consulted their village priest. The result was that Elizabeth Lavenza became a member of my parents' household — more than my sister — the beautiful and adored companion of all my interests and pleasures.

Everyone loved Elizabeth. The passionate, almost reverential devotion everyone felt for her became my pride and delight. The evening before she was brought to our home, my mother had said playfully, "I have a pretty present for my Victor — tomorrow he shall have it." And when, the next morning, she presented Elizabeth to me as her promised gift, I — with childish seriousness — took her words literally and looked upon Elizabeth as mine. Mine to protect, love, and cherish. Every compliment paid to her, I received as praise of my own treasure. We called each other cousin. But no word could capture the bond between us — she was more than a sister, for until death she was to be mine alone.

chapters.title: Chapter 2
paragraphs: We grew up together with barely a year between our ages. We never knew disagreement or conflict. Harmony was the soul of our companionship. The differences in our characters only drew us closer. Elizabeth was calmer and more focused. But despite all my passion, I was capable of more intense concentration and was more deeply driven by a thirst for knowledge. She occupied herself with the imaginative creations of poets. In the magnificent scenery that surrounded our Swiss home — the towering mountains, the changing seasons, storms and calm, winter's silence, and the wild energy of our Alpine summers — she found endless sources of wonder and delight. While Elizabeth contemplated the grand appearance of things with a serious, satisfied spirit, I delighted in investigating their causes. The world was a secret I wanted to unlock. Curiosity, passionate research into nature's hidden laws, a joy close to rapture as they were revealed to me — these are among my earliest memories.

When my parents had a second son, seven years younger than me, they gave up their wandering life entirely and settled in their native country. We had a house in Geneva and a country estate at Belrive, on the eastern shore of the lake, about three miles from the city. We lived mainly at the latter. My parents' lives were spent in considerable seclusion. My temperament led me to avoid crowds and attach myself deeply to a few people. I was indifferent to my schoolmates in general. But I formed the closest friendship with one of them. Henry Clerval was the son of a Geneva merchant. He was a boy of remarkable talent and imagination. He loved adventure, hardship, and even danger for its own sake. He was deeply read in books of chivalry and romance. He wrote heroic songs and began many tales of enchantment and knightly adventure. He tried to make us act out plays and pageants, with characters drawn from the heroes of Roncesvalles, King Arthur's Round Table, and the crusaders who shed their blood to reclaim the Holy Land.

No one could have had a happier childhood than mine. My parents embodied kindness and indulgence. We felt they weren't tyrants ruling our lives by whim but the creators of all the delights we enjoyed. When I mixed with other families, I clearly saw how fortunate I was. Gratitude deepened my love for them.

My temperament was sometimes violent, and my passions intense. But by some quirk of nature, these energies weren't directed toward childish pursuits but toward an eager desire to learn — and not to learn everything randomly. I confess that neither languages, nor government, nor politics held any attraction for me. What I wanted were the secrets of heaven and earth. Whether it was the outward substance of things or the inner spirit of nature and the mysterious depths of the human mind, my inquiries were always directed toward the fundamental secrets of the world.

Meanwhile, Clerval occupied himself with the moral dimensions of life. The busy stage of human affairs, the virtues of heroes, and the deeds of great men were his subjects. His hope and dream was to become one of those whose names are remembered as brave and generous benefactors of humanity. Elizabeth's saintly soul shone like a lamp in our peaceful home. Her sympathy was ours. Her smile, her soft voice, the sweet light of her celestial eyes — these were always there to bless and uplift us. She was the living spirit of love, softening and attracting. I might have grown sullen in my studies or rough through the intensity of my nature, but she was there to draw out my gentleness. And Clerval — could anything have corrupted his noble spirit? Perhaps. But he might not have been so perfectly humane, so generous and kind amid his passion for adventure, had she not shown him the true beauty of doing good and made it the highest aim of his ambition.

I take real pleasure in dwelling on memories of childhood, before misfortune poisoned my mind and turned its bright visions of purpose into gloomy, self-centered reflections. Besides, in painting the picture of my early days, I'm also tracing the events that led, step by invisible step, to my later tale of misery. When I try to account for the birth of the passion that came to rule my destiny, I find it rising like a mountain river from humble, nearly forgotten sources. But as it flowed onward, it swelled into a torrent that swept away all my hopes and joys.

Natural philosophy is the force that shaped my fate. So in this account, I need to explain what drew me to that science. When I was thirteen, we all went on a pleasure trip to the baths near Thonon. Bad weather forced us to stay indoors at an inn for a day. There I happened to find a book by Cornelius Agrippa. I opened it with little interest, but his theories and the extraordinary claims he made quickly filled me with excitement. A new light seemed to dawn on my mind. Bursting with joy, I told my father about my discovery. My father glanced casually at the title page and said, "Ah! Cornelius Agrippa! My dear Victor, don't waste your time on this. It's worthless nonsense."

If instead of that dismissal my father had taken the time to explain that Agrippa's principles had been completely disproven — that modern science had far greater, real powers, while Agrippa's were imaginary — I would certainly have tossed the book aside and returned eagerly to my previous studies. The entire course of my ideas might never have taken the fatal turn that led to my ruin. But his quick glance at my book didn't convince me he knew what was in it. I kept reading with the greatest eagerness.

When I got home, my first task was to get everything this author had written, and then the works of Paracelsus and Albertus Magnus. I read and studied the wild ideas of these writers with delight. They seemed like treasures known to few besides myself. I've described myself as always having a burning desire to penetrate nature's secrets. Despite the intense labor and wonderful discoveries of modern scientists, I always came away from my studies feeling dissatisfied. Isaac Newton reportedly said he felt like a child picking up shells beside the great unexplored ocean of truth. His successors in every branch of natural science seemed to me — even with my boyish understanding — like beginners pursuing the same quest.

The uneducated farmer knew the elements around him and their practical uses. The most learned scientist knew little more. He'd partially unveiled Nature's face, but her immortal features remained a mystery. He could dissect, analyze, and name things. But the underlying causes — not to mention any ultimate cause — were utterly unknown to him. I'd looked at the walls and barriers that seemed to keep humans from entering nature's fortress, and I'd foolishly resented them.

But here were books, and here were men who had penetrated deeper and knew more. I took them at their word and became their disciple. It may seem strange that this happened in the eighteenth century. But while I followed the standard curriculum in Geneva's schools, I was largely self-taught in my favorite subjects. My father wasn't a scientist, and I was left to struggle with a child's blindness combined with a student's thirst for knowledge. Under the guidance of my new teachers, I threw myself into the search for the philosopher's stone and the elixir of life. The latter soon captured my full attention. Wealth was a lesser goal. But imagine the glory of banishing disease from the human body and making people immune to everything but violent death!

These weren't my only fantasies. My favorite authors also promised the ability to summon ghosts and demons, a promise I eagerly pursued. When my attempts always failed, I blamed my own inexperience rather than any fault in my teachers. So for a time I was occupied with discredited systems, mixing a thousand contradictory theories together and floundering in a swamp of confused knowledge. I was guided only by a passionate imagination and childish reasoning — until an accident changed the direction of my thoughts.

When I was about fifteen, we were at our house near Belrive when we witnessed an incredibly violent thunderstorm. It came from behind the Jura mountains. Thunder crashed from every direction at once with terrifying force. I watched its progress with curiosity and delight. As I stood at the door, I suddenly saw a stream of fire shoot from an old, beautiful oak tree about twenty yards from our house. The moment the dazzling light vanished, the oak had disappeared. Nothing remained but a charred stump. When we examined it the next morning, the tree had been shattered in a strange way — not splintered by the blast but reduced entirely to thin ribbons of wood. I'd never seen anything so utterly destroyed.

I already knew something about electricity. On this occasion, a man of great scientific knowledge was visiting us. Excited by what had happened, he explained a theory he'd developed about electricity and galvanism. It was completely new and astonishing to me. Everything he said made Cornelius Agrippa, Albertus Magnus, and Paracelsus — the lords of my imagination — seem irrelevant. But by some twist of fate, the overthrow of these men killed my interest in pursuing my old studies. It seemed to me as if nothing could ever truly be known. Everything that had occupied me for so long suddenly felt worthless. In one of those sudden shifts of mind that we're perhaps most prone to in youth, I gave up my former interests entirely. I dismissed natural history and all its offshoots as a deformed creation and felt the greatest contempt for a so-called science that could never even step across the threshold of real knowledge. In this mood, I turned to mathematics and related subjects as being built on solid foundations and worthy of my attention.

How strangely our minds are made, and by what thin threads we're bound to prosperity or ruin. Looking back, it seems to me as if this almost miraculous change of direction was the last effort of my guardian angel to prevent the storm that was already gathering in the stars, ready to engulf me. Her victory was announced by an unusual calm and gladness of soul that followed my abandonment of those ancient, tormenting studies. I was being taught to associate evil with their pursuit and happiness with their neglect.
It was a strong effort of the spirit of good, but it was not enough. Destiny was too powerful, and her unchangeable laws had decreed my utter and terrible destruction.

chapters.title: Chapter 3
paragraphs: When I was seventeen, my parents decided I should attend the university at Ingolstadt. I'd been educated in Geneva's schools until then, but my father thought I needed exposure to customs beyond our own country. My departure was set for an early date. But before that day could arrive, the first misfortune of my life struck — an omen of the misery to come.

Elizabeth had caught scarlet fever. Her illness was severe, and she was in the greatest danger. Many arguments were made to persuade my mother not to nurse her. She yielded to our pleas at first. But when she heard that Elizabeth's life was threatened, she could no longer control her anxiety. She went to the sickbed. Her devoted care triumphed over the disease — Elizabeth was saved. But the consequences were fatal for her rescuer. On the third day, my mother fell ill. Her fever came with the most alarming symptoms. Her doctors' faces predicted the worst. On her deathbed, the courage and kindness of this best of women did not desert her. She joined Elizabeth's hand with mine. "My children," she said, "my greatest hope for future happiness was the prospect of your union. This will now be your father's consolation. Elizabeth, my love, you must take my place with the younger children. Alas! I'm sorry to be taken from you. Happy and beloved as I've been, it's hard to leave you all. But these aren't fitting thoughts. I'll try to accept death cheerfully and hold onto the hope of meeting you in another world."

She died peacefully. Her face expressed love even in death. I don't need to describe the feelings of those whose dearest bonds are torn apart by that most irreparable evil — the void it leaves in the soul, the despair written on every face. It takes so long for the mind to accept that someone we saw every day, whose very existence seemed part of our own, is gone forever — that the brightness of a beloved eye has been extinguished and a voice so familiar and dear will never be heard again. These are the thoughts of the first days. But when time confirms the reality of the loss, the true bitterness of grief begins. Yet who hasn't had someone dear torn away? Why should I describe a sorrow everyone has felt and must feel? Eventually, grief becomes more of an indulgence than a necessity. The smile that plays on the lips, though it might seem like a sacrilege, is not banished. My mother was dead, but we still had duties to fulfill. We had to continue our lives and learn to count ourselves fortunate that at least some of our loved ones had been spared.

My departure for Ingolstadt, delayed by these events, was now set again. I asked my father for a few weeks' reprieve. It felt wrong to leave the quiet, death-like atmosphere of our mourning house so soon and rush into the thick of life. Grief was new to me, but no less frightening for that. I was reluctant to leave those who remained, and above all, I wanted to see my sweet Elizabeth find some comfort.

She hid her grief and tried to comfort us all. She looked steadily at life and took up its duties with courage and determination. She devoted herself to those she'd been taught to call her uncle and cousins. She'd never been more captivating than during this time, when she gathered up the sunshine of her smiles and spent them on us. She forgot her own sorrow in her efforts to make us forget ours.

The day of my departure finally arrived. Clerval spent the last evening with us. He'd tried to persuade his father to let him come with me as a fellow student, but without success. His father was a narrow-minded tradesman who saw only idleness and ruin in his son's ambitions. Henry felt the injustice of being denied a liberal education deeply. He said little, but when he spoke, I could read in his bright eyes and animated expression a restrained but firm resolve not to be chained to the petty details of commerce.

We stayed up late. We couldn't tear ourselves away from each other or bring ourselves to say "farewell." It was finally said, and we went to bed pretending to seek rest, each believing the other was fooled. But when I came down to the carriage at dawn, they were all there — my father to bless me once more, Clerval to press my hand one last time, Elizabeth to renew her pleas that I write often and to give her last tender attentions to her friend and playmate.

I threw myself into the carriage and gave in to the most melancholy thoughts. I, who had always been surrounded by loving companions, constantly trying to make each other happy — I was now alone. At the university I would have to make my own friends and be my own protector. My life had been remarkably sheltered and domestic, which gave me a deep resistance to new faces. I loved my brothers, Elizabeth, and Clerval — these were my "old familiar faces." I believed myself totally unfit for the company of strangers. These were my thoughts as I began my journey. But as I went on, my spirits and hopes rose. I deeply wanted knowledge. I'd often thought it hard to spend my youth confined to one place and had longed to enter the wider world. Now my wishes were being fulfilled. It would have been foolish to regret it.

I had plenty of time for these and many other reflections during the long, tiring journey to Ingolstadt. At last the town's tall white steeple came into view. I got out and was taken to my room to spend the evening as I wished.

The next morning I delivered my letters of introduction and visited some of the chief professors. Chance — or rather the evil influence that had claimed power over me from the moment I left my father's door — led me first to Professor Krempe, who taught natural philosophy. He was a rough man, but deeply versed in his science. He asked me several questions about my progress in various branches of natural science. I answered carelessly and mentioned the names of my alchemist authors as the main writers I'd studied. The professor stared. "Have you," he said, "really spent your time studying such nonsense?"

I said I had. "Every minute," Professor Krempe continued with heat, "every instant you wasted on those books is utterly and entirely lost. You've stuffed your memory with discredited theories and worthless names. Good God! What desert did you grow up in, where no one was kind enough to tell you that these ideas you so eagerly absorbed are a thousand years old and as stale as they are ancient? In this age of science and enlightenment, I hardly expected to find a follower of Albertus Magnus and Paracelsus. My dear sir, you must begin your studies entirely from scratch."

With that, he stepped aside and wrote a list of books on natural philosophy for me to buy. He dismissed me after mentioning that the following week he'd begin a lecture course on natural philosophy in general, and that Professor Waldman, a colleague, would lecture on chemistry on alternate days.

I went home not disappointed — I'd long considered those authors useless, as the professor said. But I was no more inclined to return to those studies in any form. Professor Krempe was a short, squat man with a harsh voice and unpleasant face. The teacher didn't endear me to his subject. Looking back with perhaps too much philosophical clarity, I'd already drawn my own conclusions about science in my early years. As a child, I wasn't satisfied with what modern scientists promised. In my confusion — understandable given my youth and lack of guidance — I'd retraced the path of knowledge backward through time, exchanging modern discoveries for the dreams of forgotten alchemists. Besides, I had contempt for the goals of modern natural science. When the old masters sought immortality and power, their aims were grand, even if futile. But now everything had changed. Modern scientists seemed content to demolish the very visions that had first drawn me to science. I was being asked to trade boundless dreams for trivial realities.

These were my thoughts during my first few days at Ingolstadt, which I spent mostly getting to know the place and its residents. But as the following week began, I thought about what Professor Krempe had said about the lectures. I couldn't bring myself to go hear that smug little man hold forth from a lectern. But I remembered what he'd said about Professor Waldman, whom I hadn't met since he'd been away.

Partly from curiosity and partly from having nothing better to do, I went to the lecture hall. Professor Waldman entered shortly after. He was nothing like his colleague. He appeared about fifty years old, with a face full of kindness. A few gray hairs covered his temples, but those at the back were nearly black. He was short but remarkably upright, and his voice was the sweetest I'd ever heard. He began with a survey of the history of chemistry and the contributions of various scholars, speaking the names of the greatest discoverers with genuine passion. Then he gave an overview of the current state of the science and explained many of its basic concepts. After a few demonstrations, he concluded with a tribute to modern chemistry that I shall never forget:

"The ancient teachers of this science," he said, "promised impossible things and accomplished nothing. The modern masters promise very little. They know that metals can't be turned into gold and that the elixir of life is a fantasy. But these scientists, whose hands seem made only for test tubes and microscopes, have truly performed miracles. They penetrate into nature's inner workings and reveal how she operates in her most hidden places. They reach into the heavens. They've discovered how blood circulates and what the air we breathe is made of. They've gained new and nearly unlimited powers. They can command the lightning, mimic the earthquake, and even mock the invisible world with its own shadows."

Those were the professor's words — or rather, let me say, the words of fate — spoken to destroy me. As he continued, I felt as if my soul were wrestling with something tangible. One by one, various keys were touched that formed the mechanism of my being. String after string was struck. Soon my mind was filled with one thought, one vision, one purpose. So much has been done, cried the soul of Frankenstein — more, far more, will I achieve. Following in the steps already marked, I will pioneer a new way, explore unknown powers, and reveal to the world the deepest mysteries of creation.

I didn't close my eyes that night. My mind was in a state of upheaval and turmoil. I sensed that order would emerge from the chaos, but I had no power to make it happen. Gradually, after dawn, sleep came. When I woke, the previous night's thoughts felt like a dream. Only a resolution remained: to return to my old studies and devote myself to a science for which I believed I had a natural gift. That same day I visited Professor Waldman. His manner in private was even more warm and inviting than in public. The certain dignity he carried in the lecture hall was replaced at home by the greatest friendliness and kindness. I gave him roughly the same account of my former studies as I'd given his colleague. He listened attentively and smiled at the names of Cornelius Agrippa and Paracelsus — but without Professor Krempe's contempt. He said, "These were men to whose tireless dedication modern scientists owe most of the foundations of their knowledge. They left us the easier task of giving new names and organizing the facts they were largely responsible for bringing to light. The work of brilliant minds, however wrongly directed, almost always ends up benefiting humanity." I listened to this fair, unpretentious statement, then told him his lecture had removed my prejudice against modern chemistry. I spoke carefully, with the modesty a young student owes his teacher, without revealing the enthusiasm that was already driving my intended work. I asked his advice about which books to get.

"I'm happy," said Professor Waldman, "to have gained a student. If your effort matches your ability, I have no doubt you'll succeed. Chemistry is the branch of natural science where the greatest advances have been and may yet be made, which is why I've made it my specialty. But at the same time, I haven't neglected the other branches. A man who studied only chemistry would make a poor chemist. If you truly want to become a scientist and not merely a petty experimenter, I'd advise you to study every branch of natural philosophy, including mathematics."

He then took me into his laboratory and explained his various instruments. He told me what I should buy and promised I could use his own equipment once I'd advanced far enough not to damage it. He also gave me the book list I'd requested, and I took my leave.
So ended a day that was to be memorable for me. It decided my future destiny.

chapters.title: Chapter 4
paragraphs: From that day, natural philosophy — and chemistry in particular, in the broadest sense — became nearly my only occupation. I read eagerly the works of genius and insight that modern scientists had written. I attended lectures and cultivated the acquaintance of the university's men of science. I found even in Professor Krempe a great deal of sound knowledge and real information, despite his unpleasant appearance and manner. In Professor Waldman I found a true friend. His gentleness was never tainted by arrogance, and his teaching was delivered with such openness and good nature that it banished any hint of stuffiness. In a thousand ways he smoothed my path to knowledge, making the most complex subjects clear and accessible. My effort was unsteady at first, but it gained strength as I went on and soon became so intense that the stars often faded into morning light while I was still working in my laboratory.

Given my dedication, my progress was naturally rapid. My passion astonished the other students, and my skill impressed the professors. Professor Krempe often asked me, with a sly smile, how Cornelius Agrippa was getting along, while Professor Waldman expressed the greatest delight in my progress. Two years passed this way. I paid no visit to Geneva, being engaged heart and soul in pursuing discoveries I hoped to make. Only those who've experienced it can understand the pull of science. In other fields, you go as far as others have gone before, and there's nothing more to learn. But in science, there's always something new to discover and marvel at. A mind of moderate ability that closely pursues one subject must inevitably achieve great skill in it. And I, who continually chased a single goal with complete focus, improved so quickly that by the end of two years I'd made some discoveries in chemical instrumentation that earned me great recognition at the university. When I'd learned as much theory and practice as any professor at Ingolstadt could teach me, I thought about going home — until an incident extended my stay.

One phenomenon had particularly captured my attention: the structure of the human body, and indeed any living creature. Where, I often asked myself, does the principle of life come from? It was a bold question, one that has always been considered a mystery. Yet how many truths hover just beyond our grasp, kept at bay only by our cowardice or carelessness? I thought this over and resolved to focus specifically on the branches of natural philosophy related to physiology. Without an almost supernatural passion, this study would have been unbearable. To examine the causes of life, we must first turn to death. I studied anatomy, but that wasn't enough. I also had to observe the natural decay and corruption of the human body. My father had been careful to ensure my mind was never haunted by supernatural fears. I'd never trembled at ghost stories or feared apparitions. Darkness had no effect on me. A graveyard was simply a place where bodies, once the seat of beauty and strength, became food for worms. Now I was led to examine the process of decay and forced to spend days and nights in vaults and charnel houses. I fixed my attention on every detail most repulsive to human feeling. I watched the fine form of man degrade and waste away. I saw the flush of life give way to the corruption of death. I watched how worms inherited the wonders of the eye and brain. I paused, examining and analyzing every detail of this transformation from life to death and death to life — until, from the midst of this darkness, a sudden light broke upon me. A light so brilliant and yet so simple that, while I was dizzy with the immensity of what it revealed, I was stunned that among so many brilliant scientists who had pursued the same questions, I alone should be the one to discover so astonishing a secret.

Remember, I'm not describing the ravings of a madman. The sun doesn't shine more certainly in the sky than this truth I'm about to tell you. Some miracle might have produced it, yet the stages of the discovery were clear and logical. After days and nights of incredible labor and exhaustion, I succeeded in discovering the cause of life. More than that — I became capable of bringing lifeless matter to life.

The astonishment I first felt at this discovery soon gave way to delight and ecstasy. After so much painful work, to arrive at the summit of my desires was the most gratifying reward I could imagine. But the discovery was so immense and overwhelming that all the steps that had led me to it were wiped from my mind. I saw only the result. What the wisest men in history had sought since the creation of the world was now within my grasp. Not that it all opened before me at once, like a magic scene. The knowledge I'd gained was better suited to direct my efforts toward a goal than to present that goal as already achieved. I was like the man in the old tale who was buried alive with the dead and found a passage to life, aided only by one faint, flickering light.

I can see from your eagerness and the wonder and hope in your eyes, my friend, that you expect me to share this secret. I cannot. Listen patiently to the end of my story, and you'll easily understand why I hold back. I won't lead you, unguarded and passionate as I was then, to your destruction and certain misery. Learn from me — if not from my words, then from my example — how dangerous the pursuit of knowledge can be, and how much happier is the man who believes his small town is the whole world than the one who tries to become greater than nature allows.

When I found such astonishing power in my hands, I hesitated a long time over how to use it. Although I could give life, preparing a body to receive it — with all its intricate fibers, muscles, and veins — remained enormously difficult. I debated whether to attempt a being like myself or something simpler. But my imagination was too inflamed by my first success to doubt my ability to create something as complex and wonderful as a human being. The materials I had seemed barely adequate for such an ambitious project, but I didn't doubt I would ultimately succeed. I prepared myself for countless setbacks. My work might be repeatedly thwarted, and the final result might be imperfect. Yet when I considered the daily improvements in science and technology, I was encouraged to hope that my present attempts would at least lay the foundation for future success. I couldn't let the magnitude and complexity of my plan serve as an argument against it. With these feelings, I began the creation of a human being. Since the smallness of the parts would greatly slow my work, I decided — contrary to my first intention — to make the being of enormous size: about eight feet tall and proportionally large. After making this decision and spending some months collecting and preparing my materials, I began.

No one can imagine the storm of feelings that drove me forward in those first days of success. Life and death seemed to me like imaginary boundaries I would break through first, flooding our dark world with light. A new species would bless me as its creator and source. Many happy and excellent beings would owe their existence to me. No father could deserve his children's gratitude as completely as I would deserve theirs. And if I could give life to dead matter, I might eventually — though it seemed impossible now — learn to restore life where death had claimed it.

These thoughts sustained me while I pursued my work with relentless drive. My cheeks grew pale from study. My body wasted from confinement. Sometimes, on the very edge of success, I failed. Yet I still clung to the hope that the next day or the next hour might deliver the breakthrough. The one secret I possessed was the hope I'd dedicated myself to. The moon watched over my midnight labors while, with breathless, unrelenting eagerness, I tracked nature to her hiding places. Who can imagine the horrors of my secret work as I dug among the foul dampness of graves or tortured living animals to give life to lifeless clay? My limbs tremble and my eyes blur at the memory. But then, a resistless, almost frantic impulse drove me on. I seemed to have lost all feeling except for this one pursuit. It was only a passing frenzy that made me feel the horror all the more sharply once the unnatural stimulus wore off and my old self returned. I collected bones from charnel houses. With unholy fingers, I disturbed the deepest secrets of the human body. In a solitary room at the top of the house — really more of a cell, separated from all other rooms by a gallery and staircase — I kept my workshop of filthy creation. My eyes were nearly starting from their sockets as I labored over the details. The dissecting room and the slaughterhouse provided many of my materials. Often my humanity recoiled from my work. But still, driven by an eagerness that kept growing, I brought my creation near to completion.

The summer months passed while I was engaged, heart and soul, in this single pursuit. It was a beautiful season. The fields had never produced a more plentiful harvest, nor the vines a more abundant vintage. But my eyes were blind to nature's beauty. The same obsession that made me ignore the world around me also caused me to forget the friends who were so many miles away and whom I hadn't seen in so long. I knew my silence worried them. I remembered my father's words: "I know that while you're pleased with yourself, you'll think of us with affection, and we'll hear from you regularly. If your letters stop coming, I'll have to assume you're neglecting your other duties too."

I knew well how my father would feel, but I couldn't tear my thoughts from my work. It was loathsome in itself, yet it had seized an irresistible hold on my mind. I wanted to push aside everything related to my emotions until the great project that consumed my every instinct was finished.

I later thought my father would be unfair to blame me for vice or weakness. But I'm now convinced he was right to suspect I wasn't entirely blameless. A person should always maintain a calm and peaceful mind and never let passion or fleeting desire disturb that peace. I don't think the pursuit of knowledge is an exception to this rule. If a study tends to weaken your affections and destroy your taste for simple pleasures, then that study is certainly wrong — unfit for the human mind. If this rule were always followed, if no one let any pursuit interfere with domestic love, Greece would not have been enslaved, Caesar would have spared his country, America would have been discovered more gradually, and the empires of Mexico and Peru would not have been destroyed.
But I'm moralizing at the most exciting part of my tale, and your expression reminds me to continue.

My father didn't reproach me in his letters. He only noticed my silence by asking about my work in greater detail. Winter, spring, and summer passed during my labors. But I didn't watch the blossoms open or the leaves unfold — sights that had once given me supreme delight. I was that deeply absorbed. The leaves of that year had withered before my work neared completion. Every day showed me more clearly how well I had succeeded. But my enthusiasm was dampened by anxiety. I seemed more like a slave condemned to toil in a mine than an artist at his beloved work. Every night I was gripped by a slow fever. I became nervously sensitive to a painful degree. The fall of a leaf startled me. I avoided other people as if I were guilty of a crime. Sometimes I was alarmed at the wreck I was becoming. Only the driving force of my purpose kept me going. My work would end soon, I told myself, and then exercise and recreation would cure my creeping illness. I promised myself both of these when my creation was complete.

chapters.title: Chapter 5
paragraphs: It was on a dreary night in November that I saw the result of my labors. With an anxiety bordering on agony, I gathered the instruments of life around me, ready to spark a glimmer of being into the lifeless thing at my feet. It was already one in the morning. Rain pattered dismally against the windows. My candle was nearly burned out. Then, by the flickering half-light, I saw the creature's dull yellow eye open. It drew a hard breath, and a convulsive movement shook its limbs.

How can I describe my feelings at this catastrophe? How can I capture the wretch I had worked so hard to create? His limbs were in proportion. I had chosen features I considered beautiful. Beautiful! Good God! His yellow skin barely covered the muscles and arteries beneath. His hair was lustrous black and flowing. His teeth were pearly white. But these fine details only made a more horrible contrast with his watery eyes — nearly the same color as the pale sockets they sat in — his shriveled complexion, and straight black lips.

The twists of life are not as changeable as human emotions. I had worked relentlessly for nearly two years with the sole purpose of bringing a lifeless body to life. I had sacrificed my rest and my health. I had wanted it with a passion beyond all moderation. But now that I was finished, the beauty of the dream vanished. Breathless horror and disgust filled my heart. Unable to bear the sight of the being I'd created, I rushed from the room. I paced my bedroom for a long time, unable to calm my mind enough to sleep. Eventually exhaustion overcame the turmoil I'd endured, and I threw myself on the bed fully clothed, trying to find a few moments of forgetfulness. But it was useless. I slept, but the wildest dreams tormented me. I thought I saw Elizabeth, glowing with health, walking through the streets of Ingolstadt. Delighted and surprised, I embraced her. But as I pressed my first kiss to her lips, they turned the color of death. Her features seemed to change, and I realized I was holding the corpse of my dead mother in my arms. A shroud wrapped her body, and I saw grave-worms crawling in the folds of the cloth. I woke with horror. Cold sweat covered my forehead. My teeth chattered. Every limb convulsed. Then, by the dim yellow moonlight forcing through the shutters, I saw the wretch — the miserable monster I had created. He was holding up the bed curtain. His eyes — if you could call them eyes — were fixed on me. His jaw opened. He mumbled some inarticulate sounds. A grin wrinkled his cheeks. He might have spoken, but I didn't hear. One hand reached out, seemingly to hold me, but I broke free and rushed downstairs. I took shelter in the courtyard, where I stayed for the rest of the night, pacing back and forth in the greatest agitation, listening intently, catching and dreading each sound as if it might herald the approach of the monstrous corpse to which I had so miserably given life.

Oh! No mortal could bear the horror of that face. A reanimated mummy could not have been so hideous. I had looked at him while he was still unfinished — he was ugly then. But when those muscles and joints were brought to life, he became something not even Dante could have imagined.

I passed the night in wretchedness. Sometimes my pulse beat so fast and hard that I could feel every artery throb. Other times I nearly collapsed from exhaustion and extreme weakness. Mingled with the horror was the bitterness of disappointment. Dreams that had been my nourishment and comfort for so long had become my hell. The change was so sudden, the collapse so complete!

Morning — gray and wet — finally revealed to my sleepless, aching eyes the church of Ingolstadt with its white steeple and clock showing six o'clock. The porter opened the courtyard gates that had been my refuge through the night. I went out into the streets, walking quickly as if I were trying to avoid the wretch I feared would appear around every corner. I didn't dare return to my apartment. I felt driven to keep moving, though drenched by rain falling from a black, comfortless sky.

I kept walking like this for some time, trying to ease my mental burden through physical exercise. I wandered the streets with no clear idea of where I was going or what I was doing. My heart hammered with fear. I hurried on with irregular steps, not daring to look around:
Like one who, on a lonely road, Doth walk in fear and dread, And, having once turned round, walks on, And turns no more his head; Because he knows a frightful fiend Doth close behind him tread.
[Coleridge's "Ancient Mariner."]

Continuing this way, I eventually came to the inn where carriages usually stopped. I paused, not knowing why, and stood for several minutes staring at a coach approaching from the other end of the street. As it drew closer, I recognized the Swiss coach. It stopped right where I stood. The door opened, and I saw Henry Clerval, who instantly jumped out. "My dear Frankenstein!" he cried. "How glad I am to see you! How lucky that you're here just as I arrive!"

Nothing could match my delight at seeing Clerval. His presence brought back thoughts of my father, Elizabeth, and all the beloved scenes of home. I grasped his hand. In an instant, I forgot my horror and misery. For the first time in many months, I felt sudden, calm, pure joy. I welcomed my friend with the greatest warmth. We walked toward my college. Clerval talked for some time about our mutual friends and his own good fortune in being allowed to come to Ingolstadt. "You can imagine," he said, "how hard it was to convince my father that all necessary knowledge isn't found in bookkeeping. I think he remained unconvinced to the end. His constant reply to my pleas was the same as the Dutch schoolmaster's in The Vicar of Wakefield: 'I have ten thousand florins a year without Greek, I eat heartily without Greek.' But his love for me finally overcame his dislike of learning, and he's let me set off on a voyage of discovery to the land of knowledge."
"It's wonderful to see you. But tell me, how did you leave my father, my brothers, and Elizabeth?"

"Very well and very happy, though a little worried because they hear from you so rarely. By the way, I plan to scold you on their behalf. But my dear Frankenstein," he continued, stopping short and studying my face, "I didn't notice before how terribly ill you look. So thin and pale — you look as if you haven't slept for days."

"You've guessed right. I've been so deeply occupied with one project that I haven't allowed myself enough rest, as you can see. But I hope — I sincerely hope — that all these labors are now finished and I'm finally free."

I trembled violently. I couldn't bear to think of, much less mention, what had happened the night before. I walked quickly, and we soon reached my college. Then the thought struck me — and it made me shiver — that the creature I'd left in my apartment might still be there, alive and walking about. I dreaded seeing the monster, but I feared even more that Henry might see him. I begged him to wait a few minutes at the bottom of the stairs, then raced up to my room. My hand was on the lock before I caught myself. I paused, and a cold shudder ran through me. I threw the door open violently, the way children do when they expect a ghost waiting on the other side. But nothing was there. The apartment was empty. My bedroom was free of its hideous occupant. I could hardly believe my luck. When I was sure my enemy had truly fled, I clapped my hands for joy and ran back down to Clerval.

We went up to my room. The servant soon brought breakfast, but I couldn't contain myself. It wasn't just joy that possessed me. My skin tingled with excess sensation. My pulse raced. I couldn't stay still for a single moment. I jumped over chairs, clapped my hands, and laughed aloud. Clerval first attributed my wild spirits to happiness at his arrival. But when he looked more closely, he saw a wildness in my eyes he couldn't account for. My loud, uncontrolled, frantic laughter frightened and bewildered him.
"My dear Victor," he cried, "what in God's name is the matter? Don't laugh like that. You're ill! What's causing all this?"

"Don't ask me," I cried, covering my eyes, for I thought I saw the dreaded specter glide into the room. "_He_ can tell. Oh, save me! Save me!" I imagined the monster seizing me. I struggled wildly and collapsed in a fit.

Poor Clerval! What must he have felt? A reunion he'd looked forward to with such joy had turned suddenly to bewilderment. But I didn't witness his distress, for I was unconscious and didn't recover my senses for a long, long time.

This was the beginning of a nervous fever that confined me for several months. During all that time, Henry was my only nurse. I later learned that, knowing my father's age made a long journey inadvisable and how much my illness would distress Elizabeth, he spared them this grief by hiding how sick I really was. He knew I couldn't have a kinder or more attentive nurse than himself. Confident I would recover, he believed that rather than doing harm, he was performing the kindest possible act toward them.

But I was genuinely very ill. Only Henry's limitless, tireless care could have brought me back to life. The image of the monster I'd created was constantly before my eyes. I raved endlessly about him. My words must have puzzled Henry. At first he took them for the wanderings of a fevered mind. But my persistent return to the same subject convinced him that my illness truly had its origin in some terrible event.

Very slowly, with frequent relapses that alarmed my friend, I recovered. I remember the first time I could look at the world around me with any kind of pleasure. I noticed that the fallen leaves had disappeared and young buds were sprouting from the trees outside my window. It was a divine spring, and the season greatly helped my recovery.
