I felt joy and affection revive in my heart. My gloom faded. Soon I was as cheerful as I'd been before that fatal passion seized me.

"Dearest Clerval," I exclaimed, "how kind, how incredibly good you are to me. Instead of studying this whole winter as you'd planned, you've spent it in my sick room. How can I ever repay you? I feel terrible about the disappointment I've caused you. But please forgive me."
"You'll repay me completely if you just get well as fast as you can and don't upset yourself. Since you seem to be in such good spirits, may I mention one thing?"
I trembled. One thing! What could it be? Could he be referring to the subject I didn't dare even think about?

"Relax," said Clerval, noticing my change of color. "I won't bring it up if it upsets you. But your father and cousin would be very happy to receive a letter from you in your own handwriting. They barely know how ill you've been, and your long silence has worried them."
"Is that all, dear Henry? How could you think my first thought wouldn't fly to those dear, dear friends I love and who deserve my love so much?"
"If that's how you feel, you'll perhaps be glad to see a letter that's been waiting here for you for some days. It's from your cousin, I believe."

chapters.title: Chapter 6
paragraphs: Clerval then put the following letter into my hands. It was from my own Elizabeth:
"My dearest Cousin,

"You have been ill, very ill, and even dear kind Henry's constant letters aren't enough to reassure me. You're forbidden to write or even hold a pen. Yet one word from you, dear Victor, is all we need to calm our fears. I've been expecting that word with every post, and I've managed to stop my uncle from making the long journey to Ingolstadt. I've spared him the difficulties and possible dangers of such a trip, yet how often I've wished I could go myself! I imagined some hired nurse attending your sickbed — someone who could never guess your needs or care for you with the love your poor cousin would. But that's over now. Clerval writes that you're getting better. I eagerly hope you'll confirm this soon in your own handwriting.

"Get well and come home. You'll find a happy, cheerful household and friends who love you dearly. Your father is in good health. He asks only to see you and to know you're well. Not a single worry will cloud his kind face. How pleased you'd be to see how Ernest has grown! He's sixteen now, full of energy and spirit. He wants to be a true Swiss and enter military service abroad. But we can't let him go, at least not until his elder brother returns. My uncle doesn't like the idea of a military career in a distant country. But Ernest never had your powers of concentration. He thinks of study as a hateful burden. He spends his time outdoors, climbing hills or rowing on the lake. I'm afraid he'll become an idler unless we give in and let him pursue the career he's chosen.

"Little has changed besides the children growing up. The blue lake and snow-capped mountains never change. I think our peaceful home and contented hearts are governed by the same timeless laws. My small occupations fill my time and amuse me. I'm rewarded by seeing nothing but happy, kind faces around me. Since you left, only one change has occurred in our household. Do you remember when Justine Moritz came to our family? Probably not, so let me tell you her story briefly. Her mother, Madame Moritz, was a widow with four children. Justine was the third. She had always been her father's favorite, but through a strange cruelty, her mother couldn't stand her. After Monsieur Moritz died, her mother treated her terribly. My aunt noticed this, and when Justine was twelve, persuaded her mother to let her live with us. The democratic institutions of our country have created simpler, happier manners than those of the great monarchies around us. The differences between social classes are smaller here. The lower classes, being neither so poor nor so despised, have more refined and moral habits. Being a servant in Geneva doesn't mean the same thing as being a servant in France or England. Justine joined our family and learned a servant's duties — a role which, in our fortunate country, doesn't imply ignorance or loss of human dignity.

"You may remember that Justine was a great favorite of yours. I recall you once said that if you were in a bad mood, one look from Justine could fix it, for the same reason Ariosto gives for Angelica's beauty — she looked so open-hearted and happy. My aunt grew very fond of her and gave her a better education than she'd originally planned. Justine repaid this kindness fully. She was the most grateful creature in the world. Not that she made speeches about it — I never heard one leave her lips. But you could see in her eyes that she nearly worshipped her protectress. Though she was cheerful and sometimes careless by nature, she paid the closest attention to every gesture my aunt made. She thought my aunt was the model of perfection and tried to imitate her way of speaking and behaving. Even now she often reminds me of her.

"When my dearest aunt died, everyone was too consumed by their own grief to notice poor Justine, who had nursed her through her final illness with the most devoted care. Poor Justine was very ill herself. But other trials awaited her.

"One by one, her brothers and sister died. Her mother, left with only her neglected daughter, was now childless except for her. The woman's conscience troubled her. She began to think these deaths were heaven's punishment for her favoritism. She was a Roman Catholic, and I believe her confessor encouraged this idea. So, a few months after you left for Ingolstadt, Justine's repentant mother called her home. Poor girl! She wept when she left our house. She was much changed since my aunt's death. Grief had softened her and given her a quiet sweetness that replaced her former liveliness. Living with her mother didn't restore her spirits. The poor woman swung back and forth in her repentance — sometimes begging Justine to forgive her cruelty, but more often accusing her of causing her siblings' deaths. This constant emotional abuse eventually threw Madame Moritz into a decline that at first increased her bitterness but ended with her death at the start of this past winter. Justine has just returned to us. I assure you I love her dearly. She's very clever, gentle, and extremely pretty. As I mentioned, her manner and expression constantly remind me of my dear aunt.

"I must also say a few words about little darling William. I wish you could see him! He's very tall for his age, with sweet laughing blue eyes, dark eyelashes, and curly hair. When he smiles, two little dimples appear on each rosy, healthy cheek. He already has one or two little sweethearts, but his favorite is Louisa Biron, a pretty little girl of five.

"Now, dear Victor, I'm sure you want some gossip about the good people of Geneva. The pretty Miss Mansfield has already received congratulations on her upcoming marriage to a young Englishman, John Melbourne, Esq. Her plain sister, Manon, married Monsieur Duvillard, the rich banker, last autumn. Your favorite schoolmate, Louis Manoir, has suffered several misfortunes since Clerval left Geneva. But he's recovered his spirits and is reportedly about to marry a lively, pretty Frenchwoman, Madame Tavernier. She's a widow, much older than Manoir, but she's greatly admired and a favorite with everyone.

"Writing this has put me in better spirits, dear cousin. But my anxiety returns as I finish. Write, dearest Victor — one line, one word would be a blessing to us. Ten thousand thanks to Henry for his kindness, his love, and his many letters. We're sincerely grateful. Farewell, my cousin! Take care of yourself, and I beg you — write!
"Elizabeth Lavenza.
"Geneva, March 18th, 17—."

"Dear, dear Elizabeth!" I exclaimed when I'd finished her letter. "I'll write immediately and relieve their anxiety." I wrote, and the effort greatly tired me. But my recovery had begun and continued steadily. Within another two weeks I was able to leave my room.

One of my first duties after recovering was to introduce Clerval to the university professors. This put me through a kind of ordeal ill-suited to the wounds my mind had suffered. Ever since that fatal night — the end of my labors and the beginning of my misfortunes — I'd developed a violent hatred for even the name of natural philosophy. Merely seeing a chemical instrument would bring back all the agony of my nervous breakdown. Henry recognized this and removed all my equipment from sight. He'd also moved me to a different room, sensing my hatred for the one that had been my laboratory. But these precautions were useless when I visited the professors. Professor Waldman tortured me when he praised, with kindness and warmth, the astonishing progress I'd made in science. He soon noticed my discomfort but didn't guess the real cause. Attributing my reaction to modesty, he changed the subject from my achievements to the science itself, clearly hoping to draw me out. What could I do? He meant to be kind, and he was tormenting me. I felt as if he were carefully placing before me, one by one, the instruments that would later be used to kill me slowly. I squirmed under his words but didn't dare show my pain. Clerval, whose sharp eyes always read others' feelings, steered the conversation away by pleading complete ignorance of the subject. I silently thanked him from the depths of my heart. I could clearly see his surprise, but he never tried to extract my secret. Though I loved him with boundless affection and reverence, I could never bring myself to confide in him about the event that haunted my memory. I feared that telling someone else would only imprint it more deeply on my mind.

Professor Krempe was less tactful. In my almost unbearably sensitive state, his blunt, harsh compliments caused me even more pain than Professor Waldman's kind praise. "Damn the fellow!" he cried. "Monsieur Clerval, I assure you he's surpassed us all. Yes, stare if you like, but it's true. A young man who just a few years ago believed in Cornelius Agrippa as firmly as the gospel has now put himself at the head of the university. If we don't pull him down soon, we'll all be put to shame. Ah, yes," he continued, noticing my expression of discomfort, "Monsieur Frankenstein is modest. An excellent quality in a young man. Young men should be modest, Monsieur Clerval. I was modest myself once, but that wears off quickly."
Professor Krempe had now launched into praising himself, which thankfully steered the conversation away from a subject that was agony for me.

Clerval had never shared my interest in natural science. His scholarly pursuits were completely different from mine. He'd come to the university to master the Oriental languages, which would help him realize his life plan. Determined to pursue a distinguished career, he'd turned his gaze toward the East as a field for his ambitious spirit. Persian, Arabic, and Sanskrit occupied his attention. I was easily persuaded to join him in these studies. Idleness had always been unbearable to me. Now that I wanted to escape my own thoughts and hated my old studies, I found great relief in being a fellow student with my friend. The works of the Orientalists gave me not just learning but consolation. I didn't try to master the languages critically, as Henry did, since I only intended them as temporary distraction. I read simply for meaning, and they amply rewarded my efforts. Their melancholy is soothing and their joy uplifting to a degree I'd never experienced in any other literature. When you read their writings, life seems to consist of a warm sun and a garden of roses — the smiles and frowns of a beautiful adversary, and the fire consuming your own heart. How different from the bold, heroic poetry of Greece and Rome!

Summer passed in these activities. My return to Geneva was planned for late autumn. But several delays pushed it back. Winter came, the roads became impassable, and my journey was postponed until spring. I felt this delay keenly, for I longed to see my hometown and my beloved friends. I'd only stayed so long because I was reluctant to leave Clerval in a strange place before he'd made acquaintances. The winter passed cheerfully, though. And when spring finally came — uncommonly late — its beauty made up for the wait.

May had already begun. I was expecting the letter that would set my departure date when Henry proposed a walking tour of the countryside around Ingolstadt, so I could say a personal farewell to the area I'd lived in so long. I happily agreed. I was fond of exercise, and Clerval had always been my favorite companion on such outings in our native country.

We spent two weeks on this ramble. My health and spirits had long since recovered, and they gained extra strength from the fresh air, the natural sights along our way, and my friend's conversation. Study had previously cut me off from other people and made me unsociable. But Clerval drew out the better feelings in my heart. He taught me again to love nature's beauty and children's cheerful faces. Excellent friend! How genuinely you loved me and tried to lift my mind to the level of your own. A selfish obsession had cramped and narrowed me until your gentleness and warmth opened my senses again. I became the same happy person who, a few years earlier, loved and was loved by all, with no sorrow or care. When I was happy, nature could give me the most delightful feelings. A clear sky and green fields filled me with bliss. This season was truly divine — spring flowers blooming in the hedges, summer buds already forming. I was free of the thoughts that had weighed on me the previous year despite my efforts to shake them off.

Henry rejoiced in my cheerfulness and shared my feelings wholeheartedly. His mind was remarkably alive on these occasions. His conversation sparkled with imagination. Often, imitating the Persian and Arabic writers, he invented tales of wonderful fantasy and passion. Other times he recited my favorite poems or drew me into debates, which he conducted with great cleverness.

We returned to the university on a Sunday afternoon. Peasants were dancing. Everyone we met seemed happy and cheerful. My own spirits were high. I strode along with feelings of unbounded joy and delight.

chapters.title: Chapter 7
paragraphs: On my return, I found the following letter from my father:
"My dear Victor,

"You've probably been waiting impatiently for a letter setting the date of your return. I was tempted at first to write just a few lines mentioning when to expect you. But that would be a cruel kindness, and I can't do it. What would your surprise be, my son, if instead of a happy welcome you found tears and misery? And how, Victor, can I tell you about our tragedy? Absence can't have made you indifferent to our joys and sorrows. How shall I deliver such pain to my long-absent son? I want to prepare you for the terrible news, but I know it's impossible. Even now your eye is racing across the page, searching for the words that will tell you the horrible truth.
"William is dead! That sweet child whose smiles warmed and delighted my heart, who was so gentle yet so full of life! Victor, he was murdered!
"I won't try to console you. I'll simply describe what happened.

"Last Thursday, May 7th, I went walking in Plainpalais with my niece and your two brothers. The evening was warm and pleasant, and we stayed out longer than usual. It was already getting dark before we thought about heading home. That's when we realized William and Ernest, who had gone ahead, were nowhere to be found. We sat down to wait for them. Soon Ernest came back and asked if we'd seen his brother. He said they'd been playing together, that William had run off to hide, and that he'd searched for him in vain and waited a long time, but William never came back.

"This alarmed us. We kept searching until nightfall, when Elizabeth guessed he might have gone home. He hadn't. We went out again with torches. I couldn't rest knowing my sweet boy might be lost, exposed to the damp and cold of night. Elizabeth suffered extreme anguish too. Around five in the morning, I found my lovely boy — whom I'd seen just the night before, so full of life and health — lying on the grass, pale and motionless. The murderer's fingermarks were on his neck.

"He was carried home. The anguish on my face gave away the secret to Elizabeth. She desperately wanted to see the body. I tried to stop her at first, but she insisted. Entering the room where he lay, she quickly examined the victim's neck. Clasping her hands, she cried, 'Oh God! I've murdered my darling child!'

"She fainted and was revived only with the greatest difficulty. When she came to, she could only weep. She told me that the same evening, William had begged her to let him wear a very valuable miniature portrait she had of your mother. The picture is gone. It was undoubtedly what lured the murderer to the deed. We have no trace of him yet, though we're searching tirelessly. But nothing will bring back my beloved William!

"Come, dearest Victor. You alone can console Elizabeth. She weeps constantly and blames herself as the cause of his death. Her words pierce my heart. We're all miserable. But won't that be one more reason for you, my son, to come home and comfort us? Your dear mother! Alas, Victor! I find myself saying, thank God she didn't live to see the cruel, miserable death of her youngest child!

"Come, Victor — not with thoughts of vengeance against the murderer, but with feelings of peace and gentleness that will heal, rather than worsen, our wounds. Enter this house of mourning, my friend, with kindness and love for those who care about you, not with hatred for your enemies.
"Your affectionate and afflicted father,
"Alphonse Frankenstein.
"Geneva, May 12th, 17—."

Clerval had been watching my face as I read. He was startled to see the despair that replaced the joy I'd first shown at receiving news from my friends. I threw the letter on the table and covered my face with my hands.
"My dear Frankenstein," cried Henry, seeing my bitter tears, "must you always be unhappy? My dear friend, what's happened?"
I motioned him to read the letter while I paced the room in extreme agitation. Tears streamed from Clerval's eyes too as he read the account of my tragedy.
"I can offer you no comfort, my friend," he said. "Your loss is beyond repair. What do you plan to do?"
"Go to Geneva immediately. Come with me, Henry, to arrange the horses."

As we walked, Clerval tried to say a few consoling words. He could only express his deepest sympathy. "Poor William!" he said. "Dear, lovely child. He sleeps now with his angel mother! Who that saw him — so bright and joyful in his young beauty — could help but weep at his untimely loss! To die so horribly, to feel the murderer's grip! How much worse that someone could destroy such innocent radiance! Poor little fellow! We have one consolation: his friends mourn and weep, but he is at rest. The agony is over. His suffering has ended forever. He's covered by earth now and knows no pain. We can no longer pity him. We must save that for his miserable survivors."

Clerval said this as we hurried through the streets. His words impressed themselves on my mind, and I remembered them later in solitude. But for now, as soon as the horses arrived, I jumped into a carriage and said goodbye to my friend.

My journey was deeply sad. At first I wanted to hurry, longing to console my loved ones. But as I approached my hometown, I slowed down. I could barely endure the flood of feelings crowding into my mind. I passed through scenes familiar from my youth, scenes I hadn't seen in nearly six years. How much might have changed in that time! One sudden, devastating event had struck. But a thousand small circumstances might have worked other changes — quieter ones, but no less significant. Fear overcame me. I didn't dare go forward, dreading a thousand nameless horrors I couldn't define.

I stayed two days at Lausanne in this painful state of mind. I gazed at the lake. The water was calm. Everything around was peaceful, and the snowy mountains — the palaces of nature — were unchanged. Gradually the calm, heavenly scene restored me, and I continued toward Geneva.

The road ran alongside the lake, which grew narrower as I approached home. I could see the dark slopes of the Jura more clearly, and the bright summit of Mont Blanc. I wept like a child. "Dear mountains! My own beautiful lake! How do you welcome your wanderer? Your peaks are clear, the sky and lake are blue and still. Is this a promise of peace, or are you mocking my unhappiness?"

I'm afraid, my friend, that I'll bore you by dwelling on these details. But they were days of relative happiness, and I think of them with pleasure. My country, my beloved country! Only a native can know the delight I took in seeing your streams, mountains, and above all, your lovely lake!

Yet as I drew closer to home, grief and fear overwhelmed me again. Night was falling. When I could barely see the dark mountains, I felt even gloomier. The landscape seemed like a vast, dim scene of evil. I sensed that I was destined to become the most wretched of human beings. Alas! I prophesied truly, and failed only in one thing: in all the misery I imagined and dreaded, I didn't conceive a hundredth part of the anguish I was destined to endure.

It was completely dark when I reached the outskirts of Geneva. The city gates were already shut, so I had to spend the night at Secheron, a village about a mile and a half away. The sky was clear. Unable to rest, I decided to visit the spot where poor William had been murdered. Since I couldn't pass through town, I crossed the lake by boat to reach Plainpalais. During the short crossing, I saw lightning playing on Mont Blanc's summit in the most beautiful patterns. The storm seemed to be approaching quickly. When I landed, I climbed a low hill to watch its progress. It advanced. The sky clouded over. I soon felt large drops of rain, and its violence quickly increased.

I left my seat and walked on, though the darkness and storm grew worse by the minute. Thunder crashed directly over my head with terrific force. Echoes bounced from Mount Saleve, the Jura, and the Alps of Savoy. Vivid lightning flashes blinded me, illuminating the lake like a vast sheet of fire, then plunging everything into pitch darkness until my eyes could recover. The storm appeared in several parts of the sky at once, as often happens in Switzerland. The most violent part hung exactly north of the town, over the lake between Belrive and Copet. Another lit up the Jura with faint flashes. A third alternately revealed and hid the Mole, a peaked mountain east of the lake.

While I watched the tempest — so beautiful yet so terrifying — I walked on quickly. This noble war in the sky lifted my spirits. I clasped my hands and cried aloud, "William, dear angel! This is your funeral. This is your requiem!" As I said these words, I spotted a figure stealing from behind a clump of trees near me. I stopped and stared. I couldn't be mistaken. A flash of lightning illuminated it clearly: its gigantic height and the deformity of its appearance, more hideous than any human face. I knew instantly that it was the wretch, the filthy demon to whom I had given life. What was he doing there? Could he be — I shuddered at the thought — the murderer of my brother? No sooner did that idea cross my mind than I was certain of it. My teeth chattered. I had to lean against a tree for support. The figure passed quickly and vanished into the darkness. Nothing in human form could have destroyed that innocent child. _He_ was the murderer! I was sure of it. The mere thought carried irresistible proof. I considered chasing the monster, but it would have been hopeless. Another flash revealed him clinging to the rocks of the nearly vertical face of Mount Saleve. He quickly reached the summit and disappeared.

I stood motionless. The thunder stopped, but the rain continued. The scene was wrapped in impenetrable darkness. I turned over in my mind the events I had tried to forget: the entire course of my journey toward the creation, the appearance of my handiwork at my bedside, its departure. Nearly two years had passed since the night I first gave it life. Was this its first crime? Alas! I had turned loose upon the world a depraved wretch whose joy was in destruction and misery. Had he not murdered my brother?

No one can imagine the anguish I suffered through the rest of that night, spent cold and wet in the open air. But I didn't feel the weather. My imagination was consumed with scenes of evil and despair. I thought about the being I had cast among humanity, endowed with the will and power to carry out purposes of horror. I saw it almost as my own vampire, my own spirit let loose from the grave, forced to destroy everything dear to me.

Day broke, and I headed toward town. The gates were open. I hurried to my father's house. My first instinct was to reveal what I knew about the murderer and have him pursued immediately. But I hesitated when I considered the story I'd have to tell. A being I myself had created and given life had met me at midnight on the slopes of an inaccessible mountain. I also remembered the nervous fever that had seized me just after the creation — a detail that would make an already impossible story sound like pure madness. I knew that if anyone else had told me such a tale, I'd have dismissed it as insane. Besides, the creature's strange nature would let it escape any pursuit, even if my family believed me enough to begin one. And what would be the point? Who could arrest a creature capable of climbing the sheer face of Mount Saleve? These thoughts made up my mind, and I resolved to stay silent.
It was about five in the morning when I entered my father's house. I told the servants not to wake the family and went to the library to wait for the usual hour of rising.

Six years had passed — lived as a dream except for one indelible mark — and I stood in the same spot where I'd last embraced my father before leaving for Ingolstadt. Beloved parent! He still remained to me. I gazed at the portrait of my mother that hung above the mantelpiece. It was a historical painting, commissioned by my father, showing Caroline Beaufort in an agony of despair, kneeling by her dead father's coffin. Her clothes were simple, her cheek pale, but there was an air of dignity and beauty that barely permitted pity. Below this painting was a miniature of William. Tears flowed when I looked at it. While I stood there, Ernest entered. He'd heard me arrive and rushed to welcome me. "Welcome, my dearest Victor," he said. "Ah! I wish you'd come three months ago. You would have found us all joyful and happy. You come now to share a misery nothing can ease. But your presence will, I hope, revive our father, who seems to be sinking under his grief. And maybe you can persuade poor Elizabeth to stop her endless, tormenting self-blame. Poor William! He was our darling and our pride!"

Uncontrolled tears fell from my brother's eyes. A sense of mortal agony crept over me. Before, I'd only imagined the wretchedness of our destroyed home. Now reality hit me as a new, equally terrible disaster. I tried to calm Ernest and asked about my father and then about my cousin.
"She needs consolation most of all," said Ernest. "She's accused herself of causing my brother's death, and that's made her terribly unhappy. But since the murderer has been discovered—"

"The murderer discovered! Good God! How? Who could possibly pursue him? It's impossible — like trying to outrun the wind or stop a mountain stream with a straw. I saw him too. He was free last night!"

"I don't know what you mean," replied my brother in confusion. "But for us, this discovery has completed our misery. No one wanted to believe it at first. Even now Elizabeth won't be convinced, despite all the evidence. Who would have thought that Justine Moritz — so kind and devoted to the whole family — could suddenly commit such a horrible, appalling crime?"
"Justine Moritz! Poor, poor girl — she's the accused? But it's wrong! Everyone must know that. Surely no one believes it, Ernest?"

"No one did at first. But several things came to light that have almost forced us to believe it. And her own confused behavior has added weight to the evidence. I'm afraid it leaves no room for doubt. But she'll be tried today, and then you'll hear everything."

He then told me that on the morning William's murder was discovered, Justine had fallen ill and been confined to bed for several days. During this time, a servant examining the clothes she'd worn that night found the portrait of my mother in her pocket — the miniature that was thought to be the murderer's motive. The servant immediately showed it to another, who went straight to a magistrate without telling the family. Based on their statements, Justine was arrested. When confronted with the evidence, the poor girl's extreme confusion only deepened the suspicion.
This was a strange story, but it didn't shake my belief. I replied firmly, "You're all wrong. I know who the murderer is. Justine, poor, good Justine, is innocent."

At that moment my father entered. I saw deep unhappiness on his face, but he tried to welcome me cheerfully. After we'd exchanged our sad greetings, he would have changed the subject, but Ernest exclaimed, "Good God, Papa! Victor says he knows who murdered poor William."
"Unfortunately, we do too," replied my father, "for I would rather have remained ignorant forever than discover such depravity and ingratitude in someone I valued so highly."
"My dear father, you're mistaken. Justine is innocent."
"If she is, God forbid she should suffer as guilty. She's to be tried today, and I sincerely hope she'll be acquitted."

This calmed me. I was firmly convinced that Justine — and indeed every human being — was guiltless of this murder. I had no fear that any circumstantial evidence could be strong enough to convict her. My own tale was impossible to tell publicly. Its astounding horror would be dismissed as madness by everyone. Did anyone besides me — the creator — even believe in the existence of the living monument to arrogance and reckless ignorance that I had let loose on the world?

We were soon joined by Elizabeth. Time had changed her since I'd last seen her. She was more beautiful than in her girlhood. She had the same sincerity, the same liveliness, but paired with an expression of deeper intelligence and feeling. She welcomed me with the greatest warmth. "Your arrival, dear cousin," she said, "fills me with hope. Perhaps you'll find some way to prove my poor Justine innocent. Alas! Who is safe if she's convicted? I believe in her innocence as firmly as I believe in my own. Our misfortune is doubly hard. We've not only lost our lovely darling boy, but this poor girl — whom I sincerely love — faces an even worse fate. If she's condemned, I'll never know joy again. But she won't be. I'm sure she won't. And then I'll be happy again, even after the sad death of my little William."
"She is innocent, my Elizabeth," I said, "and that will be proved. Don't be afraid. Take heart from the certainty of her acquittal."
"How kind and generous you are! Everyone else believes she's guilty, and that made me hopeless — because I knew it was impossible. Seeing everyone else convinced of it left me in despair." She wept.
"Dearest niece," said my father, "dry your tears. If she is, as you believe, innocent, trust in the justice of our laws and in my determination to prevent the slightest hint of unfairness."

chapters.title: Chapter 8
paragraphs: We spent a few sad hours until eleven o'clock, when the trial was set to begin. My father and the rest of the family had to attend as witnesses, so I went with them to the court. Throughout this wretched mockery of justice, I suffered living torture. The verdict would decide whether my curiosity and reckless experiments would cause the death of two people: one an innocent, smiling baby, the other far more cruelly murdered, with every possible aggravation of injustice making her death memorable in its horror. Justine was a girl of merit whose qualities promised a happy life. Now everything was to be destroyed in a shameful grave — and I was the cause! A thousand times I would rather have confessed to the crime myself. But I'd been absent when it happened. Such a declaration would be dismissed as madness and wouldn't save Justine.

Justine appeared calm. She wore mourning, and her face — always appealing — was made exquisitely beautiful by the depth of her feelings. Yet she seemed confident in her innocence and didn't tremble, though thousands stared at her with hatred. All the sympathy her beauty might have aroused was destroyed by the spectators' certainty of the monstrous crime she supposedly committed. She was composed, though clearly forcing herself to appear courageous. Her earlier confusion had already been cited as proof of guilt, so she steeled her mind to show courage. When she entered the court, she looked around and quickly found where we were sitting. A tear seemed to dim her eye when she saw us, but she quickly recovered. A look of sorrowful affection seemed to declare her complete innocence.

The trial began. After the prosecutor stated the charge, several witnesses were called. The facts that emerged were damning — enough to have shaken anyone who didn't have the proof of her innocence that I had. She had been out all night on the night of the murder. Toward morning, she'd been spotted by a market woman near where the body was later found. When asked what she was doing there, she looked strange and gave a confused, unintelligible answer. She returned to the house around eight o'clock. When someone asked where she'd been all night, she said she'd been looking for the child and urgently asked if there was any news of him. When shown the body, she fell into violent fits and was bedridden for several days. Then the miniature portrait was produced — the one the servant found in her pocket. When Elizabeth, in a faltering voice, confirmed it was the same picture she'd hung around William's neck an hour before he disappeared, a murmur of horror and outrage filled the courtroom.

Justine was called to defend herself. As the trial progressed, her expression had changed. Surprise, horror, and misery were written on her face. Sometimes she fought back tears. But when asked to plead, she gathered her strength and spoke in an audible, though unsteady, voice.

"God knows," she said, "how completely innocent I am. But I don't expect my protests alone to clear me. I rest my innocence on a plain and simple explanation of the facts that have been presented against me. I hope the character I've always maintained will lead my judges to interpret any doubtful or suspicious circumstances in my favor."

She then explained that she had spent the evening of the murder at the house of an aunt in Chene, a village about three miles from Geneva, with Elizabeth's permission. On her way back, around nine o'clock, she met a man who asked if she'd seen a lost child. Alarmed, she spent several hours searching for him. When the city gates were shut, she was forced to spend the night in a barn, unwilling to disturb the cottage owners, who knew her well. She spent most of the night awake there. Toward morning she believed she slept a few minutes before being woken by footsteps. At dawn she left her shelter to search again. If she'd gone near the spot where his body lay, she didn't know it. Her confusion when questioned by the market woman wasn't surprising — she'd had a sleepless night, and William's fate was still unknown. As for the portrait, she had no explanation.

"I know," the unhappy victim continued, "how heavily this one piece of evidence weighs against me. But I have no way to explain it. When I've declared my complete ignorance, all I can do is guess how it might have been placed in my pocket. But even here I'm stuck. I believe I have no enemy on earth. Surely no one would try to destroy me for no reason. Did the murderer put it there? I know of no chance he would have had. And even if he did, why would he steal the jewel only to immediately give it away?

"I place my fate in the hands of my judges. Yet I see no reason for hope. I ask permission to have a few witnesses speak to my character. If their testimony can't outweigh my supposed guilt, then I must be condemned — though I would stake my salvation on my innocence."

Several witnesses who had known her for years were called, and they spoke well of her. But fear and hatred of the crime made them timid and reluctant to come forward. Elizabeth saw even this last hope — Justine's excellent character and spotless record — about to fail her. Although deeply shaken, she asked permission to address the court.

"I am," she said, "the cousin of the murdered child — or rather his sister, for I was raised by his parents and have lived with them since long before his birth. It may seem improper for me to speak at this trial. But when I see a fellow human being about to die through the cowardice of her supposed friends, I must speak up and say what I know of her character. I know the accused well. I lived in the same house with her — for five years at one time and nearly two years at another. During all that time she seemed to me the most kind and generous person imaginable. She nursed my aunt, Madame Frankenstein, in her final illness with the greatest love and care. Afterward she nursed her own mother through a long illness in a way that inspired everyone's admiration. Then she lived again in my uncle's house, where every member of the family loved her. She was warmly devoted to the child who is now dead and treated him like the most affectionate mother. For my own part, I don't hesitate to say that despite all the evidence against her, I believe absolutely in her innocence. She had no reason for such an act. As for the trinket that forms the main evidence — if she had wanted it, I would gladly have given it to her. That's how much I value and respect her."

A murmur of approval followed Elizabeth's simple, powerful appeal. But it was inspired by her generous courage, not by any shift in feeling toward poor Justine. The public's rage actually turned on her with renewed force, accusing her of the darkest ingratitude. Justine herself wept as Elizabeth spoke but didn't respond. My own agitation and anguish during the entire trial were extreme. I believed in her innocence — I knew it. Could the demon who had murdered my brother — I didn't doubt it for a minute — also have framed an innocent person for death? I couldn't bear the horror of my situation. When I saw that public opinion and the judges' faces had already condemned the poor girl, I rushed from the courtroom in agony. The suffering of the accused didn't equal mine. She was sustained by innocence. But the fangs of remorse tore at my heart and wouldn't let go.

I spent a night of unrelieved wretchedness. In the morning I went back to the court. My lips and throat were parched. I didn't dare ask the fatal question, but the officers knew me and guessed why I was there. The votes had been cast. They were all guilty. Justine was condemned.

I can't describe what I felt then. I'd experienced horror before and tried to put it into words. But no language can convey the heartsick despair I endured. The official I spoke to added that Justine had already confessed. "That confession," he observed, "was hardly necessary in such a clear-cut case. But I'm glad of it. None of our judges likes to condemn anyone on circumstantial evidence alone, no matter how decisive."

This was strange and unexpected news. What could it mean? Had my eyes deceived me? Was I really as mad as the whole world would think if I revealed what I suspected? I hurried home. Elizabeth demanded to know the result.
"My cousin," I replied, "it's been decided as you might have expected. All judges would rather let ten innocent people suffer than let one guilty person escape. But she has confessed."

This was a devastating blow to poor Elizabeth, who had relied firmly on Justine's innocence. "Alas!" she said. "How shall I ever believe in human goodness again? Justine, whom I loved like a sister — how could she have worn that mask of innocence only to betray us? Her gentle eyes seemed incapable of cruelty or deceit, yet she's committed murder."

Soon we heard that the poor victim had asked to see my cousin. My father urged Elizabeth not to go, but left it to her own judgment. "Yes," said Elizabeth, "I'll go, even though she's guilty. And you, Victor, must come with me. I can't go alone." The thought of this visit was torture to me, but I couldn't refuse.

We entered the gloomy prison cell and found Justine sitting on some straw at the far end, her hands in shackles, her head resting on her knees. She stood when she saw us. When we were left alone with her, she threw herself at Elizabeth's feet, weeping bitterly. My cousin wept too.
"Oh, Justine!" she said. "Why did you rob me of my last consolation? I trusted your innocence. I was already wretched, but not as miserable as I am now."
"Do you too believe I'm so terribly wicked? Do you too join my enemies in crushing me, condemning me as a murderer?" Her voice was choked with sobs.

"Stand up, my poor girl," said Elizabeth. "Why kneel if you're innocent? I'm not your enemy. I believed you guiltless despite all the evidence, until I heard that you'd confessed your guilt yourself. You say that report is false. Be certain, dear Justine, that nothing can shake my faith in you except your own confession."

"I did confess — but I confessed a lie. I confessed to obtain absolution. But now that falsehood weighs on my heart more heavily than all my other sins. God in heaven forgive me! Ever since I was condemned, my confessor has pressured me relentlessly. He threatened and terrorized me until I almost started to believe I was the monster he said I was. He threatened excommunication and hellfire in my last moments if I didn't give in. Dear lady, I had no one to support me. Everyone looked on me as a wretch doomed to shame and damnation. What could I do? In a weak moment I agreed to a lie. Only now am I truly miserable."

She paused, weeping, then continued, "I thought with horror, my sweet lady, that you might believe your Justine — whom your blessed aunt honored so highly, and whom you loved — was capable of a crime only the devil himself could commit. Dear William! Dearest blessed child! I'll see you again soon in heaven, where we'll all be happy. That thought consoles me, even as I go to face disgrace and death."

"Oh, Justine! Forgive me for doubting you, even for a moment. Why did you confess? But don't grieve, dear girl. Don't be afraid. I'll proclaim your innocence. I'll prove it. I'll melt the stony hearts of your enemies with my tears and prayers. You shall not die! You — my playmate, my companion, my sister — you won't die on the scaffold! No! No! I could never survive such a horror."

Justine shook her head sadly. "I'm not afraid to die," she said. "That terror has passed. God gives me strength to endure the worst. I'm leaving a sad and bitter world. If you remember me and think of me as someone unjustly condemned, I accept my fate. Learn from me, dear lady, to submit with patience to heaven's will."

During this conversation, I'd retreated to a corner of the cell to hide the horrible anguish consuming me. Despair! Who dared speak of that? The poor victim, who would cross the terrible boundary between life and death tomorrow, didn't feel the deep, bitter agony I felt. I ground my teeth together and groaned from the depths of my soul. Justine started at the sound. When she saw who it was, she approached me and said, "Dear sir, you're very kind to visit me. I hope you don't believe I'm guilty?"
I couldn't answer. "No, Justine," said Elizabeth. "He's even more convinced of your innocence than I was. Even when he heard you'd confessed, he didn't believe it."

"I truly thank him. In these last moments, I feel the sincerest gratitude toward those who think of me with kindness. How sweet is others' affection to a wretch like me! It takes away more than half my misery. I feel as if I could die in peace now that you, dear lady, and your cousin believe I'm innocent."

So the poor victim tried to comfort others and herself. She did achieve the resignation she sought. But I — the true murderer — felt the never-dying worm alive in my heart, allowing no hope or consolation. Elizabeth also wept and was unhappy, but hers was the misery of innocence — like a cloud passing over the fair moon, temporarily hiding but never dimming its brightness. Anguish and despair had penetrated to the core of my heart. I bore a hell within me that nothing could extinguish. We stayed several hours with Justine. Elizabeth could barely tear herself away. "I wish," she cried, "that I could die with you. I can't live in this world of misery."

Justine put on an air of cheerfulness while struggling to hold back her bitter tears. She embraced Elizabeth and said, in a voice of barely controlled emotion, "Farewell, sweet lady, dearest Elizabeth, my beloved and only friend. May heaven bless and preserve you. May this be the last misfortune you ever suffer! Live, and be happy, and make others happy too."

The next day, Justine died. Elizabeth's heartbreaking eloquence failed to move the judges from their conviction. My passionate, indignant protests were ignored. When I heard their cold replies and their harsh, unfeeling logic, the confession I'd been about to make died on my lips. All I would accomplish was declaring myself a madman without saving Justine. She died on the scaffold, branded as a murderess.

From the tortures of my own heart, I turned to watch Elizabeth's deep, silent grief. This too was my doing! And my father's suffering, and the ruin of our once-happy home — all were the work of my cursed hands! You weep, unhappy ones, but these are not your last tears! You'll raise the funeral cry again and again! Frankenstein — your son, your kinsman, your early and dearly loved friend, who would give every drop of his blood for you, who has no thought of joy except as reflected in your dear faces, who would fill the air with blessings and spend his life serving you — he tells you to weep, to shed countless tears. He hopes only that if enough tears fall, inexorable fate may be satisfied and that destruction may stop before the peace of the grave finally succeeds your sad torment.
So spoke my prophetic soul, as, torn by remorse, horror, and despair, I watched those I loved grieve helplessly over the graves of William and Justine, the first victims of my unholy experiments.

chapters.title: Chapter 9
paragraphs: Nothing is more painful to the human mind than the dead calm that follows after emotions have been whipped up by a rapid series of events — a stillness that robs the soul of both hope and fear. Justine was dead. She was at rest. But I was alive. Blood flowed freely through my veins, yet a crushing weight of despair and remorse sat on my heart that nothing could lift. Sleep fled from me. I wandered like an evil spirit, for I had committed deeds of indescribable horror — and more, much more, I was sure, was yet to come. Yet my heart overflowed with kindness and a love of virtue. I'd begun life with good intentions and longed for the moment when I could put them into practice and be useful to others. Now all was destroyed. Instead of the clear conscience that had once let me look back with satisfaction and look forward with hope, I was gripped by guilt and remorse that dragged me into a hell of torment beyond what language can express.

This mental state ate away at my health, which had perhaps never fully recovered from its first collapse. I avoided other people. Any sound of joy or contentment was torture to me. Solitude was my only comfort — deep, dark, deathlike solitude.

My father noticed the change in my mood and habits with pain. He tried to inspire me with courage, drawing on his own clear conscience and blameless life. "Victor," he said, "do you think I don't suffer too? No one could love a child more than I loved your brother" — tears came to his eyes — "but isn't it our duty to the survivors to control our grief? Excessive sorrow prevents improvement or enjoyment, or even the ability to fulfill daily duties. Without that, no man is fit for society."

This advice, though good, didn't apply to my situation at all. I should have been the first to hide my grief and comfort my friends — if remorse hadn't mixed its bitterness, and terror its alarm, with everything else I felt. All I could do was look at my father in despair and try to hide from his sight.

Around this time, we moved to our house at Belrive. This change was especially welcome to me. Geneva's gates shut regularly at ten, and being confined within the city walls had become unbearable. Now I was free. Often, after the rest of the family had gone to bed, I took the boat and spent hours on the water. Sometimes the wind filled my sails and carried me along. Sometimes I rowed to the middle of the lake, then let the boat drift while I gave in to my miserable thoughts. I was often tempted — when all around me was peaceful and I was the only restless creature wandering through such beauty, except perhaps a bat or the frogs whose harsh croaking I heard only near the shore — I was often tempted to plunge into the silent lake, to let the water close over me and my suffering forever. But I held back. I thought of Elizabeth, whom I loved dearly and whose life was bound to mine. I thought of my father and surviving brother. Should I desert them through cowardice and leave them unprotected against the monster I'd let loose among them?

In those moments I wept bitterly and wished for peace — if only so I could bring comfort and happiness to my family. But that was impossible. Remorse destroyed every hope. I had caused irreversible evil, and I lived in daily fear that the monster would commit some new atrocity. I had a persistent feeling that it wasn't over — that he would still commit some monstrous crime that would almost erase the memory of what had come before. As long as anyone I loved still lived, there was always room for fear. My hatred of this creature was beyond description. When I thought of him, I gnashed my teeth, my eyes burned, and I wished desperately to destroy the life I had so thoughtlessly given. When I considered his crimes and malice, my hatred and desire for revenge burst all bounds. I would have made a pilgrimage to the highest peak of the Andes if I could have thrown him from the summit. I longed to see him again so I could unleash the full force of my hatred and avenge the deaths of William and Justine.

Ours was a house of mourning. My father's health was deeply shaken by recent events. Elizabeth was sad and despairing. She no longer took pleasure in anything. All enjoyment seemed wrong, a sin against the dead. Endless tears and grief, she felt, were the only fitting tribute to innocence so cruelly destroyed. She was no longer the happy girl who had once walked with me along the lake, talking excitedly about our future. The first sorrow sent to teach us that earth is not heaven had reached her, and its shadow had dimmed her brightest smiles.

"When I think, dear cousin," she said, "about the miserable death of Justine Moritz, I no longer see the world as I used to. Before, I read about vice and injustice in books or heard about it from others, and it seemed like ancient history or imaginary evil — remote and more real to my reason than to my feelings. But now misery has come home. People seem to me like monsters thirsting for each other's blood. Yet I know I'm being unfair. Everyone believed that poor girl was guilty. If she had committed the crime, she would have been the most depraved creature alive. To have murdered the son of her benefactor — a child she'd nursed from birth and seemed to love as her own — for a few jewels! I couldn't consent to anyone's death, but I would certainly have thought such a person unfit to live among others. But she was innocent. I know it. I feel it. You agree with me, which confirms what I know. Alas! Victor, when lies can look so much like truth, who can feel certain of happiness? I feel as if I'm walking on the edge of a cliff, with thousands pushing me toward the abyss. William and Justine were killed, and the murderer walks free — perhaps even respected. But even if I were condemned to the scaffold for the same crimes, I wouldn't trade places with such a wretch."

I listened to this with the most extreme anguish. I — not directly, but in effect — was the true murderer. Elizabeth read the anguish on my face and, gently taking my hand, said, "My dearest friend, you must calm yourself. These events have affected me deeply, God knows. But I'm not as wretched as you are. There's an expression of despair — and sometimes revenge — in your face that frightens me. Dear Victor, drive away these dark passions. Remember the friends who love you and center all their hopes on you. Haven't we lost the power to make you happy? Ah! While we love each other, while we remain true to each other, here in this land of peace and beauty — your native country — we can enjoy every blessing. What can disturb our peace?"

And couldn't such words, from the person I treasured above all others, be enough to drive away the monster lurking in my heart? Even as she spoke, I drew close to her in terror, afraid the destroyer might be near to snatch her from me at that very moment.

So neither the tenderness of friendship, nor the beauty of earth or sky, could save my soul from suffering. Even the words of love were powerless. I was enveloped in a cloud that no good influence could penetrate. The wounded deer dragging its dying limbs to some hidden thicket, there to stare at the arrow that pierced it and die — that was my image.

Sometimes I could cope with the sullen despair that overwhelmed me. But sometimes the storm of passions in my soul drove me to seek relief through physical exercise and change of scenery. It was during one of these fits that I suddenly left home and headed toward the nearby Alpine valleys. In the magnificence and permanence of those scenes, I hoped to forget myself and my fleeting, human sorrows. My wanderings took me toward the valley of Chamonix. I'd visited it often as a boy. Six years had passed since then. _I_ was a wreck, but nothing had changed in those savage, enduring landscapes.

I traveled the first part of the journey on horseback, then hired a mule as more sure-footed on these rough mountain roads. The weather was fine. It was about the middle of August, nearly two months after Justine's death — that miserable turning point from which I dated all my suffering. The weight on my spirit lightened as I plunged deeper into the gorge of the Arve. The immense mountains and cliffs that towered over me on every side, the sound of the river crashing among rocks, the roar of waterfalls — all spoke of a power as mighty as God himself. I stopped fearing or bowing before anything less than the force that had created and ruled these elements, here displayed in their most terrifying form. Still, as I climbed higher, the valley grew more magnificent. Ruined castles clinging to the cliffs of pine-covered mountains, the wild Arve river, cottages peeking out among the trees — all formed a scene of extraordinary beauty. But the mighty Alps overshadowed everything, their white, shining peaks and domes towering above as if they belonged to another earth, the home of another race of beings.

I crossed the bridge at Pelissier, where the river gorge opened before me, and began ascending the mountain above it. Soon I entered the valley of Chamonix — more wonderful and sublime than the valley of Servox I'd just passed through, but not as beautiful or picturesque. The high, snowy mountains formed its immediate boundaries. I saw no more ruined castles or fertile fields. Immense glaciers came right to the road. I heard the rumbling thunder of falling avalanches and saw the smoke of their passage. Mont Blanc — supreme and magnificent — rose from the surrounding peaks, its tremendous dome overlooking the valley.

A tingling, long-lost sense of pleasure came over me during this journey. Some turn in the road, some sudden new sight, reminded me of days gone by and was linked to the lighthearted joy of boyhood. The very winds seemed to whisper comfort, and mother Nature told me to weep no more. Then the kind spell would break, and I'd find myself chained to grief again, wallowing in all the misery of reflection. Then I'd spur my animal on, trying to forget the world, my fears, and above all myself — or, more desperately, I'd dismount and throw myself on the grass, crushed by horror and despair.

At last I reached the village of Chamonix. Extreme exhaustion of both body and mind overcame me. For a short time I stood at the window, watching pale lightning flicker above Mont Blanc and listening to the rush of the Arve flowing noisily below. These same soothing sounds acted as a lullaby to my overwrought senses. When I put my head on the pillow, sleep crept over me. I felt it come and blessed the giver of oblivion.

chapters.title: Chapter 10
paragraphs: I spent the following day roaming through the valley. I stood beside the sources of the Arveiron, which rises from a glacier slowly advancing down from the mountain summit to block the valley. The sheer walls of vast mountains rose before me. The icy cliff of the glacier hung over me. A few shattered pines were scattered around. The solemn silence of this glorious presence-chamber of nature was broken only by the rushing water, the crash of some great falling fragment, the thunder of an avalanche, or the cracking of the accumulated ice as it split and tore under immutable natural laws — as if it were merely a toy in their hands. These sublime, magnificent scenes gave me the greatest comfort I was capable of receiving. They lifted me above all pettiness and, though they didn't remove my grief, they calmed and softened it. To some degree they also diverted my mind from the thoughts that had consumed me for the past month. I went to bed that night, and my sleep was attended by the grand visions I'd absorbed during the day. They gathered around me — the spotless snowy peak, the glittering spire, the pine forests, the jagged ravine, the eagle soaring among the clouds — and bade me be at peace.

But where had they gone when I woke the next morning? All that had inspired my soul fled with sleep. Dark melancholy clouded every thought. Rain poured in torrents. Thick mist hid the mountain summits, so I couldn't even see my mighty friends. But I would penetrate their misty veil and seek them in their cloudy retreats. What were rain and storm to me? My mule was brought to the door, and I resolved to climb to the top of Montanvert. I remembered the effect the sight of the tremendous, ever-moving glacier had produced on my mind when I'd first seen it. It had filled me with a sublime ecstasy that gave wings to my soul, letting it soar above the dark world to light and joy. The sight of the awesome and majestic in nature had always made my mind solemn and helped me forget the petty cares of life. I decided to go without a guide. I knew the path well, and another person would destroy the solitary grandeur of the scene.

The climb is steep, but the path winds in short, continual turns that let you conquer the mountain's sheer face. The landscape is terrifyingly desolate. In a thousand spots you can see the marks of winter avalanches — trees lying broken and scattered, some completely destroyed, others bent against jutting rocks or leaning on other trees. Higher up, the path crosses snow-filled gullies where stones constantly roll down from above. One is especially dangerous — the slightest sound, even a loud voice, can trigger enough movement in the air to bring rocks crashing down on the speaker. The pines aren't tall or lush, but they're dark and add severity to the scene. I looked down at the valley below. Vast mists rose from the rivers and curled in thick wreaths around the opposite mountains, whose peaks were hidden in uniform clouds. Rain fell from the dark sky, deepening my melancholy. Alas! Why does man boast of senses superior to animals? It only makes us more vulnerable. If our urges were limited to hunger, thirst, and desire, we might be nearly free. But as it is, we're moved by every passing wind and every chance word or scene.

We rest; a dream has power to poison sleep. We rise; one wandering thought pollutes the day. We feel, conceive, or reason; laugh or weep, Embrace fond woe, or cast our cares away; It is the same: for, be it joy or sorrow, The path of its departure still is free. Man's yesterday may ne'er be like his morrow; Nought may endure but mutability!

It was nearly noon when I reached the top. For some time I sat on the rock overlooking the sea of ice. Mist covered it and the surrounding mountains. Then a breeze scattered the clouds, and I descended onto the glacier. The surface is very uneven — rising like the waves of a stormy sea, dipping into hollows, split by crevasses that plunge deep. The ice field is nearly a league wide, but I spent almost two hours crossing it. The opposite mountain is a bare, vertical cliff. From where I stood, Montanvert was directly across, about three miles away, and above it rose Mont Blanc in awful majesty. I stayed in a sheltered hollow in the rock, gazing at this stupendous scene. The vast river of ice wound among the surrounding mountains, whose towering peaks hung over its depths. Their icy, glittering summits shone in the sunlight above the clouds. My heart, which had been heavy, swelled with something like joy. I cried out: "Wandering spirits, if you truly wander and do not rest in your narrow graves, grant me this small happiness — or take me as your companion, away from the joys of life."

As I said this, I suddenly saw the figure of a man in the distance, moving toward me with superhuman speed. He bounded over the crevasses in the ice that I'd crossed with caution. As he drew closer, his height seemed to exceed that of any normal person. I was alarmed. Mist came over my eyes and I felt faint, but the cold mountain air quickly revived me. I could see, as the shape came nearer — and the sight was terrible and loathsome — that it was the wretch I had created. I trembled with rage and horror, resolving to wait for him and then engage him in mortal combat. He approached. His face showed bitter anguish combined with contempt and malice, while its inhuman ugliness made it almost too horrible to look at. But I barely noticed. Rage and hatred had first robbed me of speech. When I recovered, I overwhelmed him with words of furious hatred and contempt.

"Devil!" I cried. "How dare you approach me? Don't you fear the fierce vengeance of my arm? Begone, vile insect! Or better — stay, so I can trample you to dust! Oh, if only I could, by destroying your miserable existence, restore the victims you have so monstrously murdered!"

"I expected this reception," said the creature. "All men hate the wretched. How much more must I be hated — I, who am miserable beyond all living things! Yet you, my creator, despise and reject me, your creature, to whom you're bound by ties that only the destruction of one of us can break. You plan to kill me. How dare you play with life this way? Do your duty toward me, and I'll do mine toward you and the rest of humanity. If you agree to my terms, I'll leave you and everyone else in peace. But if you refuse, I'll gorge the jaws of death with the blood of your remaining friends."

"Loathsome monster! Fiend! The tortures of hell are too mild a punishment for your crimes. Wretched devil! You blame me for creating you? Come, then, and let me extinguish the spark I so carelessly gave you."
My rage was beyond bounds. I sprang at him, driven by every feeling that can arm one being against another.
He easily dodged me and said,

"Calm yourself! I beg you to hear me before you unleash your hatred. Haven't I suffered enough already — must you try to increase my misery? Life, even if it's nothing but an accumulation of pain, is dear to me. I'll defend it. Remember: you made me more powerful than yourself. I'm taller and stronger. But I won't pit myself against you. I am your creature, and I'll be obedient and docile to my natural master — if you'll also fulfill your obligations to me. Oh, Frankenstein, be fair to everyone else if you must, but don't trample only on me — me, to whom your justice, your mercy, and your love are most owed. Remember that I am your creature. I should be your Adam, but instead I'm the fallen angel, driven from joy for no sin. Everywhere I see happiness, from which I alone am forever excluded. I was good and kind. Misery made me a monster. Make me happy, and I'll be good again."
"Begone! I won't listen. There can be nothing between us. We are enemies. Leave, or let us fight to the death."

"How can I reach you? Won't any plea make you look on your creature with kindness? Believe me, Frankenstein — I was good. My soul glowed with love and compassion. But am I not alone, miserably alone? You, my creator, despise me. What hope can I find in your fellow humans, who owe me nothing? They reject and hate me. The barren mountains and empty glaciers are my refuge. I've wandered here for days. The ice caves, which I alone don't fear, are my home — the only one that no human grudges me. I welcome these bleak skies because they're kinder to me than people. If all humanity knew I existed, they would arm themselves against me as you do. Shouldn't I hate those who hate me? I won't keep peace with my enemies. I'm miserable, and they'll share my misery. Yet it's in your power to save them. Make up for what you've done. Don't reject me. Listen to my story. When you've heard it, judge whether I deserve your contempt or your compassion. But hear me. The guilty are allowed, by human law, to speak in their own defense before they're condemned. Listen to me, Frankenstein. You accuse me of murder, yet you would destroy your own creation with a clear conscience. Oh, praise the eternal justice of man! But I don't ask you to spare me. Just listen. If you can still condemn me after hearing my story, then destroy the work of your hands."

"Why do you remind me," I replied, "of things I shudder to recall — that I was the miserable cause and author of all this? Cursed be the day, loathsome devil, that you first saw light! Cursed — though I curse myself — be the hands that formed you! You've made me wretched beyond words. You've left me unable to even judge whether I owe you anything. Get out! Remove your hated form from my sight."

"Then I'll remove it, my creator," he said, and placed his despised hands over my eyes. I flung them away violently. "This way I spare you a sight you hate. But you can still listen. Grant me your compassion. By the goodness I once possessed, I demand this. Hear my tale. It's long and strange, and this place is too cold for your delicate constitution. Come to the hut on the mountain. The sun is still high. Before it sets behind these snowy peaks to light another world, you'll have heard my story and can decide. It rests with you whether I leave the company of men forever and live a harmless life, or become the scourge of your fellow creatures and the architect of your own swift destruction."

As he said this, he led the way across the ice. I followed. My heart was heavy, and I didn't answer. But as we walked, I weighed the various arguments he'd made and decided at least to listen to his tale. I was partly driven by curiosity, and compassion confirmed my decision. Until now I'd assumed he'd murdered my brother, and I was desperate for confirmation or denial. For the first time, I also felt what duties a creator owes to his creation — that I should make him happy before complaining of his wickedness. These reasons convinced me to agree. We crossed the ice and climbed the opposite rock. The air was cold, and rain began again. We entered the hut. The creature wore an expression of triumph. I entered with a heavy heart and crushed spirits. But I agreed to listen. Seating myself by the fire my detestable companion had lit, he began his tale.

chapters.title: Chapter 11
paragraphs: "It's very difficult for me to remember the earliest period of my existence. Everything from that time appears confused and blurred. A strange flood of sensations seized me. I saw, felt, heard, and smelled all at once. It took a long time before I learned to separate these different senses. Gradually, I remember, a stronger light pressed on my eyes, forcing me to shut them. Darkness troubled me, but then I found that by opening my eyes, light poured in again. I walked and, I believe, went down some stairs. Soon I noticed a big change in what I felt. Before, dark, solid objects had surrounded me — impossible to touch or see through. Now I could wander freely, with no obstacles I couldn't avoid or get past. The light grew more and more intense, and the heat wore me down. I looked for shade and found it in the forest near Ingolstadt. I lay by a brook to rest, until hunger and thirst roused me from my half-sleeping state. I ate berries hanging from trees or lying on the ground, drank from the brook, and lay down again. Sleep overcame me.

"It was dark when I woke. I felt cold and half-frightened, instinctively, at finding myself so alone. Before leaving your apartment, feeling cold, I'd covered myself with some clothes. But they weren't enough to protect me from the night dew. I was a poor, helpless, miserable wretch. I knew nothing, could tell nothing apart. Pain attacked me from all sides. I sat down and wept.

"Soon a gentle light crept across the sky and gave me a feeling of pleasure. I started up and saw a radiant form rising from among the trees. [The moon] I stared at it in wonder. It moved slowly, but it lit my path. I went out again in search of berries. I was still cold when I found a large cloak under one of the trees. I wrapped myself in it and sat on the ground. No clear thoughts filled my mind. Everything was confused. I felt light and hunger and thirst and darkness. Countless sounds rang in my ears. Various smells surrounded me. The only thing I could make out was the bright moon, and I fixed my eyes on it with pleasure.

"Several days and nights passed. The moon shrank noticeably before I began to tell my sensations apart from one another. Gradually I could see the clear stream that gave me water and the trees that shaded me. I was delighted when I first realized that a pleasant sound I often heard came from the throats of the little winged animals that sometimes blocked the light from my eyes. I also began to observe more carefully the shapes around me and to sense the boundaries of the bright roof of light overhead. Sometimes I tried to imitate the birds' pleasant songs but couldn't. Sometimes I wanted to express my feelings in my own way, but the rough, inarticulate sounds that burst from me frightened me into silence.

"The moon disappeared from the night sky, then returned smaller. I was still in the forest. My senses had become distinct by this time, and my mind received new ideas every day. My eyes adjusted to the light and could perceive objects in their true forms. I could tell an insect from a plant and, gradually, one plant from another. I discovered that the sparrow made only harsh sounds, while the blackbird and thrush sang sweetly.

"One day, feeling cold, I found a fire left by some wandering beggars. I was overjoyed at its warmth. In my delight I thrust my hand into the glowing embers — and quickly pulled it out with a cry of pain. How strange, I thought, that the same thing could cause such opposite effects! I examined what the fire was made of and was pleased to find it was wood. I quickly gathered some branches, but they were wet and wouldn't burn. This frustrated me. I sat watching the fire. The wet wood I'd placed near the heat dried out and caught flame. I thought about this. By touching various branches, I figured out why. Then I busied myself collecting a large supply of wood to dry and burn. When night came, I was terrified that my fire might go out. I carefully covered it with dry wood and leaves, placed wet branches on top, then spread my cloak and lay down to sleep.

"In the morning, my first concern was the fire. I uncovered it, and a gentle breeze quickly fanned it into flame. I noticed this and made a fan of branches to revive the embers when they were nearly dead. That night I discovered fire gave light as well as heat, and that this discovery was useful for cooking — I found that some scraps left by the travelers tasted much better roasted than the raw berries I'd been gathering. So I tried cooking my food the same way, placing it on live coals. The berries were ruined by this, but the nuts and roots were greatly improved.

"Food, however, grew scarce. I often spent entire days searching in vain for a few acorns to ease the pain of hunger. When I realized this, I decided to leave my home and find a place where my basic needs could be met more easily. I was deeply sorry to lose the fire I'd stumbled on by accident, since I didn't know how to start a new one. I spent several hours seriously thinking about this problem but couldn't solve it. Wrapping myself in my cloak, I set out through the woods toward the setting sun. I walked for three days. Eventually I found open country. Heavy snow had fallen the night before. The fields were all white. The scene was bleak. My feet ached from the cold, damp ground.

"It was about seven in the morning. I longed for food and shelter. At last I spotted a small hut on a rise — probably built for some shepherd's convenience. This was new to me. I examined it curiously. Finding the door open, I entered. An old man sat inside, near a fire, preparing his breakfast. He turned when he heard me. Seeing me, he screamed loudly and fled from the hut across the fields with a speed his frail body hardly seemed capable of. His appearance — so different from anything I'd seen before — and his flight surprised me. But I was enchanted by the hut. Here, snow and rain couldn't reach me. The ground was dry. It seemed as divine a retreat to me then as the finest palace. I eagerly devoured the old man's breakfast — bread, cheese, milk, and wine (though I didn't like the wine). Then, overcome by tiredness, I lay down on some straw and fell asleep.

"It was noon when I woke. Drawn by the warmth of the sun shining brightly on the white ground, I decided to keep traveling. I put the remains of the breakfast in a bag I found and walked across the fields for several hours. At sunset I reached a village. How incredible it looked! The huts, the neat cottages, the grand houses each caught my admiration. The vegetables in gardens and the milk and cheese displayed in cottage windows made me hungry. I entered one of the best-looking cottages. But the moment I stepped inside, the children screamed and one of the women fainted. The whole village came out. Some people ran. Others attacked me, pelting me with stones and other objects until, badly bruised, I escaped to the open country. I fearfully took refuge in a low hovel — bare and wretched-looking compared to the houses I'd seen in the village. But this hovel was attached to a neat, pleasant-looking cottage. After my costly experience, I didn't dare enter it. My shelter was built of wood, so low I could barely sit upright. The floor was bare earth, but it was dry. Despite the wind whistling through countless cracks, it was a welcome haven from the snow, rain, and cruelty of men.

"I retreated here and lay down, glad to have found shelter — however miserable — from the weather and, even more, from human savagery. As soon as morning came, I crept from my hiding place to examine the cottage next door and figure out if I could stay. It backed up against my hovel. On the exposed sides, a pigsty and a clear pool of water surrounded it. One side was open — the way I'd crept in. But now I blocked every crack through which I might be seen, using stones and wood arranged so I could move them to get in and out. All my light came through the pigsty, and it was enough.

"Having arranged my dwelling and carpeted it with clean straw, I retreated, for I saw a man in the distance and remembered too well what had happened in the village to trust myself in anyone's power. But first I'd secured food for the day — a stolen loaf of coarse bread and a cup I could use to drink more conveniently from the clean water flowing past my retreat. The floor was slightly raised, keeping it dry. Its closeness to the cottage chimney kept it reasonably warm.

"I decided to stay in this hovel until something changed my mind. It was a paradise compared to the bleak forest, the dripping branches, and the cold, damp earth. I ate my breakfast with pleasure and was about to move a plank to get some water when I heard a footstep. Looking through a small crack, I saw a young woman passing my hovel with a pail on her head. She was young and gentle-looking — unlike any peasant or farm servant I've since met. She was dressed simply in a coarse blue skirt and linen jacket. Her fair hair was braided but unadorned. She looked patient but sad. I lost sight of her, and in about fifteen minutes she returned with the pail partly filled with milk. As she walked, obviously struggling with the weight, a young man met her. His face expressed even deeper sadness. With a few melancholy words, he took the pail from her head and carried it to the cottage himself. She followed, and they disappeared. Soon the young man came out again with tools and crossed the field behind the cottage. The girl busied herself, sometimes inside the house, sometimes in the yard.

"Looking more carefully at my dwelling, I found that one of the cottage windows had once extended into it, but the panes had been filled in with wood. In one board was a tiny, almost invisible crack through which I could just see into the room. It was a small, whitewashed space, clean but nearly bare of furniture. In one corner, near a small fire, sat an old man with his head in his hands, looking utterly dejected. The young girl was tidying the room. Then she took something from a drawer — some kind of handwork — and sat beside the old man. He took up an instrument and began to play sounds sweeter than any birdsong I'd heard. It was a beautiful sight, even to a wretch like me who had never seen anything beautiful before. The old man's silver hair and kind face filled me with reverence. The girl's gentle manner stirred my love. He played a sweet, mournful melody that drew tears from his companion's eyes. The old man didn't notice until she sobbed aloud. Then he spoke a few words, and the girl left her work and knelt at his feet. He raised her and smiled with such kindness and warmth that I felt emotions I'd never experienced — a strange mixture of pain and pleasure unlike hunger or cold, warmth or food. I pulled away from the window, unable to bear these feelings.

"Soon after, the young man returned, carrying a load of firewood on his shoulders. The girl met him at the door and helped him. She carried some of the wood inside and put it on the fire.
