Then the two went to a corner of the cottage, where he showed her a large loaf of bread and a piece of cheese. She seemed pleased and went into the garden for some roots and greens, which she put in water over the fire. She returned to her work while the young man went into the garden, digging and pulling up roots. After about an hour the young woman joined him, and they went inside together.

"Meanwhile, the old man had been sitting in thought. When the others appeared, he brightened. They sat down to eat. The meal was quickly finished. The young woman tidied up again. The old man walked outside in the sun for a few minutes, leaning on the young man's arm. Nothing could exceed the beauty of the contrast between these two. One was old, with silver hair and a face beaming with goodness and love. The other was young, slight, and graceful, his features perfectly formed — yet his eyes and bearing expressed the deepest sadness. The old man went back inside. The young man picked up different tools and headed across the fields.

"Night fell quickly. To my amazement, I discovered that the cottagers could extend the day using candles. I was delighted that sunset didn't end the pleasure I took in watching my human neighbors. In the evening, the young girl and the man were busy with tasks I didn't understand. The old man took up his instrument again and made the divine sounds that had enchanted me that morning. When he finished, the young man began — not playing music, but making sounds that were monotonous, unlike either the old man's instrument or birdsong. I later learned he was reading aloud, but at the time I knew nothing of words or letters.
"The family soon put out their lights and went to rest, as I guessed, for the night."

chapters.title: Chapter 12
paragraphs: "I lay on my straw but couldn't sleep. I thought over the day's events. What struck me most was the gentle manner of these people. I longed to join them but didn't dare. I remembered too well how the villagers had treated me and resolved, whatever I might eventually decide to do, to stay quietly in my hovel for now — watching and trying to understand what motivated their actions.
"The cottagers rose before dawn the next morning. The young woman arranged the cottage and prepared food. The young man left after the first meal.

"This day passed exactly like the one before. The young man worked constantly outdoors. The girl did various hard tasks inside. The old man, whom I soon realized was blind, spent his leisure playing his instrument or sitting in thought. Nothing could exceed the love and respect the younger cottagers showed their elderly companion. They performed every small act of affection and duty with gentleness, and he rewarded them with kind smiles.

"They weren't entirely happy. The young man and the girl often went aside and seemed to weep. I saw no cause for their unhappiness, but it affected me deeply. If such lovely people could be miserable, it was less surprising that I — an imperfect, solitary being — should be wretched. But why were these gentle creatures unhappy? They possessed a delightful house (it seemed so to my eyes) and every luxury. They had fire for warmth and delicious food when hungry. They were well dressed. And most importantly, they had each other's company, exchanging looks of love and kindness every day. What did their tears mean? Did they really express pain? At first I couldn't answer these questions, but careful observation over time explained many things that had initially puzzled me.

"After some time I discovered one cause of the family's distress: poverty, which they suffered severely. Their food consisted entirely of garden vegetables and milk from one cow, which gave very little in winter when the owners could barely feed it. The two younger ones often went hungry. Several times I saw them place food before the old man while keeping none for themselves.

"This act of kindness moved me greatly. I'd been stealing food from their supplies at night for myself. When I realized I was causing them pain, I stopped and lived on berries, nuts, and roots from the nearby woods.

"I also found another way to help them. I noticed the young man spent much of each day gathering firewood. During the night, I often took his tools — I quickly figured out how to use them — and brought home enough fuel to last several days.

"The first time I did this, the young woman was astonished to find a large pile of wood outside her door in the morning. She called out in surprise, and the young man joined her, equally amazed. I noticed with pleasure that he didn't go to the forest that day but spent it repairing the cottage and working in the garden.

"Gradually I made an even more important discovery. I found that these people had a way of communicating their thoughts and feelings through speech. I noticed that words sometimes brought pleasure or pain, smiles or sadness, to the listener. This was a godlike power, and I desperately wanted to learn it. But every attempt failed me. Their speech was rapid, and the words they used had no obvious connection to visible objects. I couldn't find any pattern. With great effort, however, after spending many months in my hovel, I managed to learn the names given to some of the most familiar things: _fire, milk, bread,_ and _wood._ I also learned the cottagers' names. The young man and woman each had several names, but the old man had only one: _father._ The girl was called _sister_ or _Agatha,_ and the young man _Felix, brother,_ or _son._ I can't describe the delight I felt when I learned what each of these sounds meant and could say them myself. I picked up other words too, without fully understanding them yet: _good, dearest, unhappy._

"I spent the winter this way. The cottagers' gentle manners and beauty made me grow deeply fond of them. When they were sad, I felt sad. When they were happy, I shared their joy. I saw few other people, and whenever a stranger entered the cottage, their rough manners only highlighted how much better my friends were. The old man often tried to cheer up his children, as he sometimes called them. He'd speak in a warm, encouraging tone that gave even me pleasure. Agatha listened respectfully, her eyes sometimes filling with tears she tried to hide. But after listening to her father's words, she usually seemed more cheerful. Felix was always the saddest of the three. Even to my untrained eye, he seemed to have suffered more deeply than the others. But although his face was more sorrowful, his voice was more cheerful than his sister's — especially when he spoke to the old man.

"I could list countless small examples that revealed these kind people's natures. Despite their poverty, Felix took pleasure in bringing his sister the first little white flower that appeared through the snow. Early in the morning, before she was up, he cleared the snow from her path to the cowshed, drew water from the well, and brought wood from the shed — where, to his constant amazement, he always found the supply replenished by an invisible hand. During the day he sometimes worked for a neighboring farmer, since he often left and came back without firewood. At other times he worked in the garden, but since there was little to do in the cold months, he read aloud to the old man and to Agatha.

"This reading had confused me greatly at first. But gradually I realized he was making many of the same sounds when reading as when talking. I guessed he was finding signs for speech on paper and desperately wanted to understand them too. But how could I, when I didn't even understand the sounds the signs represented? I improved steadily in this science, though not enough to follow actual conversation. I applied my whole mind to the task. I could clearly see that, although I longed to reveal myself to the cottagers, I shouldn't attempt it until I'd mastered their language. If I could speak well, they might overlook my physical ugliness — a subject the constant contrast with their beauty had made painfully clear to me.

"I had admired my cottagers' graceful forms, their beauty and delicate features. But what horror I felt when I saw myself reflected in a clear pool! At first I recoiled, unable to believe it was really me in the mirror. When I finally accepted that I was indeed the monster I am, I was filled with the bitterest despair and shame. Alas! I didn't yet fully grasp the fatal effects of this miserable deformity.

"As the sun grew warmer and days grew longer, the snow vanished. I saw bare trees and black earth. From then on, Felix was busier, and the heartbreaking signs of approaching hunger disappeared. Their food, as I later learned, was coarse but nourishing and sufficient. New plants sprouted in the garden. The signs of comfort increased daily as the season advanced.

"The old man, leaning on his son's arm, walked at noon each day when it wasn't raining — which happened frequently. But a strong wind would quickly dry the earth, and the season became far more pleasant.

"My life in the hovel followed a routine. In the morning I watched the cottagers. When they scattered to their various tasks, I slept. The rest of the day I spent observing my friends. When they went to bed, if there was moonlight or starlight, I went into the woods to collect my own food and fuel for the cottage. When necessary, I cleared their path and did the chores I'd seen Felix do. I later found out these labors, performed by an invisible hand, astonished them greatly. Once or twice I heard them use the words _good spirit_ and _wonderful,_ though I didn't yet know what those words meant.

"My thoughts grew more active. I longed to understand what drove these lovely people — why Felix seemed so sad and Agatha so sorrowful. I thought — foolishly — that it might be in my power to restore their happiness. When I slept or was away, the images of the kind blind father, gentle Agatha, and excellent Felix appeared before me. I saw them as superior beings who would decide my destiny. In my imagination, I rehearsed a thousand versions of introducing myself to them, picturing their reactions. I imagined they'd be disgusted — until my gentle manner and kind words won first their favor, then their love.

"These thoughts energized me and drove me to study language with renewed passion. My voice was indeed harsh, but flexible. Though it was nothing like the soft music of their speech, I could pronounce the words I knew with reasonable ease. I was like the donkey compared to the lapdog in the fable — but surely the gentle donkey, whose intentions were kind despite his rough manners, deserved better than blows and curses.

"The pleasant spring rains and warm weather completely changed the look of the earth. People who had seemed to hide in caves during winter now scattered and busied themselves with farming. Birds sang more cheerfully. Leaves began to bud on the trees. Happy, happy earth! A fit home for gods — yet just a short time before, it had been bleak, damp, and inhospitable. My spirits rose with the beauty of nature. The past was wiped from my memory. The present was calm. The future glowed with bright rays of hope and the promise of joy."

chapters.title: Chapter 13
paragraphs: "I now come to the most important part of my story. I'll describe events that transformed me from what I was into what I am.

"Spring advanced quickly. The weather turned fine and the skies cleared. I was surprised that what had been so barren and gloomy now bloomed with the most beautiful flowers and greenery. My senses were refreshed by a thousand delightful scents and a thousand lovely sights.

"It was on one of those days when the cottagers rested from work — the old man played his guitar while the children listened — that I noticed Felix looked deeply melancholy. He sighed frequently. Once his father paused his music, and I guessed from his manner that he was asking about his son's sadness. Felix replied cheerfully, and the old man was starting his music again when someone knocked at the door.

"It was a lady on horseback, accompanied by a country man as a guide. She wore a dark outfit and was covered with a thick black veil. Agatha asked a question. The stranger replied only by pronouncing, in a sweet accent, the name of Felix. Her voice was musical but different from either of my friends'. Hearing this name, Felix rushed to the lady. When she saw him, she threw up her veil, and I saw a face of angelic beauty. Her hair was shining black and intricately braided. Her eyes were dark but gentle and lively. Her features were perfectly proportioned. Her complexion was wonderfully fair, each cheek touched with a lovely pink.

"Felix seemed overwhelmed with joy when he saw her. Every trace of sorrow vanished from his face, replaced by an ecstatic happiness I could hardly have imagined. His eyes sparkled. His cheeks flushed with pleasure. At that moment I thought him as beautiful as the stranger. She seemed to feel differently. Wiping tears from her lovely eyes, she offered her hand to Felix. He kissed it rapturously and called her — as far as I could make out — his sweet Arabian. She didn't seem to understand him, but smiled. He helped her dismount. After dismissing her guide, he led her into the cottage. Some conversation took place between Felix and his father. The young stranger knelt at the old man's feet and would have kissed his hand, but he raised her up and embraced her warmly.

"I soon noticed that although the stranger spoke and seemed to have her own language, she couldn't understand the cottagers, nor they her. They made many gestures I didn't understand, but her presence clearly brought joy to the cottage, banishing their sadness the way the sun clears morning mist. Felix seemed especially happy, welcoming his Arabian with beaming smiles. Agatha, ever gentle, kissed the stranger's hands and pointed to her brother, making signs that seemed to mean he'd been sad until she came. Several hours passed this way. The cause of their happiness escaped me, but I could see it on their faces. Then I noticed the stranger was trying to learn their language, repeating sounds they said to her. The idea instantly struck me that I could use the same lessons. The stranger learned about twenty words in the first session. Most were ones I already knew, but I benefited from the rest.

"As night came, Agatha and the Arabian retired early. When they parted, Felix kissed the stranger's hand and said, 'Good night, sweet Safie.' He stayed up much longer talking with his father. From the frequent mention of her name, I guessed their lovely guest was the subject of their conversation. I desperately wanted to understand them, but found it completely impossible.

"The next morning, Felix went to work. After Agatha finished her usual tasks, the Arabian sat at the old man's feet. Taking his guitar, she played music so hauntingly beautiful that it drew tears of both sorrow and joy from my eyes. She sang, and her voice flowed in rich waves, swelling or dying away like a nightingale in the woods.

"When she finished, she gave the guitar to Agatha, who at first declined it. She played a simple tune and sang in a sweet voice, but without the stranger's extraordinary skill. The old man seemed transported with delight. He said some words that Agatha tried to explain to Safie — apparently expressing how much joy her music brought him.

"The days now passed as peacefully as before, with the only change being that joy had replaced sadness on my friends' faces. Safie was always cheerful. She and I improved rapidly in the language, so that within two months I could understand most of what my protectors said.

"Meanwhile, the black earth was covered with new growth. The green banks were dotted with countless flowers — sweet-scented and beautiful, like pale stars among the moonlit woods. The sun grew warmer. The nights became clear and balmy. My nighttime rambles were a great pleasure, although they were cut short by the late setting and early rising of the sun. I never ventured out during daylight, fearing a repeat of my earlier treatment in the village.

"My days were spent in close study so I could master the language more quickly. I can honestly say I improved faster than the Arabian, who understood very little and spoke in broken fragments, while I could comprehend and imitate nearly every word.
"While I improved in speech, I also learned the science of reading, as it was taught to the stranger. This opened a vast new world of wonder and delight.

"The book Felix used to teach Safie was Volney's _Ruins of Empires_. I wouldn't have understood it if Felix hadn't provided very detailed explanations as he read. He'd chosen this work, he said, because its grand, declamatory style was modeled on Eastern authors. Through this book I gained a basic knowledge of history and an overview of the world's empires. I learned about the manners, governments, and religions of different nations. I heard about the lazy Asiatics, the stupendous genius of the Greeks, the wars and extraordinary virtue of the early Romans — their later decline and the fall of that mighty empire — chivalry, Christianity, and kings. I heard about the discovery of the Americas and wept with Safie over the tragic fate of the native peoples.

"These wonderful stories stirred strange feelings in me. Was man really at once so powerful, so virtuous and magnificent, yet so vicious and base? He appeared at one moment a mere offshoot of evil, and at another the noblest, most godlike being imaginable. Being a great and virtuous person seemed the highest honor a conscious being could achieve. Being base and vicious seemed the lowest degradation — worse than a blind mole or harmless worm. For a long time I couldn't understand how one person could go out and murder another, or even why there were laws and governments. But when I heard the details of human cruelty and bloodshed, my wonder ceased. I turned away with disgust and horror.

"Every conversation in the cottage now opened new wonders for me. From Felix's lessons to the Arabian, I learned about the strange system of human society — the division of property, immense wealth alongside crushing poverty, rank, bloodlines, and noble birth.

"These words forced me to look at myself. I learned that what your fellow creatures valued most was high, pure ancestry combined with wealth. A man might be respected with just one of these, but without either he was considered — with rare exceptions — a vagrant and a slave, doomed to waste his abilities for the benefit of the privileged few! And what was I? I knew absolutely nothing about my creation or creator. I had no money, no friends, no property of any kind. I was also cursed with a hideously deformed body. I wasn't even the same kind of being as man. I was faster and could survive on rougher food. I endured extremes of heat and cold with less harm. I was far taller than any human. When I looked around, I saw and heard of no one like me. Was I, then, a monster? A stain upon the earth, from which all men fled and which all men rejected?

"I can't describe the agony these thoughts caused me. I tried to push them away, but sorrow only grew with knowledge. Oh, if only I had stayed forever in my native forest, never knowing or feeling anything beyond hunger, thirst, and warmth!

"What a strange thing knowledge is! Once it takes hold of the mind, it clings like lichen on rock. I sometimes wished I could shake off all thought and feeling. But I learned there was only one way to overcome pain, and that was death — a state I feared but didn't understand. I admired virtue and good feeling. I loved the gentle manners and kind qualities of my cottagers. But I was shut out from any real connection with them, except through the stolen, secret glimpses I took when unseen and unknown — and these only increased my longing to be one of them. Agatha's gentle words and the charming Arabian's bright smiles were not for me. The old man's mild encouragement and Felix's lively conversation were not for me. Miserable, unhappy wretch!

"Other lessons struck me even more deeply. I heard about the differences between the sexes, and the birth and growth of children — how the father doted on the infant's smiles and the older child's playfulness, how the mother's whole life and care wrapped around this precious charge, how the young mind expanded and gained knowledge — of brothers, sisters, and all the various bonds that tie human beings to one another.

"But where were my own family and friends? No father had watched over my infancy. No mother had blessed me with smiles and tenderness. Or if they had, my entire past was a blank, a dark emptiness in which I could make out nothing. From my earliest memory, I'd been as I was now in height and build. I'd never seen anyone who resembled me or claimed any connection with me. What was I? The question kept returning, answered only by groans.

"I'll soon explain where these feelings led. But first, let me return to the cottagers, whose story stirred such varied feelings in me — outrage, delight, and wonder — all of which ended in deeper love and reverence for my protectors (for so I loved, in an innocent, half-painful self-deception, to call them)."

chapters.title: Chapter 14
paragraphs: "Some time passed before I learned my friends' full history. It was a story that couldn't fail to make a deep impression on someone as utterly inexperienced as I was.

"The old man's name was De Lacey. He came from a good family in France, where he'd lived for many years in comfort, respected by those above him and loved by his peers. His son had served his country, and Agatha had ranked among the highest ladies of society. A few months before I arrived, they'd lived in a large, luxurious city called Paris, surrounded by friends and possessing every advantage that virtue, intelligence, and a moderate fortune could provide.

"Safie's father had caused their ruin. He was a Turkish merchant who had lived in Paris for many years. For some reason I couldn't learn, he'd fallen out with the government. He was arrested and thrown into prison on the very day Safie arrived from Constantinople to join him. He was tried and sentenced to death. The injustice of this sentence was outrageous. All Paris was furious. It was widely believed that his religion and wealth, rather than the crime he was charged with, had been the real cause of his condemnation.

"Felix happened to be present at the trial. His horror and outrage were uncontrollable when he heard the verdict. He immediately swore a solemn vow to free the prisoner, then looked for ways to do it. After many failed attempts to get into the prison, he found a heavily barred window in an unguarded part of the building. It opened into the dungeon of the unfortunate Muslim, who waited in chains for his barbarous execution. Felix visited this window at night and told the prisoner his plans. The Turk, amazed and delighted, tried to secure Felix's loyalty with promises of reward and wealth. Felix rejected these with contempt. But when he saw beautiful Safie, who was allowed to visit her father and whose gestures expressed her deep gratitude, the young man couldn't help recognizing that this captive possessed a treasure that would fully reward his effort and risk.

"The Turk quickly saw the impression his daughter had made on Felix. He tried to bind Felix more firmly to his cause by promising Safie's hand in marriage once they reached safety. Felix was too honorable to accept this outright. But he looked forward to it as the fulfillment of his happiness.

"During the preparations for the escape, several letters from the lovely girl further warmed Felix's devotion. She'd found a way to express her thoughts in her lover's language with the help of an old servant of her father's who knew French. She thanked Felix in the most passionate terms for his efforts to help her father. At the same time, she gently mourned her own fate.

"I have copies of these letters. I found writing materials during my time in the hovel, and the letters were often in Felix's or Agatha's hands. I'll give them to you before I leave. They'll prove the truth of my story. But since the sun is already low, I'll only have time to summarize their contents.

"Safie told how her mother was a Christian Arab who had been captured and enslaved by the Turks. Her beauty won the heart of Safie's father, who married her. The young girl spoke with pride and passion about her mother, who had been born free and rejected the bondage she was now subjected to. She taught her daughter the principles of her Christian faith and instilled in her a desire for intellectual independence and freedom of spirit — things forbidden to Muslim women. When this lady died, her lessons remained indelibly imprinted on Safie's mind. Safie was sickened by the prospect of returning to Asia, where she'd be confined to a harem and allowed only childish amusements ill-suited to her character, which had grown accustomed to grand ideas and noble ambitions. The prospect of marrying a Christian and staying in a country where women held a place in society enchanted her.

"The day set for the Turk's execution arrived, but the night before, he escaped from prison. By morning he was many leagues from Paris. Felix had obtained passports in his own name, his father's, and his sister's. He had already told his father the plan. The old man left his house under the pretense of a trip and hid with his daughter in a remote part of Paris.
"Felix led the fugitives through France to Lyons, over the Alps to Leghorn, where the merchant planned to wait for a chance to reach Turkish territory.

"Safie decided to stay with her father until he left. Meanwhile the Turk renewed his promise that she would marry her rescuer. Felix stayed with them, enjoying the company of the Arabian, who showed him the simplest and most tender affection. They talked through an interpreter, and sometimes communicated with looks alone. Safie sang to him the divine music of her homeland.

"The Turk allowed this closeness and encouraged the young lovers' hopes — while secretly planning something quite different. He despised the idea of his daughter marrying a Christian but feared Felix's anger if he seemed reluctant, knowing Felix still had the power to betray him to the Italian authorities. He devised a thousand schemes to keep up the deception until it was no longer necessary, planning to secretly take his daughter with him when he left. His plans were helped by news from Paris.

"The French government was enraged by the prisoner's escape and spared no effort to find and punish his rescuer. Felix's role was quickly discovered. De Lacey and Agatha were thrown into prison. The news reached Felix and shattered his happiness. His blind, aging father and gentle sister were in a foul dungeon while he enjoyed freedom and the company of his beloved. This thought was torture. He quickly arranged with the Turk that if the latter found a chance to escape before Felix could return to Italy, Safie would stay at a convent in Leghorn. Then, leaving his beloved Arabian, he rushed to Paris and surrendered himself to the law, hoping to free his father and sister.
"He failed. They were imprisoned for five months before the trial, which stripped them of their fortune and condemned them to permanent exile from France.

"They found a miserable refuge in the cottage in Germany where I discovered them. Felix soon learned that the treacherous Turk — the man for whom he and his family had endured such unimaginable suffering — had turned traitor upon discovering his rescuer was ruined. He'd left Italy with his daughter, insultingly sending Felix a small sum of money to help with some future plan.

"These were the events that weighed on Felix's heart and made him, when I first saw him, the most miserable of the family. He could have endured poverty. When it was the price of virtue, he gloried in it. But the Turk's ingratitude and the loss of his beloved Safie were blows too bitter and final to bear. The Arabian's arrival now breathed new life into his soul.

"When the news reached Leghorn that Felix had lost his wealth and position, the merchant ordered his daughter to forget her lover and prepare to return home. Safie's generous spirit was outraged by this command. She tried to argue with her father, but he stormed off, repeating his tyrannical order.

"A few days later, the Turk burst into his daughter's room and told her urgently that his hiding place in Leghorn had been discovered and that the French government might seize him at any moment. He'd hired a ship to take him to Constantinople and would sail within hours. He planned to leave his daughter with a trusted servant, who would follow later with most of his property, which hadn't yet reached Leghorn.

"Left alone, Safie considered what to do. A life in Turkey was unbearable to her. Both her religion and her feelings were against it. Through some of her father's papers that fell into her hands, she learned of her lover's exile and the name of the place where he now lived. She wavered for a time, but finally made her decision. Taking some jewels and a sum of money, she left Italy with an attendant — a woman from Leghorn who spoke Turkish — and headed for Germany.

"She arrived safely at a town about sixty miles from the De Lacey cottage, where her attendant fell dangerously ill. Safie nursed her with the utmost devotion, but the poor woman died. The Arabian was left alone, unable to speak the local language and completely ignorant of how the world worked. But she fell into good hands. The Italian woman had mentioned their destination before she died, and the woman of the house where they'd been staying made sure Safie reached her lover's cottage safely."

chapters.title: Chapter 15
paragraphs: "That was the history of my beloved cottagers. It made a deep impression on me. From its picture of human society, I learned to admire their virtues and condemn humanity's vices.

"At that time I still saw crime as a distant evil. Kindness and generosity were always before me, inspiring a desire to play my own part in the busy world where so many admirable qualities were displayed. But in describing the development of my mind, I must mention something that happened in early August.

"One night, during my usual trip to the woods to gather food and firewood, I found a leather bag on the ground containing some clothes and several books. I eagerly grabbed this prize and took it to my hovel. Fortunately, the books were written in the language I'd been learning at the cottage. They were _Paradise Lost_, a volume of _Plutarch's Lives_, and _The Sorrows of Young Werther_. Possessing these treasures gave me immense delight. I studied them constantly while my friends were busy with their daily work.

"I can barely describe the effect these books had on me. They produced a flood of new images and emotions that sometimes lifted me to ecstasy but more often plunged me into the deepest misery. In _The Sorrows of Werther_, beyond the gripping simplicity of the story, so many opinions were explored and so much light thrown on subjects that had been dark to me that I found in it an endless source of wonder and reflection. Its descriptions of gentle domestic life and lofty feeling matched my experience of my protectors and the longings alive in my own heart. But I thought Werther himself a more magnificent being than I'd ever seen or imagined. His character was unpretentious yet deeply moving. His reflections on death and suicide filled me with awe. I didn't presume to judge the merits of his case, but I leaned toward his views, and I wept at his death without precisely understanding it.

"As I read, I constantly applied what I found to my own feelings and situation. I found myself both similar to and strangely different from the people I read about. I could sympathize with them and partly understand them, but my mind was unformed. I depended on no one and was related to no one. 'The path of my departure was free,' and there was no one who would mourn my destruction. My body was hideous and my size enormous. What did this mean? Who was I? What was I? Where did I come from? What was my purpose? These questions kept returning, answered only by groans.

"_Plutarch's Lives_ had a very different effect. From Werther I learned despondency and gloom. But Plutarch taught me to think nobly. He lifted me above my own wretched existence to admire and love the heroes of ancient times. Much of what I read was beyond my understanding and experience. I had only a vague idea of kingdoms, vast countries, mighty rivers, and boundless seas. I knew nothing about towns or large gatherings of people. The cottage was the only place I'd ever studied human nature. But Plutarch opened new and mightier scenes. I read of men in public life, governing or slaughtering their own species. I felt the greatest desire for virtue rise within me, and the deepest horror at vice — as far as I understood those terms, which for me were still tied simply to pleasure and pain. This led me to admire peaceful lawmakers like Numa, Solon, and Lycurgus over conquerors like Romulus and Theseus. My protectors' peaceful lives reinforced these feelings. Perhaps if my first encounter with humanity had been through a young soldier burning for glory and blood, I would have felt very differently.

"But _Paradise Lost_ stirred far deeper emotions. I read it — as I read the others — as true history. It filled me with every feeling of wonder and awe that the picture of an all-powerful God warring with his creatures could produce. I constantly compared the various situations to my own. Like Adam, I seemed connected to no other being in existence. But his condition was utterly different from mine in every other way. He had been created perfect by God — happy, fortunate, specially protected. He was allowed to speak with and learn from beings higher than himself. But I was wretched, helpless, and alone. Many times I saw Satan as a better image of my condition. Like him, when I saw the happiness of my protectors, bitter envy rose within me.

"Another discovery deepened these feelings. Soon after arriving at the hovel, I found some papers in the pocket of the clothes I'd taken from your laboratory. At first I'd ignored them. Now that I could read, I studied them carefully. They were your journal of the four months before my creation. You described every step of your work in detail, mixed with accounts of your daily life. You certainly remember these papers. Here they are. Everything about my cursed origin is in them — the complete, disgusting story of how I was made. The most minute description of my hideous body is given, in language that painted your own horror and made mine permanent. I felt sick as I read. 'Hateful day when I received life!' I cried in anguish. 'Cursed creator! Why did you make a monster so hideous that even _you_ turned away in disgust? God, in his mercy, made man beautiful, in his own image. But my form is a filthy copy of yours, made even more horrible by the very resemblance. Satan at least had companions — fellow demons to admire and encourage him. But I am utterly alone and despised.'

"These were my thoughts in hours of despair and isolation. But when I thought about my cottagers' virtues, their kind and generous natures, I convinced myself that when they learned of my admiration, they would pity me and overlook my physical ugliness. Could they really turn away someone, however monstrous, who asked for their compassion and friendship? I resolved not to give up hope but to prepare myself in every way for the encounter that would decide my fate. I kept postponing it — the stakes were too high and the fear of failure too great. Besides, my understanding improved every day, and I didn't want to attempt it until a few more months had sharpened my mind.

"Meanwhile, changes took place in the cottage. Safie's presence had spread happiness. Felix and Agatha spent more time in conversation and entertainment, helped by servants. They weren't rich, but they were content and at peace. Their feelings were calm, while mine grew more turbulent every day. Growing knowledge only showed me more clearly what a wretched outcast I was. I held onto hope, but it vanished whenever I saw my reflection in water or my shadow in moonlight — as fleeting and unreal as those images themselves.

"I tried to crush these fears and steel myself for the trial I'd resolved to face. Sometimes I let my thoughts wander unchecked into dreams of paradise, imagining kind, lovely beings who understood my feelings and eased my darkness. Their angelic faces smiled with comfort. But it was all fantasy. No Eve soothed my sorrows or shared my thoughts. I was alone. I remembered Adam's plea to his Creator. But where was mine? He had abandoned me. In the bitterness of my heart, I cursed him.

"Autumn passed. I watched with surprise and sadness as the leaves decayed and fell and nature put on the barren, bleak appearance it had worn when I first saw the woods. Yet I didn't mind the cold weather. My body was better suited to endure cold than heat. But my greatest pleasures had been flowers, birds, and all the bright display of summer. When these vanished, I turned with more attention to the cottagers. Their happiness wasn't diminished by summer's absence. They loved each other, and their joys depended on one another, undisturbed by what happened around them. The more I saw of them, the more I longed for their acceptance and love. To see their kind faces turned toward me with affection was the highest dream I could imagine. I didn't dare think they would look at me with contempt and horror. The poor who came to their door were never turned away. I asked, it's true, for more than a little food or rest. I needed kindness and understanding. But I didn't believe myself entirely unworthy of it.

"Winter came, and a full year had passed since I first woke into life. My attention was now focused entirely on my plan to introduce myself to the cottagers. I considered many approaches. The one I settled on was to enter the cottage when the blind old man was alone. I was smart enough to realize that my unnatural ugliness was the main source of horror for those who had seen me. My voice, though harsh, had nothing terrible about it. So I reasoned that if I could win the old man's goodwill in his children's absence, he might mediate on my behalf with the younger members of the family and prepare them for my appearance.

"One day, when the sun shone on the red leaves scattered on the ground and spread a cheerfulness that contradicted the cold, Safie, Agatha, and Felix left for a long walk in the country. The old man, at his own request, was left alone. When they'd gone, he took up his guitar and played several mournful but sweet melodies — sweeter and sadder than I'd ever heard from him. At first his face was lit with pleasure, but as he played on, thoughtfulness and sadness took over. Finally, setting aside the instrument, he sat absorbed in reflection.

"My heart beat fast. This was the hour that would determine my hopes or confirm my fears. The servants had gone to a nearby fair. Everything was silent in and around the cottage. It was the perfect opportunity. Yet when I moved to carry out my plan, my legs buckled and I collapsed to the ground. I rose again, summoned every ounce of courage I possessed, and removed the planks I'd placed over my hovel entrance to hide my retreat. Fresh air revived me. With renewed determination, I approached the cottage door.
"I knocked. 'Who is there?' said the old man. 'Come in.'
"I entered. 'Forgive the intrusion,' I said. 'I'm a traveler who needs a little rest. You'd greatly oblige me if you'd let me warm myself by your fire for a few minutes.'
"'Come in,' said De Lacey. 'I'll try to help however I can. But unfortunately my children are away from home, and since I'm blind, I'm afraid I can't easily find you food.'
"'Please don't trouble yourself, kind sir. I have food. I need only warmth and rest.'
"I sat down. A silence followed. I knew every minute was precious, yet I couldn't decide how to begin. Then the old man spoke.
"'From your language, stranger, I take it you're my countryman. Are you French?'
"'No, but I was educated by a French family and understand only that language. I'm now on my way to seek the protection of some friends whom I love dearly and in whose kindness I have some hope.'
"'Are they Germans?'

"'No, they're French. But let me change the subject. I'm an unfortunate and abandoned creature. I look around and have no relative or friend on earth. These kind people I'm going to have never seen me and know little of me. I'm full of fear, because if they reject me, I'll be an outcast forever.'

"'Don't despair. Being friendless is certainly a misfortune. But the hearts of men, when not clouded by self-interest, are full of brotherly love and charity. Trust in your hopes. If your friends are good and kind, don't give up.'

"'They are kind — they're the most excellent people in the world. But unfortunately they're prejudiced against me. I have good intentions. My life has been harmless and even somewhat beneficial. But a fatal prejudice blinds them. Where they should see a feeling, kind friend, they see only a detestable monster.'
"'That is indeed unfortunate. But if you're truly blameless, can't you set them right?'

"'I'm about to try exactly that. And it's this attempt that fills me with such overwhelming dread. I love these friends dearly. For many months, unknown to them, I've done them daily kindnesses. But they believe I mean them harm. That's the misunderstanding I'm trying to overcome.'
"'Where do these friends live?'
"'Near this very spot.'

"The old man paused, then continued: 'If you confide in me fully, perhaps I can help set things right. I'm blind and can't judge your face, but there's something in your voice that convinces me you're sincere. I'm poor and an exile, but it would give me true pleasure to help a fellow human being.'
"'Excellent man! I thank you and accept your generous offer. You lift me from the dust with this kindness. I trust that with your help, I won't be driven from the company of your fellow creatures.'

"'Heaven forbid! Even if you were guilty of a crime — for that can only drive you to desperation, not inspire virtue. I too am unfortunate. My family has been condemned, though innocent. So judge whether I can't feel for your troubles.'

"'How can I thank you, my best and only friend? Yours is the first voice of kindness ever directed at me. I'll be grateful forever. Your goodness assures me I'll succeed with the friends I'm about to meet.'
"'May I know their names and where they live?'

"I paused. This was the moment of truth — the moment that would grant or destroy my happiness forever. I fought for the strength to answer, but the effort broke me. I collapsed into the chair and sobbed aloud. Just then I heard the footsteps of my younger protectors. There wasn't a moment to lose. Seizing the old man's hand, I cried, 'Now is the time! Save and protect me! You and your family are the friends I seek. Don't abandon me in this hour of need!'
"'Great God!' exclaimed the old man. 'Who are you?'

"At that instant the cottage door opened, and Felix, Safie, and Agatha entered. Who can describe their horror and shock at seeing me? Agatha fainted. Safie, unable to help her friend, rushed out of the cottage. Felix lunged forward and, with superhuman force, tore me from his father's knees where I clung. In a fury, he threw me to the ground and beat me violently with a stick. I could have torn him limb from limb, as a lion tears its prey. But my heart sank with bitter anguish, and I held back. When I saw him about to strike again, overcome by pain and grief, I fled the cottage. In the confusion, I escaped unnoticed to my hovel."

chapters.title: Chapter 16
paragraphs: "Cursed, cursed creator! Why did I live? Why didn't I extinguish in that instant the spark of existence you had so carelessly given me? I don't know. Despair hadn't yet taken hold of me. What I felt was rage and a desire for revenge. I could gladly have destroyed the cottage and its inhabitants, gorging myself on their screams and misery.

"When night came I left my hiding place and wandered through the woods. No longer restrained by fear of being discovered, I gave voice to my anguish in terrible howls. I was like a wild beast that had broken free, destroying everything in my path and racing through the forest with the speed of a deer. Oh, what a miserable night! The cold stars shone in mockery. The bare trees waved their branches above me. Now and then a bird sang amid the universal silence. Everything was at rest or happy — except me. Like the devil himself, I carried a hell within me. Finding no one who understood or cared, I wanted to tear up the trees, spread destruction everywhere, and then sit down among the ruins and savor the wreckage.

"But this luxury of sensation couldn't last. I grew exhausted from the violence of my exertions and sank onto the wet grass in the helpless misery of despair. Among all the millions of people on earth, not one would pity or help me. Should I feel kindness toward my enemies? No. From that moment, I declared eternal war against the human species — and above all, against the one who had made me and abandoned me to this unbearable misery.
"The sun rose. I heard voices and knew it was impossible to return to my hovel during daylight. I hid in thick underbrush, planning to use the hours for thinking about my situation.

"The pleasant sunshine and fresh air gradually calmed me. When I thought about what had happened at the cottage, I couldn't help thinking I'd been too hasty. I had certainly acted foolishly. My conversation had clearly interested the old man. But I'd been a fool to expose myself to his children's horror. I should have won the old man over gradually and revealed myself to the rest of the family only after they'd been prepared. My mistakes didn't seem beyond repair. After much thought, I resolved to return to the cottage, find the old man, and try again to win his support.

"These thoughts calmed me. In the afternoon I fell into a deep sleep. But fever in my blood wouldn't let me rest peacefully. The horrible scene of the day before played over and over before my eyes — the women fleeing, the enraged Felix tearing me from his father's feet. I woke exhausted. Finding it was already night, I crept out in search of food.

"When my hunger was satisfied, I headed down the familiar path to the cottage. Everything was quiet there. I crept into my hovel and waited silently for the family to rise at their usual hour. That hour came. The sun climbed high in the sky. But the cottagers didn't appear. I trembled violently, sensing some terrible disaster. The cottage was dark inside. I heard no movement. The suspense was agonizing.

"Soon two country men passed by. They paused near the cottage and entered into conversation, using animated gestures. I couldn't understand them, since they spoke the local language, which was different from my protectors'. Shortly after, Felix approached with another man. I was surprised, since I knew he hadn't left the cottage that morning. I waited anxiously to learn from their conversation what was happening.

"'Do you realize,' the man said to Felix, 'that you'll have to pay three months' rent and lose the produce of your garden? I don't want to take unfair advantage, so please take a few days to reconsider.'

"'It's completely useless,' Felix replied. 'We can never live in your cottage again. My father's life is in the greatest danger because of the dreadful event I've described. My wife and my sister will never recover from the shock. I beg you not to argue with me anymore. Take your property back and let me flee this place.'
"Felix trembled violently as he said this. He and his companion went into the cottage, stayed a few minutes, then left. I never saw any member of the De Lacey family again.

"I spent the rest of the day in my hovel in a state of complete, numbing despair. My protectors had gone. They had broken the only link that connected me to the world. For the first time, hatred and revenge filled my heart, and I didn't try to fight them. I let myself be carried along by the current. I bent my mind toward destruction and death. When I thought of my friends — the old man's gentle voice, Agatha's tender eyes, the Arabian's exquisite beauty — those thoughts vanished into tears that briefly soothed me. But then I remembered that they had rejected and abandoned me. Anger returned — a rage of anger. Unable to hurt anything human, I turned my fury on objects. As night advanced, I placed piles of dry material around the cottage. After destroying every trace of cultivation in the garden, I waited with forced patience until the moon had set to begin.

"As the night grew deeper, a fierce wind rose from the woods and quickly scattered the clouds. The blast tore along like a mighty avalanche, producing a kind of madness in my spirit that shattered all restraint of reason. I lit a dry branch from a tree and danced with fury around the cottage. My eyes were fixed on the western horizon, where the moon's edge was about to disappear. A sliver of it was hidden. I waved my torch. It sank. With a loud scream, I set fire to the straw and brush I'd piled up. The wind fanned the flames. The cottage was quickly engulfed. Fire clung to it and licked it with forked, destroying tongues.
"As soon as I was sure nothing could save the building, I left the scene and sought refuge in the woods.

"And now, with the whole world before me, where should I go? I decided to flee far from the scene of my misery. But to me — hated and despised everywhere — every country would be equally horrible. Then I thought of you. I'd learned from your papers that you were my father, my creator. To whom could I turn more fittingly than the one who had given me life? Among the lessons Felix had given Safie, geography hadn't been neglected. I'd learned the relative positions of different countries on the earth. You had mentioned Geneva as your hometown. I resolved to go there.

"But how would I find my way? I knew I had to travel southwest, but the sun was my only guide. I didn't know the names of the towns along the way, and I couldn't ask a single person for directions. Yet I didn't give up. You were my only hope — even though I felt nothing but hatred toward you. Heartless creator! You had given me thoughts and feelings, then cast me out as an object of scorn and horror. But you alone owed me pity and justice, and from you I was determined to get it.

"My journey was long and the suffering intense. It was late autumn when I left the region where I'd lived so long. I traveled only at night, afraid of encountering any human face. Nature was dying around me. The sun grew cold. Rain and snow poured down. Mighty rivers froze. The ground was hard, cold, and bare. I found no shelter. Oh, earth! How often I cursed the cause of my existence! The gentleness of my nature had fled. Everything within me had turned to bitterness. The closer I got to your home, the more deeply I felt revenge burning in my heart. Snow fell. The waters hardened. But I didn't rest. A few landmarks guided me. I had a map, but I often wandered far off course. The agony of my feelings allowed no peace. Every incident fed my rage and misery. But one event that happened on the borders of Switzerland, when the sun had regained its warmth and the earth was turning green again, confirmed the bitterness and horror of my feelings in a special way.

"I usually rested during the day and traveled only at night. One morning, however, finding my path through a deep wood, I dared to continue after sunrise. The day was one of the first of spring. It cheered even me with its sunshine and mild air. I felt emotions of gentleness and pleasure that had long seemed dead. Half-surprised by the novelty of these feelings, I let myself be carried along by them. Forgetting my solitude and ugliness, I dared to feel happy. Soft tears ran down my cheeks. I even raised my wet eyes with thankfulness toward the blessed sun.

"I continued through the woods until I reached its edge, where a deep, rapid river ran. Many trees bent their budding branches over the water. I paused here, unsure which way to go, when I heard voices that made me hide under a cypress tree. I'd barely hidden when a young girl came running toward me, laughing, as if she were being playfully chased. She ran along the steep riverbank. Suddenly her foot slipped, and she fell into the rushing water. I sprang from my hiding place and, with tremendous effort against the current, pulled her to shore. She was unconscious. I tried every way I knew to revive her — when suddenly a man appeared. He was probably the person she'd been running from. When he saw me, he rushed forward, tore the girl from my arms, and headed for the deeper part of the woods. I followed, hardly knowing why. When the man saw me approaching, he aimed a gun at me and fired. I fell to the ground. My attacker fled with greater speed into the woods.

"This was the reward for my kindness! I had saved a human life, and in return I now writhed in the agony of a wound that shattered flesh and bone. The feelings of gentleness I'd felt just moments before gave way to hellish rage and gnashing of teeth. Inflamed by pain, I vowed eternal hatred and vengeance against all humanity. But the agony of my wound overcame me. I fainted.

"For several weeks I lived miserably in the woods, trying to heal my wound. The bullet had entered my shoulder, and I didn't know if it was still lodged there. I had no way to remove it. My suffering was worsened by the unbearable sense of injustice. Every day I swore revenge — a deep and deadly revenge that alone could compensate for the outrages I'd endured.

"After some weeks my wound healed, and I continued my journey. The sun's warmth and spring breezes no longer soothed me. All joy was just a mockery that insulted my desolate state and made me feel more painfully that I was not meant for pleasure.
"But my journey was nearing its end. Within two months I reached the outskirts of Geneva.

"It was evening when I arrived. I hid in the fields to think about how to approach you. I was worn down by exhaustion and hunger, far too miserable to enjoy the gentle evening breeze or the sight of the sun setting behind the magnificent mountains of the Jura.

"I dozed lightly, finding brief relief from the pain of my thoughts. I was startled awake by the approach of a beautiful child, running into my hiding place with all the playfulness of youth. Suddenly, as I looked at him, an idea seized me: this little creature was unprejudiced, too young to have learned a horror of ugliness. If I could take him and raise him as my companion and friend, I wouldn't be so alone in this crowded world.

"Driven by this impulse, I grabbed the boy as he passed and pulled him toward me. As soon as he saw me, he covered his eyes and screamed. I pulled his hand from his face and said, 'Child, what does this mean? I don't intend to hurt you. Listen to me.'
"He struggled violently. 'Let me go!' he screamed. 'Monster! Ugly wretch! You want to eat me and tear me apart. You're an ogre. Let me go, or I'll tell my papa.'
"'Boy, you'll never see your father again. You must come with me.'
"'Hideous monster! Let me go. My papa is a syndic — he's Monsieur Frankenstein — he'll punish you. You wouldn't dare keep me.'
"'Frankenstein! You belong to my enemy — to the man I've sworn eternal revenge against. You shall be my first victim.'
"The child kept struggling and hurling insults that drove despair into my heart. I seized his throat to silence him. In a moment he lay dead at my feet.

"I stared at my victim. My heart swelled with triumph and hellish joy. Clapping my hands, I cried, 'I too can create devastation! My enemy is not invulnerable. This death will bring despair to him, and a thousand other miseries shall torment and destroy him.'

"As I stared at the child, I noticed something glittering on his chest. I took it. It was a portrait of a most beautiful woman. Despite my hatred, it softened me and drew me in. For a few moments I gazed with delight at her dark eyes, framed by deep lashes, and her lovely lips. But then my rage returned. I remembered that I would forever be denied the joy such beautiful creatures could give — and that this woman, if she ever looked at me, would replace her expression of divine kindness with one of disgust and terror.

"Can you wonder that such thoughts drove me wild with rage? I'm only surprised that in that moment, instead of venting my feelings in screams and agony, I didn't rush among humanity and die trying to destroy them.

"Overcome by these feelings, I left the murder scene and found a more secluded hiding place. I entered a barn that appeared empty. A young woman was sleeping on some straw. She wasn't as beautiful as the woman in the portrait, but she was pleasant-looking, blooming with youth and health. Here, I thought, is one of those whose joyful smiles are given to everyone but me. Then I bent over her and whispered, 'Wake, beautiful one — your lover is near, he who would give his life for one look of affection from your eyes. My beloved, awake!'

"The sleeper stirred. A thrill of terror ran through me. What if she woke and saw me and cursed me and denounced the murderer? That's exactly what she would do if she opened her eyes and saw me. The thought was madness. It stirred the devil within me. Not I, but she, would suffer. The murder I'd committed because I was forever robbed of everything she could give — she would pay for it. The crime had its source in her. Let the punishment be hers. Thanks to Felix's lessons and the bloody laws of men, I'd learned to do harm. I bent over her and tucked the portrait into a fold of her dress. She stirred again, and I fled.

"For some days I haunted the area where these events had occurred, sometimes wishing to see you, sometimes resolved to leave the world and its miseries forever. Finally I wandered toward these mountains. I've roamed through their vast wilderness, consumed by a burning passion that only you can satisfy. We cannot part until you've promised to grant my demand. I am alone and miserable. No one will associate with me. But a creature as deformed and horrible as myself wouldn't refuse me. You must create my companion."

chapters.title: Chapter 17
paragraphs: The creature finished speaking and fixed his eyes on me, waiting for a reply. But I was overwhelmed, confused, and unable to fully grasp the scope of his demand. He continued,
"You must create a female for me, with whom I can share the companionship necessary for my existence. Only you can do this, and I demand it as a right you cannot refuse."
The latter part of his story had rekindled the anger that had faded while he described his peaceful life among the cottagers. When he finished, I could no longer suppress the rage burning inside me.

"I refuse," I replied. "No torture will ever wring consent from me. You may make me the most miserable of men, but you'll never make me betray my own principles. Shall I create another like you, whose combined wickedness might devastate the world? Get out! I've given you my answer. You may torture me, but I will never agree."

"You're wrong," the creature replied, "and instead of threatening, I'm willing to reason with you. I'm cruel because I'm miserable. Am I not shunned and hated by all humanity? You, my creator, would tear me apart and celebrate. Remember that — and then tell me why I should pity mankind more than mankind pities me. You wouldn't call it murder if you could push me into one of these crevasses and destroy the body you made with your own hands. Should I respect people who condemn me? Let them live with me in mutual kindness, and instead of harm, I would shower them with every blessing, weeping tears of gratitude. But that can never be. Human senses are an insurmountable barrier between us. Yet I won't submit like a cringing slave. I'll take my revenge. If I can't inspire love, I'll cause fear — and especially toward you, my creator and greatest enemy, I swear undying hatred. Be careful. I'll work toward your destruction until I've devastated your heart so completely that you'll curse the hour of your birth."
A fiendish rage animated him as he said this. His face contorted into expressions too horrible for human eyes. But he quickly calmed himself and continued —

"I meant to reason calmly. This passion harms me, because you don't realize that _you_ are its cause. If any being showed me kindness, I would return it a hundredfold. For that one person's sake, I would make peace with the entire human race! But I'm dreaming of happiness I can never have. What I'm asking is reasonable and modest. I want a creature of the other sex, but as ugly as myself. The satisfaction is small, but it's all I can have, and it will be enough. It's true we'll be monsters, cut off from the world. But for that very reason we'll be more devoted to each other. Our lives won't be happy, but they'll be harmless and free from the misery I feel now. Oh, my creator, make me happy! Let me feel gratitude toward you for one kindness! Let me know that I matter to some living being. Don't deny me my request!"

I was moved. I shuddered at the possible consequences of agreeing. But I felt there was justice in his argument. His story and the feelings he'd expressed proved him a creature of fine sensibilities. Didn't I, as his maker, owe him whatever happiness I could provide? He saw my hesitation and continued,

"If you agree, neither you nor any other human being will ever see us again. I'll go to the vast wilderness of South America. My food isn't what humans eat. I don't slaughter lambs and goats to satisfy my hunger. Acorns and berries are enough for me. My companion will be of the same nature and content with the same food. We'll make our bed of dried leaves. The sun will shine on us as it does on everyone and ripen our food. The picture I'm painting is peaceful and humane. You can only deny it out of cruelty and abuse of power. Pitiless as you've been toward me, I now see compassion in your eyes. Let me seize this moment and persuade you to promise what I so desperately desire."

"You propose," I replied, "to flee from civilization and live in the wilderness, where wild animals will be your only companions. How can you, who long for human love and connection, persist in this exile? You'll return and seek their kindness again — and meet their hatred. Your violent impulses will be renewed. And you'll have a companion to help you destroy. This cannot be. Stop arguing. I cannot consent."

"How changeable your feelings are! Just a moment ago you were moved by my words. Why do you harden your heart against me again? I swear to you, by the earth I walk on and by you who made me, that with the companion you give me, I'll leave human society forever. I'll live, wherever chance takes me, in the most remote, savage places. My violent impulses will disappear, because I'll have someone who understands me! My life will pass quietly, and in my final moments I won't curse my maker."

His words had a strange effect on me. I pitied him and sometimes felt a wish to console him. But when I looked at him — when I saw the grotesque mass that moved and talked — my stomach turned and my feelings shifted to horror and revulsion. I tried to suppress these reactions. Since I couldn't sympathize with him, I had no right to withhold the small measure of happiness still in my power to grant.
"You swear," I said, "to be harmless. But haven't you already shown enough cruelty to make me distrust you? Might this not be a trick to make your revenge even more devastating?"

"How is this? I won't be toyed with. I demand an answer. If I have no bonds and no love, hatred and evil must be my lot. Another's love will destroy the cause of my crimes. I'll become a being whose existence nobody even knows about. My vices are the children of a forced isolation I despise. My virtues will naturally emerge when I live with an equal. I'll feel the emotions of a conscious being and become linked to the chain of existence from which I'm now excluded."

I paused for a long time to reflect on everything he'd told me and the arguments he'd used. I thought of the promise of goodness he'd shown at the beginning of his life and how it had been destroyed by the hatred and contempt his protectors had shown him. His power and threats weren't lost on me either. A creature who could survive in ice caves and hide among inaccessible cliffs was a being I couldn't hope to fight. After a long pause, I concluded that justice — both to him and to my fellow humans — required me to agree to his request. Turning to him, I said,
"I consent to your demand, on your solemn oath to leave Europe forever — and every other place near human habitation — as soon as I deliver a female companion to you."

"I swear," he cried, "by the sun, and by the blue sky of heaven, and by the fire of love that burns in my heart — if you grant my prayer, you will never see me again while they exist. Go home and begin your work. I'll watch its progress with inexpressible anxiety. Don't worry — when you're ready, I shall appear."
With that, he suddenly left me. I watched him descend the mountain faster than an eagle and quickly vanish among the ridges of the glacier.

His tale had taken the entire day. The sun was on the horizon when he departed. I knew I should hurry down to the valley before darkness surrounded me. But my heart was heavy, and my steps slow. The struggle of winding among the narrow mountain paths, placing my feet carefully as I went, was made harder by the emotions the day's events had stirred. Night was far advanced when I reached the halfway resting place and sat down beside a fountain. Stars shone through gaps in the clouds. Dark pines rose before me. Here and there a fallen tree lay on the ground. It was a scene of solemn wonder that stirred strange thoughts. I wept bitterly. Clasping my hands in anguish, I cried, "Oh, stars and clouds and winds! Are you all about to mock me? If you truly pity me, crush my consciousness and memory. Let me become nothing. But if not — go away and leave me in darkness."
These were wild, miserable thoughts. I can't describe how the eternal twinkling of the stars weighed on me, or how I listened to every gust of wind as if it were a deadly storm coming to consume me.

Morning broke before I reached the village of Chamonix. I took no rest but returned immediately to Geneva. Even in my own heart I couldn't put my feelings into words. They pressed on me with the weight of a mountain and their sheer intensity destroyed my ability to feel their pain. So I returned home. Entering the house, I presented myself to my family. My wild, haggard appearance alarmed them intensely. But I answered no questions and barely spoke. I felt as if I were under a curse — as if I had no right to their sympathy, as if I could never again enjoy their companionship. Yet I loved them with utter devotion. To save them, I resolved to dedicate myself to my most hated task. The prospect of such work made everything else in my life pass before me like a dream. That thought alone felt real.

chapters.title: Chapter 18
paragraphs: Day after day, week after week passed after my return to Geneva, and I couldn't summon the courage to begin my work. I feared the disappointed creature's vengeance, yet I couldn't overcome my revulsion for the task ahead. I realized I couldn't create a female without devoting several more months to intensive study. I'd heard that an English scientist had made discoveries essential to my success. I sometimes thought about getting my father's permission to visit England. But I clung to every excuse for delay and shrank from taking the first step in a project whose urgency seemed less pressing as time passed. A change had taken place in me. My health, which had been declining, was now much improved. My spirits, when not darkened by the memory of my terrible promise, rose accordingly. My father noticed this improvement with pleasure and turned his thoughts toward the best way of curing the lingering melancholy that still sometimes returned to blacken my days. In those dark moments, I sought the most complete solitude. I spent whole days alone on the lake in a little boat, watching clouds and listening to waves, silent and listless. But the fresh air and bright sun almost always restored some measure of calm. I returned to greet my family with a readier smile and a more cheerful heart.
It was after one of these outings that my father called me aside.

"I'm happy to see, my dear son, that you've returned to your former pleasures and seem to be becoming yourself again. And yet you're still unhappy and still avoid our company. For some time I was puzzled about the cause. But yesterday an idea struck me, and if I'm right, I beg you to be honest. Silence on such a matter would only bring triple misery on us all."
I trembled at his introduction. My father continued —

"I confess, my son, that I've always looked forward to your marriage with our dear Elizabeth as the bond of our domestic happiness and the comfort of my old age. You were attached to each other from your earliest childhood. You studied together, and in temperament and tastes you seemed perfectly suited. But I may have been blind. What I believed would help my plan may have destroyed it entirely. Perhaps you see her as a sister, with no wish that she become your wife. Or perhaps you've met someone else. If you feel bound to Elizabeth by honor while your heart is elsewhere, this inner conflict may be causing the intense misery you seem to feel."

"My dear father, reassure yourself. I love my cousin tenderly and sincerely. No woman has ever stirred my admiration and affection as Elizabeth does. My future hopes are entirely bound up in the expectation of our marriage."

"To hear you say so, dear Victor, gives me more pleasure than I've felt in a long time. If this is true, we shall surely be happy, whatever shadows may hang over us now. But it is this shadow that seems to have such a strong grip on your mind, and I wish to dispel it. Tell me — do you object to getting married soon? We've been unfortunate. Recent events have disrupted the quiet life suited to my age and health. You're younger. But I don't think that an early marriage would interfere with any future plans of yours, given that you have an adequate fortune. Don't think, however, that I'm trying to dictate your happiness, or that any delay would cause me serious concern. Speak honestly and answer me with complete sincerity."

I listened in silence, unable to answer for some time. My mind raced through a whirlwind of thoughts, trying to reach a conclusion. Alas! The idea of immediate marriage to Elizabeth filled me with horror and dread. I was bound by a solemn promise I hadn't yet kept and dared not break. If I did, what unspeakable miseries might descend on me and my family? Could I celebrate a wedding with this deadly weight hanging around my neck, dragging me to the ground? I had to fulfill my promise and let the monster depart with his mate before I could allow myself the happiness of marrying Elizabeth.

I also remembered that I needed to travel to England, or enter into a long correspondence with English scientists whose knowledge was essential for my project. The correspondence option was too slow and unsatisfying. Besides, I had an overwhelming aversion to doing this loathsome work in my father's house, surrounded by the people I loved. I knew that a thousand terrible accidents could happen, any one of which might reveal a story that would horrify everyone connected to me. I was also aware that I would often lose all self-control during such hideous work. I had to be away from everyone I loved while I was engaged in it. Once started, it could be finished quickly. Then I could return to my family in peace and happiness. My promise fulfilled, the monster would leave forever. Or — so my hopeful imagination pictured — some accident might destroy him and end my slavery.

These considerations shaped my answer. I expressed a wish to visit England, concealing the true reasons behind a cover story that raised no suspicion. I urged my request earnestly, and my father was easily persuaded to agree. After such a long period of depression that resembled madness, he was glad to see me capable of taking pleasure in the idea of a trip. He hoped that a change of scene would fully restore me.

The length of my absence was left to me — a few months, or at most a year. My father took one kind precaution: without telling me, he and Elizabeth had arranged for Clerval to join me at Strasbourg. This interfered with the solitude I needed for my work. But at the start of my journey, my friend's company wouldn't be a problem, and in truth I was glad. His presence would save me many hours of lonely, maddening reflection. Henry might even stand between me and the intrusion of my enemy. If I were alone, the creature might force his loathsome presence on me to remind me of my task or watch its progress.

To England, then, I was bound. It was understood that my marriage to Elizabeth would take place immediately on my return. My father's age made him deeply opposed to delay. For myself, I promised myself one reward from my hated labors — one consolation for my unparalleled suffering: the day when, freed from my wretched slavery, I could claim Elizabeth and forget the past in our union.

I made my travel arrangements. But one fear haunted me. During my absence, I would leave my friends unaware of their enemy's existence and unprotected from his attacks. He might be enraged by my departure. But he'd promised to follow me wherever I went. Wouldn't he come to England too? This thought was terrible in itself, but comforting insofar as it meant my friends would be safe. I agonized over the possibility that the opposite might be true. But throughout the entire period of my slavery to this creature, I allowed myself to be governed by the impulse of the moment. My current feelings strongly suggested the creature would follow me and spare my family from his schemes.

It was late September when I left my native country again. The journey had been my own idea, so Elizabeth agreed. But she was filled with anxiety about the suffering and grief I might experience while away from her. She had arranged for Clerval to accompany me — yet a man is blind to the thousand small things a woman's attentive care would notice. She longed to tell me to hurry back. A thousand conflicting emotions left her mute as she bade me a tearful, silent farewell.

I threw myself into the carriage, barely knowing where I was going and careless of everything around me. I remembered only — and the memory was bitter — to have my chemical instruments packed. Filled with dark thoughts, I passed through many beautiful scenes, but my eyes were fixed and unseeing. I could think only of my journey's purpose and the work that awaited me.

After some days of listless travel, I reached Strasbourg, where I waited two days for Clerval. He came. Alas, the contrast between us was striking! He was alive to every new sight, joyful at the beauty of the sunset, even happier watching the sunrise begin a new day. He pointed out the shifting colors of the landscape and the patterns of the sky. "This is what it means to live!" he exclaimed. "Now I truly exist! But you, my dear Frankenstein — why so gloomy and sad?" In truth, I was consumed by dark thoughts. I neither saw the evening star descend nor the golden sunrise reflected in the Rhine. You, my friend, would have found much more pleasure in Clerval's journal — for he observed the scenery with a feeling eye — than in listening to my reflections. I, a miserable wretch, was haunted by a curse that blocked every path to joy.

We'd agreed to travel down the Rhine by boat from Strasbourg to Rotterdam, then take a ship to London. During the voyage we passed many willow-covered islands and saw several beautiful towns. We stopped a day at Mannheim. On the fifth day after leaving Strasbourg, we reached Mainz. Below Mainz, the Rhine becomes much more scenic. The river descends quickly, winding between hills — not high, but steep and beautifully shaped. We saw many ruined castles on the edges of cliffs, surrounded by dark woods, high and inaccessible. This stretch of the Rhine presents a remarkably varied landscape. In one spot you see rugged hills and ruined castles overlooking sheer drops, with the dark Rhine rushing far below. Then, around a sudden bend, flourishing vineyards appear on gentle green slopes, with a winding river and busy towns filling the scene.

We traveled during the grape harvest and heard the harvesters singing as we glided downstream. Even I, depressed and constantly tormented by dark feelings — even I was pleased. I lay at the bottom of the boat. Gazing at the cloudless blue sky, I seemed to drink in a peace I hadn't felt in a long time. And if I could feel this way, imagine how Henry felt! He experienced a happiness few people ever know. "I've seen the most beautiful scenery in my own country," he said. "I've visited the lakes of Lucerne and Uri, where snowy mountains descend almost vertically to the water, casting black, impenetrable shadows. I've seen Lake Lucerne whipped up by storms, with waterspouts and waves crashing against mountain bases. I've seen the mountains of the Valais and the Pays de Vaud. But this country, Victor, pleases me more than all those wonders. The Swiss mountains are more dramatic and strange, but the banks of this divine river have a charm I've never seen equaled. Look at that castle hanging over the cliff! And that one on the island, almost hidden among lovely trees. And those workers coming from their vineyards. And that village half-concealed in the mountain hollow. Oh, surely the spirit guarding this place has a soul more in harmony with man than those who build the glaciers or hide among our own country's inaccessible peaks."

Clerval! Beloved friend! Even now it delights me to record your words and praise your remarkable qualities. He was a being formed in "the very poetry of nature." His wild, imaginative spirit was tempered by the warmth of his heart. His soul overflowed with passionate affection. His friendship was of that devoted, extraordinary kind that worldly people tell us exists only in fiction. But even human connection wasn't enough for his eager mind. The beauty of the natural world, which others merely admire, he loved with passion: —

The sounding cataract Haunted him like a passion: the tall rock, The mountain, and the deep and gloomy wood, Their colours and their forms, were then to him An appetite; a feeling, and a love, That had no need of a remoter charm, By thought supplied, or any interest Unborrow'd from the eye.
[Wordsworth's "Tintern Abbey."]

And where is he now? Is this gentle, lovely being lost forever? Has this mind — so rich with ideas, so magnificent in imagination, creating a world whose existence depended on the life of its creator — has this mind perished? Does it exist now only in my memory? No. Your divinely shaped form has decayed, but your spirit still visits and consoles your unhappy friend.
