Forgive this outpouring of grief. These inadequate words are only a small tribute to Henry's extraordinary worth. But they soothe my aching heart. I'll continue with my tale.
Beyond Cologne we descended to the plains of Holland. We decided to travel the rest of the way by coach, since the wind was against us and the river current too gentle to help.

Our journey lost the charm of beautiful scenery, but we arrived within a few days at Rotterdam. From there we sailed to England. It was a clear morning in late December when I first saw the white cliffs of Britain. The banks of the Thames were a new scene — flat but fertile. Nearly every town reminded us of some historical event. We saw Tilbury Fort and remembered the Spanish Armada. We passed Gravesend, Woolwich, and Greenwich — places I'd heard of even in my own country.
At last we saw the countless steeples of London, with St. Paul's towering above all, and the Tower, famous in English history.

chapters.title: Chapter 19
paragraphs: London was our immediate destination. We planned to stay several months in this wonderful, celebrated city. Clerval wanted to meet the brilliant thinkers flourishing there. For me, this was secondary. I was mainly concerned with gathering the scientific knowledge I needed to fulfill my promise. I quickly used the letters of introduction I'd brought, addressed to the most distinguished natural scientists.

If this trip had taken place during my happier student days, it would have given me enormous pleasure. But a curse had settled over my existence. I visited these men only for the information they could give me on the subject that so terribly consumed me. Company was unbearable. When alone, I could fill my mind with the beauty of heaven and earth. Henry's voice soothed me, and I could trick myself into temporary peace. But the busy, carefree, happy faces of strangers brought despair crashing back. I saw an impassable wall between me and other people — a wall sealed with the blood of William and Justine. Thinking about events connected to those names filled my soul with anguish.

But in Clerval I saw an image of my former self. He was eager and curious, hungry for experience and learning. The different customs he observed were an endless source of instruction and amusement. He was also pursuing a long-held goal: visiting India. He believed that his knowledge of Indian languages and society could help advance European trade and settlement. Only in Britain could he further this plan. He was always busy, and the only check on his happiness was my sorrowful, dejected state. I tried to hide this as much as possible, not wanting to rob him of the pleasures natural to someone entering a new phase of life, free from bitter memories. I often refused to join him, claiming another engagement, so I could be alone. I also began collecting materials for my new creation. This was like the torture of water slowly, endlessly dripping on my head. Every thought devoted to it was extreme anguish. Every word I spoke about it made my lips tremble and my heart pound.

After some months in London, we received a letter from a friend in Scotland — someone who had once visited us in Geneva. He praised the beauties of his native country and asked whether they weren't enough to lure us as far north as Perth, where he lived. Clerval was eager to accept. I, though I loathed society, wanted to see mountains and streams again — all the wonderful works with which nature adorns her favorite places.

We'd arrived in England at the beginning of October. It was now February. We decided to start our northward journey at the end of another month. We wouldn't follow the main road to Edinburgh but would instead visit Windsor, Oxford, Matlock, and the Cumberland lakes, planning to complete the tour around the end of July. I packed up my chemical instruments and collected materials, planning to finish my work in some remote corner of the Scottish Highlands.

We left London on March 27th and spent a few days at Windsor, wandering through its beautiful forest. This was new territory for us mountain-dwellers — the majestic oaks, the abundant game, the herds of stately deer were all novelties.

From there we went to Oxford. As we entered the city, our minds filled with memories of events that had taken place there more than a century and a half earlier. This was where Charles I had gathered his forces. The city had remained loyal to him after the rest of the nation had abandoned his cause. The memory of that unfortunate king and his companions gave a special interest to every corner of the city. The spirit of earlier days lived here, and we enjoyed tracing its footsteps. Even without these historical associations, the city was beautiful enough to earn our admiration. The colleges were ancient and picturesque. The streets were almost magnificent. The lovely River Isis flowed beside it through meadows of exquisite green, spreading into a placid expanse of water that reflected the majestic array of towers, spires, and domes nestled among ancient trees.

I enjoyed this scene, yet my pleasure was poisoned by memories of the past and fear of the future. I'd been made for peaceful happiness. In my youth, discontent never visited my mind. When boredom crept in, the sight of natural beauty or the study of human excellence could always rekindle my spirits. But I was now a blasted tree, struck by lightning to the soul. I felt then that I would survive only to exhibit what I would soon cease to be — a miserable wreck of humanity, pitiful to others and unbearable to myself.

We spent considerable time at Oxford, exploring its surroundings and trying to find every spot connected to the most stirring period of English history. We visited the tomb of the great Hampden and the field where that patriot fell. For a moment my soul was lifted from its degrading fears to contemplate the divine ideas of liberty and sacrifice that these places represented. For an instant I dared to shake off my chains and look around with a free, noble spirit. But the iron had eaten into my flesh, and I sank back, trembling and hopeless, into my miserable self.

We left Oxford with regret and went to Matlock. The countryside nearby resembled Switzerland to some degree, but everything was on a smaller scale. The green hills lacked the crown of distant white Alps that always accompanies our Swiss mountains. We visited the famous cave and the little natural history collections. When Henry mentioned the name Chamonix, I shuddered, and I rushed to leave Matlock and the terrible associations that name brought.

From Derby, continuing north, we spent two months in Cumberland and Westmorland. I could almost imagine myself among the Swiss mountains again. The patches of lingering snow on northern slopes, the lakes, the rushing rocky streams — all were familiar and dear to me. Here we also made friends who almost managed to trick me into happiness. Clerval's delight was even greater than mine. His mind expanded in the company of talented people. He discovered abilities and depths within himself he hadn't known he possessed. "I could live here forever," he told me, "and among these mountains I'd scarcely miss Switzerland and the Rhine."

But he found that a traveler's life mixes much pain with its pleasures. Your feelings are always stretched to the limit. When you begin to settle into contentment, you're forced to leave and move on to something new, which also engages your interest — only to be abandoned for the next novelty.

We'd barely explored the Cumberland and Westmorland lakes and grown fond of some of the local people when the date of our Scottish appointment approached. We left to continue our journey north. For my part, I wasn't sorry. I'd been neglecting my promise for some time and feared the creature's reaction to my delay. He might still be in Switzerland, wreaking vengeance on my family. This thought pursued and tormented me constantly. I waited for letters with feverish anxiety. When they were late, I was consumed by a thousand fears. When they arrived and I saw Elizabeth's or my father's handwriting, I hardly dared read them. Sometimes I imagined the creature was following me and might speed up my negligence by murdering my companion. When these thoughts possessed me, I wouldn't leave Henry's side for a moment but followed him like his shadow, trying to protect him from the imagined rage of his destroyer. I felt as if I'd committed some great crime — a crime whose consciousness haunted me. I was innocent, yet I'd drawn a terrible curse upon my head, as deadly as any criminal's.

I visited Edinburgh with dulled eyes and mind — though the city might have fascinated even the most unfortunate person. Clerval didn't like it as much as Oxford, preferring the latter's antiquity. But Edinburgh's beauty and regularity, its romantic castle, and its magnificent surroundings — Arthur's Seat, St. Bernard's Well, the Pentland Hills — more than compensated and filled him with admiration. But I was impatient to reach my journey's end.

We left Edinburgh within a week, passing through Coupar, St. Andrews, and along the banks of the Tay to Perth, where our friend was expecting us. But I was in no mood for socializing. I told Clerval I wanted to tour Scotland alone. "Enjoy yourself," I said. "Let this be our meeting point. I may be gone a month or two. But don't interfere with my plans, I beg you. Leave me to peace and solitude for a while. When I return, I hope it will be with a lighter heart, more suited to your own."

Henry tried to talk me out of it, but seeing I was determined, he stopped arguing. "I'd rather be with you," he said, "even on your lonely rambles, than with these Scottish people I don't know. Hurry back, dear friend, so I can feel at home again — something I can't manage without you."

Having parted from my friend, I decided to find some remote spot in Scotland to finish my work in solitude. I had no doubt the monster was following me and would reveal himself when I was done, to collect his companion.

With this resolve, I traveled through the northern Highlands and chose one of the most remote of the Orkney Islands for my laboratory. It was a fitting place — little more than a rock, its high sides battered constantly by waves. The soil was barren, barely supporting a few miserable cows. The five inhabitants survived on oatmeal, and their gaunt, scraggly limbs showed the poverty of their diet. Vegetables, bread, and even fresh water had to be brought from the mainland, about five miles away.

The whole island had only three wretched huts. One was vacant when I arrived. I rented it. It had just two rooms in a state of utter squalor. The roof had caved in. The walls were bare plaster. The door hung off its hinges. I had it repaired, bought some furniture, and moved in — an event that would surely have caused surprise had the islanders' senses not been numbed by want and misery. As it was, I lived unnoticed and undisturbed, barely thanked for the small amounts of food and clothing I gave them. Suffering had blunted even their most basic responses.

In this retreat I devoted mornings to my work. In the evenings, when weather permitted, I walked on the stony beach, listening to the waves roar and crash at my feet. It was monotonous yet ever-changing. I thought of Switzerland. It was so different from this desolate, terrifying landscape. Its hills are covered with vines. Its cottages dot the plains. Its beautiful lakes reflect a blue and gentle sky. Even when storms disturb the water, the lake's turbulence is like a child's play compared to the roaring of this giant ocean.

This was how I organized my days when I first arrived. But as my work progressed, it became more horrible and sickening with each passing day. Sometimes I couldn't force myself to enter my laboratory for days at a time. Other times I worked day and night to finish. It was truly a filthy process. During my first experiment, a kind of frenzied enthusiasm had blinded me to the horror of what I was doing. My mind had been fixed entirely on the goal, and my eyes were shut to the reality of my actions. But now I went to it in cold blood. My heart often sickened at the work of my hands.

Working in this most detestable occupation, immersed in a solitude where nothing could distract me from what I was doing, my nerves began to fray. I grew restless and anxious. Every moment I feared meeting my tormentor. Sometimes I sat with my eyes on the ground, afraid to look up in case I saw the creature I dreaded. I was afraid to wander from the sight of other people, in case the creature came to claim his companion when I was alone.
Meanwhile, my work progressed considerably. I looked toward its completion with a trembling, eager hope I dared not examine too closely — mixed with dark forebodings of evil that made my heart sick.

chapters.title: Chapter 20
paragraphs: I sat one evening in my laboratory. The sun had set. The moon was just rising from the sea. I didn't have enough light to work and sat idle, debating whether to stop for the night or push on to finish. As I sat, a chain of thoughts led me to consider the consequences of what I was doing. Three years ago, I'd been engaged in the same kind of work and had created a monster whose unparalleled cruelty had devastated my heart and filled it with bitter remorse. Now I was about to create another being whose character was equally unknown to me. She might become ten thousand times more dangerous than her mate and delight in murder for its own sake. He had sworn to leave humanity and hide in the wilderness, but she hadn't made any such promise. She would be a thinking, reasoning being and might refuse to honor a deal made before she existed. They might even hate each other. The creature already loathed his own ugliness — might he not feel even greater revulsion seeing it mirrored in a female form? She might also reject him and be drawn to the superior beauty of humans. She might leave him, and he'd be alone again — enraged by the fresh provocation of being abandoned by one of his own kind.

Even if they left Europe and lived in the wilderness, one of the first results of the companionship the creature craved would be children. A race of monsters might be unleashed upon the earth, making the very existence of the human species precarious and terrifying. Did I have the right, for my own benefit, to inflict this curse on all future generations? I'd been swayed by the creature's clever arguments. I'd been paralyzed by his threats. But now, for the first time, the wickedness of my promise struck me with full force. I shuddered to think that future ages might curse me as their plague — someone whose selfishness had bought his own peace at the price of the entire human race's survival.

I trembled. My courage failed. Looking up, I saw by moonlight the creature's face at the window. A ghastly grin twisted his lips as he watched me working at the task he'd assigned. Yes — he had followed me on my travels. He'd lurked in forests, hidden in caves, and camped on empty moors. Now he'd come to check my progress and claim the fulfillment of my promise.

As I looked at him — his face expressing the most extreme malice and treachery — I thought with something like madness of my promise to create another like him. Trembling with passion, I tore to pieces the thing I'd been working on. The creature saw me destroy the being on whose future existence his happiness depended. With a howl of devilish despair and revenge, he withdrew.

I left the room, locked the door, and made a solemn vow in my heart never to resume this work. Then, with trembling steps, I made my way to my own room. I was alone. No one was near to ease the gloom or free me from my terrible thoughts.

Several hours passed. I stood near my window, gazing at the sea. It was almost motionless. The wind had died. All nature rested under the quiet moon's gaze. A few fishing boats dotted the water. Now and then a gentle breeze carried the sound of fishermen calling to each other. I felt the silence without being fully conscious of how deep it was — until suddenly my ear caught the sound of oars paddling near the shore and someone landing close to my house.

A few minutes later, I heard the creak of my door, as if someone were trying to open it quietly. I trembled from head to foot. I sensed who it was and wanted to rouse one of the peasants living in a nearby cottage. But I was paralyzed — gripped by that helplessness you feel in nightmares when you try to flee from danger and cannot move.
Soon I heard footsteps in the passage. The door opened. The creature I dreaded appeared. Closing the door, he approached me and said in a muffled voice,

"You've destroyed the work you began. What do you intend? Do you dare break your promise? I've endured suffering and misery. I left Switzerland with you. I crept along the banks of the Rhine, through its willow islands and over the summits of its hills. I've lived for months on the moors of England and in the wilds of Scotland. I've endured unimaginable exhaustion, cold, and hunger. Do you dare destroy my hopes?"
"Go away! I am breaking my promise. I will never create another like you — equal in ugliness and evil."

"Slave! I tried to reason with you before, but you've proven yourself unworthy of my patience. Remember that I have power. You think yourself miserable, but I can make you so wretched that the light of day will be hateful to you. You are my creator, but I am your master. Obey!"

"My time of hesitation is over. Your power has reached its end. Your threats can't force me to commit evil. They only confirm my decision not to create you a companion in wickedness. Shall I deliberately unleash another demon upon the earth, one whose pleasure is death and destruction? Get out! I am firm. Your words will only increase my rage."

The monster saw my resolve in my face and gnashed his teeth with helpless anger. "Shall every man," he cried, "find a wife, and every animal have its mate, while I remain alone? I had feelings of love and tenderness, and they were met with hatred and scorn. Man! You may hate me, but beware! Your hours will be spent in dread and misery. Soon the blow will fall that will destroy your happiness forever. Are you to be happy while I suffer in the depths of wretchedness? You can crush my other passions, but revenge remains — revenge, now dearer to me than light or food! I may die, but first you, my tyrant and tormentor, shall curse the sun that shines on your misery. Be warned, for I am fearless and therefore powerful. I'll watch with the cunning of a snake, ready to strike with its venom. Man, you shall pay for the wrongs you inflict."
"Devil, stop! Don't poison the air with your malice. I've stated my decision, and I'm no coward to back down before words. Leave me. I won't be moved."
"Very well. I go. But remember — I shall be with you on your wedding night."
I lunged forward and cried, "Villain! Before you sign my death warrant, make sure you are yourself safe."
I would have seized him, but he dodged me and fled the house. Moments later I saw him in his boat, which shot across the water with the speed of an arrow and was soon lost among the waves.

Everything was silent again, but his words rang in my ears. I burned with rage. I wanted to chase the murderer of my peace and hurl him into the ocean. I paced my room, wild and agitated, while my imagination conjured a thousand tormenting images. Why hadn't I followed him and fought him to the death? But I had let him go, and he was heading toward the mainland. I shuddered to think who might be his next victim. Then I thought again of his words: "_I will be with you on your wedding night._" That, then, was when my fate would be sealed. On that night I would die, satisfying and ending his hatred. The prospect didn't frighten me. But when I thought of my beloved Elizabeth — her tears and endless grief when she found her lover so brutally taken from her — tears came to my eyes, the first I'd shed in months. I resolved not to fall before my enemy without a bitter fight.

The night passed. The sun rose from the ocean. My feelings became calmer — if you can call it calm when the violence of rage sinks into the depths of despair. I left the house, the scene of last night's confrontation, and walked on the beach. I almost saw the sea as an impassable barrier between me and civilization — and part of me wished it were true. I wanted to spend the rest of my life on that barren rock, wearily but undisturbed by sudden shocks of tragedy. If I went back, I would either be killed or watch those I loved most die at the hands of a creature I myself had made.

I walked the island like a restless ghost, cut off from everything I loved and wretched in the separation. When noon came and the sun climbed higher, I lay down on the grass and was overcome by deep sleep. I'd been awake all the previous night. My nerves were strained. My eyes were inflamed from stress and sleeplessness. The sleep refreshed me. When I woke, I felt almost human again and began to reflect on what had happened with more composure. Yet the creature's words still echoed like a death knell — vivid and oppressive as reality.

The sun had descended far when I still sat on the shore, eating an oat cake to satisfy my ravenous hunger. Then I saw a fishing boat land nearby. One of the men brought me a packet of letters from Geneva, along with one from Clerval begging me to join him. He said he was wasting his time where he was. Letters from friends he'd made in London asked him to return to complete negotiations for his India venture. He couldn't delay his departure any longer. Since his London trip might soon be followed by the longer voyage to India, he begged me to spend as much time with him as I could spare. He asked me to leave my solitary island and meet him at Perth so we could travel south together. This letter partly recalled me to life. I decided to leave the island in two days.

But before I left, there was one task I dreaded: I had to pack up my chemical instruments, which meant entering the room where I'd done my hideous work and handling equipment that sickened me. The next morning at dawn, I summoned enough courage and unlocked the laboratory door. The remains of the half-finished creature lay scattered on the floor. I almost felt as if I'd dismembered a living human being. I paused to collect myself, then entered. With trembling hands I carried the instruments out. But I realized I shouldn't leave the remains behind to horrify the islanders and arouse suspicion. I put them in a basket with a large quantity of stones. I planned to throw the basket into the sea that night. Meanwhile, I sat on the beach, cleaning and arranging my chemical equipment.

Nothing could be more complete than the change in my feelings since the creature's appearance at the window. Before, I'd viewed my promise with gloomy despair as something that must be fulfilled no matter what. Now I felt as if a veil had been lifted from my eyes. I could see clearly for the first time. The idea of resuming my work didn't even cross my mind. The threat I'd heard weighed on me, but I didn't consider that any voluntary act of mine could prevent it. I'd decided in my own heart that creating another creature like the first would be the most cowardly, despicable act of selfishness imaginable. I banished from my mind every thought that might lead to a different conclusion.

Between two and three in the morning, the moon rose. I put my basket in a small boat and sailed out about four miles from shore. The scene was perfectly solitary. A few boats were heading toward land, but I sailed away from them. I felt as if I were about to commit a terrible crime and shrank from encountering anyone. When the moon, which had been clear, was suddenly covered by a thick cloud, I seized the moment of darkness and dropped my basket into the sea. I listened to the gurgling sound as it sank, then sailed away. The sky clouded over, but the air was pure though chilled by a rising northeast wind. It refreshed me and filled me with surprisingly pleasant feelings. I decided to extend my time on the water. Fixing the rudder in a straight position, I stretched out at the bottom of the boat. Clouds hid the moon. Everything was dark. I heard only the sound of the keel cutting through water. The murmur lulled me, and soon I was deeply asleep.

I don't know how long I slept, but when I woke, the sun was already high. The wind was strong. Waves threatened my little boat's safety. I tried to change course but quickly found that doing so would swamp the boat. My only option was to run before the wind. I confess I felt a flash of terror. I had no compass. I knew so little of this region's geography that the sun was useless to me. I might be driven into the open Atlantic and face starvation, or be swallowed by the enormous waves roaring around me. I'd been adrift for many hours already. I felt the torment of burning thirst — a preview of worse suffering to come. I looked up at the sky, covered by clouds racing before the wind. I looked at the sea. It would be my grave. "Fiend," I cried, "your task is already done!" I thought of Elizabeth, of my father, of Clerval — all left behind, all at the monster's mercy. This thought plunged me into such despairing, frightful imagination that even now, as the scene is about to close before me forever, I shudder to think of it.

Hours passed. But gradually, as the sun descended, the wind dropped to a gentle breeze and the sea grew calmer. Heavy swells replaced the breakers. I felt seasick and could barely hold the rudder — when suddenly I saw a line of high land to the south.
Nearly spent with exhaustion and the terrible suspense of the last several hours, this sudden certainty of survival rushed to my heart like a flood of warm joy. Tears streamed from my eyes.

How changeable our feelings are! And how strange is our clinging love of life, even in the worst misery! I made another sail from part of my clothing and eagerly steered toward land. It looked wild and rocky, but as I drew closer, I could see signs of farming. I spotted boats near the shore and found myself suddenly back in the world of civilization. I carefully followed the coastline and spotted a church steeple rising from behind a small headland. Since I was in a state of extreme weakness, I headed straight for the town as the likeliest place to find food. Fortunately, I had money with me. As I rounded the headland, I saw a small, tidy town with a good harbor, which I entered, my heart leaping with joy at my unexpected escape.

While I was busy securing my boat and arranging the sail, several people gathered around me. They seemed very surprised by my appearance. Instead of offering help, they whispered together with gestures that might have alarmed me under other circumstances. As it was, I merely noticed they spoke English and addressed them in that language. "My good friends," I said, "would you kindly tell me the name of this town and where I am?"
"You'll know that soon enough," replied a man with a harsh voice. "Maybe you've come to a place that won't be to your liking. But you won't be asked about your lodgings, I promise you."
I was extremely surprised by this rude answer. "Why do you speak to me so roughly?" I replied. "Surely it's not the English custom to receive strangers so inhospitably."
"I don't know about the English custom," said the man, "but it's the Irish custom to hate villains."

As this strange exchange continued, the crowd grew rapidly. Their faces showed a mix of curiosity and anger that annoyed and somewhat alarmed me. I asked for directions to the inn, but no one answered. I moved forward. A murmur rose from the crowd as they followed and surrounded me. Then a rough-looking man tapped me on the shoulder and said, "Come, sir. You must follow me to Mr. Kirwin's to give an account of yourself."
"Who is Mr. Kirwin? Why must I give an account of myself? Isn't this a free country?"
"Aye, sir — free enough for honest folk. Mr. Kirwin is the magistrate. You're to give an account of the death of a gentleman who was found murdered here last night."

This answer startled me, but I quickly recovered. I was innocent. That could easily be proved. So I followed my escort in silence and was led to one of the best houses in town. I was ready to collapse from exhaustion and hunger. But surrounded by a crowd, I thought it wise to summon all my strength, so that physical weakness wouldn't be mistaken for guilt or fear. Little did I know that within minutes, a catastrophe would overwhelm me and destroy all fear of shame or death.
I must pause here. It takes all my strength to recall the terrible events I'm about to describe.

chapters.title: Chapter 21
paragraphs: I was soon brought before the magistrate, an old, kind-faced man with calm, gentle manners. He looked at me with some severity, then turned to my escorts and asked who was testifying.

About half a dozen men came forward. One, selected by the magistrate, testified that he'd been out fishing the previous night with his son and brother-in-law, Daniel Nugent. Around ten o'clock, a strong north wind rose and they headed for port. It was very dark — the moon hadn't risen yet. They didn't land at the harbor but at a creek about two miles south, as they usually did. He walked ahead carrying fishing gear, with his companions following at a distance. Walking along the sand, he tripped over something and fell flat. His companions ran to help. By lantern light they found he'd fallen on the body of a man who appeared to be dead. Their first thought was that it was a drowning victim washed ashore. But on examination they found the clothes weren't wet and the body wasn't yet cold. They carried it to a nearby old woman's cottage and tried, without success, to revive the man. He appeared to be a handsome young man of about twenty-five. He'd apparently been strangled — there was no sign of violence except the black marks of fingers on his neck.

The first part of this testimony didn't interest me at all. But when the finger marks were mentioned, I remembered my brother's murder. I became extremely agitated. My limbs trembled. A mist came over my eyes. I had to lean on a chair for support. The magistrate watched me with a sharp eye and drew an unfavorable conclusion from my reaction.

The son confirmed his father's account. But when Daniel Nugent was called, he swore that just before his companion's fall, he had seen a boat with a single man in it, a short distance from shore. As far as he could judge by the faint starlight, it was the same boat in which I had just landed.

A woman testified that she lived near the beach and had been standing at her cottage door, waiting for the fishermen, about an hour before the body was found. She had seen a boat with only one man push off from the very part of the shore where the corpse was later discovered.
Another woman confirmed that the fishermen had brought the body to her house. It wasn't cold. They put it in bed and rubbed it. Daniel went to town for a doctor, but life was completely gone.

Several other men testified about my landing. They agreed that, given the strong north wind during the night, I had probably been blown around for many hours and forced to return near the spot where I'd started. Besides, they noted, it appeared I'd brought the body from somewhere else. Since I obviously didn't know the shore, I might have put into the harbor not realizing how far the town was from where I'd left the corpse.

Mr. Kirwin, hearing this evidence, ordered that I be taken to the room where the body lay, to observe how seeing it would affect me. This was probably prompted by the extreme agitation I'd shown when the strangling was described. I was led by the magistrate and several others to the inn. I couldn't help noticing the strange coincidences of this eventful night. But knowing I'd been talking with several people on my island around the time the body was found, I was perfectly calm about the outcome.

I entered the room and was led to the coffin. How can I describe my feelings when I saw it? I still feel parched with horror. I can't think of that terrible moment without shuddering in agony. The examination, the magistrate, the witnesses — all passed like a dream from my memory when I saw the lifeless body of Henry Clerval stretched before me. I gasped for breath. Throwing myself on the body, I cried, "Have my murderous schemes robbed you too of life, my dearest Henry? Two I've already destroyed. Other victims await their fate. But you, Clerval, my friend, my benefactor —"
My body could bear no more. I was carried from the room in violent convulsions.

A fever followed. I lay for two months at the point of death. My ravings, as I later heard, were terrifying. I called myself the murderer of William, of Justine, and of Clerval. Sometimes I begged my attendants to help me destroy the monster that tormented me. Other times I felt the creature's fingers already closing around my throat and screamed with agony and terror. Fortunately, since I spoke my native language, only Mr. Kirwin understood my words. But my gestures and bitter cries were enough to frighten the other witnesses.

Why didn't I die? More miserable than any person before me, why didn't I sink into oblivion and rest? Death snatches away blooming children, the only hope of their parents. Lovers are one day in the bloom of health and the next day food for worms. What was I made of that I could withstand so many blows — each one renewing the torture like a wheel constantly turning?

But I was doomed to live. After two months I woke as if from a dream, in a prison cell, lying on a wretched bed, surrounded by jailers and bolts and all the miserable trappings of a dungeon. It was morning when I came to my senses. I'd forgotten the details of what had happened and only felt as if some great catastrophe had overwhelmed me. When I looked around and saw the barred windows and the filthy cell, everything came flooding back. I groaned bitterly.

The sound disturbed an old woman sleeping in a chair beside me. She was a hired nurse, the wife of one of the guards. Her face was hard and coarse — the face of someone accustomed to witnessing suffering without feeling it. Her tone expressed complete indifference. She spoke to me in English, and her voice sounded like one I'd heard during my illness.
"Are you feeling better now, sir?" she said.
I replied weakly, "I think so. But if everything that happened was real and not a dream, I'm sorry I'm still alive to feel this misery and horror."

"As for that," the old woman replied, "if you mean about the gentleman you murdered, I think it would be better for you if you were dead. It'll go hard with you, I expect! But that's none of my business. I'm here to nurse you and get you well. I do my duty with a clear conscience. It would be good if everyone did the same."

I turned away from this woman in disgust. But I felt weak and unable to reflect on everything that had happened. My whole life seemed like a dream. I sometimes doubted whether any of it was real, because it never presented itself to my mind with the force of reality.

As the images floating before me became clearer, I grew feverish. Darkness closed around me. No one was near to soothe me with a gentle voice of love. No dear hand supported me. The doctor came and prescribed medicines. The old woman prepared them. But the doctor showed utter carelessness, and the woman's face was marked by cruelty. Who would care about the fate of a murderer except the hangman who would earn his fee?

These were my first thoughts. But I soon learned that Mr. Kirwin had shown me great kindness. He'd arranged the best room in the prison for me — wretched as the best was — and provided a doctor and a nurse. He seldom came to see me himself. Though he deeply wanted to relieve every human being's suffering, he didn't wish to witness the agonies and delirious ravings of a supposed murderer. He came occasionally to check that I wasn't being neglected, but his visits were brief and infrequent.

One day, while I was slowly recovering, I sat in a chair, my eyes half-open, my cheeks pale as death. I was overwhelmed by gloom and misery. I often thought it would be better to seek death than to remain in a world so full of suffering. At one point I considered confessing my guilt and accepting the punishment of the law — though I was less innocent than poor Justine had been. While I was lost in these thoughts, the door opened and Mr. Kirwin entered. His face expressed sympathy and compassion. He drew a chair close to mine and addressed me in French:
"I'm afraid this place is very distressing to you. Can I do anything to make you more comfortable?"
"Thank you, but nothing you mention means anything to me. There is no comfort on this entire earth that I'm capable of receiving."

"I know that a stranger's sympathy can be little comfort to someone burdened by such strange misfortune. But I hope you'll soon leave this sad place. Evidence can surely be found to clear you of the criminal charge."
"That's the least of my concerns. Through a series of strange events, I've become the most miserable person alive. Persecuted and tortured as I am and have been, can death hold any terror for me?"

"Nothing indeed could be more unfortunate than the strange chances that have recently befallen you. You were thrown, by some astonishing accident, onto this shore — famous for its hospitality — immediately arrested and charged with murder. The first thing you saw was the body of your friend, murdered in the most incomprehensible way and placed, as it were by some demon, directly in your path."

As Mr. Kirwin said this, despite the agitation his words caused me, I was also surprised by how much he seemed to know about me. Some astonishment must have shown on my face, because he quickly added:

"As soon as you fell ill, all the papers on your person were brought to me. I examined them to find some way of notifying your family. I found several letters, including one that was clearly from your father. I wrote to Geneva immediately. Nearly two months have passed since I sent that letter. But you're ill. Even now you're trembling. You're not fit for any kind of stress."
"This uncertainty is a thousand times worse than the most horrible event. Tell me — what new scene of death has occurred? Whose murder must I now mourn?"
"Your family is perfectly well," said Mr. Kirwin gently. "And someone — a friend — has come to see you."

I don't know what chain of thought led me to this conclusion, but I was instantly convinced that the murderer had come to mock my misery and taunt me with Clerval's death as a new incentive to comply with his hellish demands. I put my hand over my eyes and cried out in agony,
"Oh! Take him away! I can't see him! For God's sake, don't let him in!"
Mr. Kirwin looked at me with concern. He clearly took my outburst as evidence of guilt and said in a rather stern tone:
"I would have thought, young man, that the presence of your father would be welcome, not inspire such violent horror."
"My father!" I cried. Every feature and muscle relaxed from anguish to joy. "Is my father really here? How kind! How incredibly kind! But where is he? Why doesn't he come to me?"

My sudden change of mood surprised and pleased the magistrate. Perhaps he thought my earlier outburst was a momentary return of delirium. He recovered his former kindness. He rose and left the room with my nurse. A moment later, my father entered.
Nothing at that moment could have given me greater pleasure. I reached out my hand and cried,
"Are you safe? And Elizabeth — and Ernest?"

My father calmed me with assurances of their well-being and tried to raise my spirits by dwelling on these subjects so dear to my heart. But he soon realized that a prison cannot be a place of cheerfulness. "What a place you're living in, my son!" he said, looking sadly at the barred windows and wretched room. "You traveled to seek happiness, but a curse seems to follow you. And poor Clerval —"
The name of my unfortunate, murdered friend was too much for my weakened state. I wept.
"Alas! Yes, my father," I replied. "Some terrible destiny hangs over me. I must live to fulfill it — otherwise I surely would have died on Henry's coffin."

We weren't allowed to talk for long. My fragile health demanded that every precaution be taken to ensure rest. Mr. Kirwin came in and insisted that my strength should not be exhausted by too much exertion. But my father's presence was to me like that of my good angel, and I gradually recovered my health.

As my sickness left me, I was consumed by a gloomy, black melancholy that nothing could shake. The image of Clerval — ghastly and murdered — was forever before me. More than once, the agitation these thoughts caused made my friends fear a dangerous relapse. Alas! Why did they save so miserable and despised a life? It was surely so that I might fulfill my destiny, which is now drawing to its close. Soon — oh, very soon — death will silence these tormented thoughts and free me from the crushing weight of anguish. Then the appearance of death seemed distant, though I constantly wished for it. I often sat for hours, motionless and speechless, wishing for some great upheaval that would bury me and my destroyer in its ruins.

The season of the court sessions approached. I'd been in prison three months. Though still weak and in constant danger of relapse, I was forced to travel nearly a hundred miles to the county seat where the trial was held. Mr. Kirwin took charge of gathering witnesses and preparing my defense. I was spared the disgrace of a public criminal trial — the case wasn't brought before the court that decides life and death. The grand jury dismissed the charges when it was proved that I was on the Orkney Islands at the hour my friend's body was found. Two weeks after being moved, I was released.

My father was overjoyed to find me freed from criminal charges, allowed to breathe fresh air again and return home. I didn't share his relief. To me, the walls of a dungeon or a palace were equally hateful. The cup of life was poisoned forever. Though the sun shone on me as it did on the happy, I saw nothing around me but dense, frightening darkness — pierced only by the glimmer of two eyes that stared at me. Sometimes they were the fading eyes of Henry, nearly closed by death, framed by long dark lashes. Sometimes they were the watery, clouded eyes of the monster, as I'd first seen them in my room at Ingolstadt.

My father tried to awaken feelings of affection in me. He spoke of Geneva, which I would soon visit, of Elizabeth and Ernest. But these words only drew deep groans from me. Sometimes I felt a flicker of desire for happiness — a melancholy delight in thoughts of my beloved cousin, or a painful longing to see the blue lake and swift Rhone that had been so dear to me in childhood. But my general state was a numbness in which a prison felt as welcome as the most divine natural scene. These fits were rarely broken except by spasms of anguish and despair. In those moments I often tried to end my life. It took constant watching to keep me from some violent act.

Yet one duty remained, and its memory finally overcame my selfish despair. I had to return to Geneva without delay to watch over those I loved, to lie in wait for the murderer, and — if chance ever led me to him, or if he dared show his face again — to destroy him with unfailing aim. My father wanted to delay our departure, fearing I couldn't endure the journey. I was a shattered wreck, the shadow of a human being. My strength was gone. I was a skeleton. Fever preyed on my wasted body day and night.

Still, I urged our departure from Ireland with such desperate impatience that my father thought it best to agree. We booked passage on a ship bound for Le Havre and sailed with a fair wind from the Irish shores. It was midnight. I lay on deck, looking at the stars and listening to the waves. I welcomed the darkness that hid Ireland from my sight. My pulse beat with feverish joy at the thought that I would soon see Geneva. The past seemed like a terrible dream. Yet the ship carrying me, the wind blowing me from that hated shore, and the sea surrounding me — all confirmed that I was not deceived by a vision, that Clerval, my friend and dearest companion, had fallen victim to me and the monster of my creation. I replayed my whole life in memory: my quiet happiness with my family in Geneva, my mother's death, my departure for Ingolstadt. I remembered, shuddering, the mad enthusiasm that drove me to create my hideous enemy, and I recalled the night he first lived. I couldn't pursue the chain of thought. A thousand feelings pressed on me, and I wept bitterly.

Since my recovery from the fever, I'd been taking a small dose of laudanum every night — the only way I could get the rest necessary to stay alive. Oppressed by the memory of my misfortunes, I now swallowed double my usual dose and soon fell into deep sleep. But sleep brought no relief from thought and misery. Nightmares presented a thousand terrifying images. Toward morning I was seized by a kind of nightmare. I felt the creature's grip on my neck and couldn't break free. Groans and cries rang in my ears. My father, who was watching over me, perceived my restlessness and woke me. The crashing waves surrounded us. The cloudy sky was above. The creature was not here. A sense of security — a feeling that a temporary truce existed between the present moment and the inevitable, catastrophic future — gave me a kind of calm forgetfulness that the human mind is uniquely capable of.

chapters.title: Chapter 22
paragraphs: The voyage ended. We landed and traveled to Paris. I soon realized I'd pushed myself too hard and needed to rest before continuing. My father's care was tireless, but he didn't know the cause of my suffering and tried the wrong remedies. He wanted me to find comfort in society. I couldn't bear the sight of other people. Oh, not because I hated them! They were my brothers and sisters, my fellow beings. I felt drawn even to the most unpleasant among them as if to angelic creatures. But I felt I had no right to share their company. I had unleashed an enemy among them whose pleasure was shedding their blood. If they knew of my unholy acts and the crimes that originated with me, they would all despise me and hunt me down.

My father eventually gave in to my desire to avoid people and tried by various arguments to banish my despair. Sometimes he thought I was deeply shamed by the murder charge and tried to prove that pride was foolish.

"Alas, my father," I said, "how little you know me. Human beings would indeed be degraded if a wretch like me felt pride. Justine, poor unhappy Justine, was as innocent as I am, and she was charged with the same crime. She died for it. And I am the cause of this — I murdered her. William, Justine, and Henry — they all died by my hand."

My father had often heard me make the same claim during my imprisonment. Sometimes he seemed to want an explanation. Other times he took it as the product of delirium — an idea that had lodged in my brain during my illness and persisted into recovery. I avoided explaining and maintained complete silence about the creature I'd created. I was convinced that I would be thought insane, and that alone would have sealed my lips. Beyond that, I couldn't bring myself to share a secret that would fill the listener with horror and make fear and revulsion the permanent inhabitants of his heart. I suppressed my desperate thirst for sympathy and stayed silent when I would have given the world to confide my fatal secret. Yet words like those I've described would burst from me involuntarily. I couldn't explain them, but their partial truth lightened the burden of my mysterious grief.
On this occasion my father said, with unbounded wonder, "My dearest Victor, what madness is this? My dear son, I beg you never to say such a thing again."

"I'm not mad," I cried with force. "The sun and the heavens, which witnessed my work, can testify that I speak the truth. I am the murderer of those most innocent victims. They died because of my schemes. A thousand times I would have shed every drop of my own blood to save their lives. But I couldn't, my father — I truly couldn't sacrifice the entire human race."

The end of this speech convinced my father that my mind was disturbed. He immediately changed the subject and tried to redirect my thoughts. He wanted to erase the memory of Ireland and never mentioned it or let me speak of my misfortunes.

As time passed, I grew calmer. Misery still lived in my heart, but I no longer spoke incoherently about my own crimes. The awareness of them was enough. Through extreme self-control, I silenced the desperate voice of wretchedness that sometimes wanted to announce itself to the whole world. My manner became calmer and more composed than at any time since my journey to the sea of ice.
A few days before we left Paris for Switzerland, I received this letter from Elizabeth:
"My dear Friend,

"It gave me the greatest pleasure to receive a letter from my uncle dated from Paris. You're no longer at such a frightening distance. I may hope to see you in less than two weeks. My poor cousin, how much you must have suffered! I expect to find you looking even worse than when you left Geneva. This winter has been utterly miserable for me, tortured by anxious suspense. Yet I hope to see peace in your face and to find that your heart is not completely empty of comfort and calm.

"But I fear the same feelings that made you so miserable a year ago may still exist — perhaps even stronger now. I wouldn't disturb you at this difficult time, when so many misfortunes weigh on you. But a conversation I had with my uncle before his departure makes some explanation necessary before we meet.

"Explanation! You may be thinking, what could Elizabeth possibly need to explain? If that's genuinely your reaction, my questions are answered and all my doubts are resolved. But you're far away, and you might dread this explanation — yet also be relieved by it. Given that possibility, I dare not delay writing what I've often wanted to say during your absence but never had the courage to begin.

"You know, Victor, that our marriage has been our parents' favorite plan since we were children. We were told this when we were young and taught to look forward to it as inevitable. We were affectionate playmates as children and, I believe, dear and valued friends as we grew older. But just as a brother and sister may feel deep love without wanting a closer bond, might the same be true for us? Tell me, dearest Victor. Answer me honestly, for the sake of our mutual happiness — do you love someone else?

"You've traveled. You spent years at Ingolstadt. I confess, my friend, that when I saw you last autumn — so unhappy, fleeing from every human being into solitude — I couldn't help thinking you might regret our engagement and feel bound by honor to fulfill your parents' wishes against your own heart. But that's wrong reasoning. I confess that I love you and that in my dreams of the future, you've been my constant friend and companion. But it's your happiness I want as much as my own. Our marriage would make me eternally miserable if it weren't your own free choice. Even now I weep to think that you, crushed as you are by the cruelest misfortunes, might force yourself — out of a sense of duty — to give up the love and happiness that could restore you. Ah, Victor! Know that your cousin and lifelong friend loves you too sincerely to be anything but miserable at such a thought. Be happy, my friend. If you honor this one request, nothing on earth will ever disturb my peace.

"Don't let this letter upset you. Don't answer tomorrow, or the next day, or even until you come, if writing would cause you pain. My uncle will keep me informed of your health. If I see even one smile on your lips when we meet — caused by this letter or anything else I do — I'll need no other happiness.
"Elizabeth Lavenza.
"Geneva, May 18th, 17—"

This letter revived in my memory what I'd forgotten: the creature's threat — "_I will be with you on your wedding night!_" That was my sentence. On that night the monster would complete his crimes with my death. So be it. A deadly struggle would take place. If he won, I'd be at peace and his power over me would end. If I won, I'd be a free man. Alas! What freedom? The kind a peasant has when his family has been slaughtered before his eyes, his cottage burned, his land destroyed — homeless, penniless, and alone, but free. Such would be my liberty, except that in Elizabeth I still possessed a treasure — weighed against the remorse and guilt that would haunt me until death.

Sweet, beloved Elizabeth! I read and reread her letter. Tender feelings crept into my heart and dared to whisper dreams of love and joy. But the apple was already eaten, and the angel's sword was raised to drive me from all hope. Yet I would die to make her happy. If the monster kept his threat, death was certain. But then I considered whether my marriage might actually hasten my fate. My destruction might come a few months earlier. But if my tormentor suspected I was postponing the wedding because of his threats, he would surely find other, perhaps more terrible, means of revenge. He had sworn to be with me on my wedding night, yet he hadn't considered that pledge as keeping him peaceful in the meantime — he'd murdered Clerval right after making his threat. I resolved, therefore, that if marrying Elizabeth would bring happiness to her or my father, my enemy's plans for my life wouldn't delay it by a single hour.

In this frame of mind I wrote to Elizabeth. My letter was calm and loving. "I fear, my beloved," I wrote, "that little happiness remains for us on earth. Yet everything I may one day enjoy is centered in you. Drive away your fears. To you alone I dedicate my life and my efforts at contentment. I have one secret, Elizabeth — a dreadful one. When I reveal it, you'll shudder with horror. Then, far from being surprised at my misery, you'll only wonder that I survived what I've endured. I'll confide this terrible tale the day after our wedding, for there must be perfect trust between us. But until then, I beg you — don't mention it or even hint at it. This I earnestly ask, and I know you'll agree."

About a week after Elizabeth's letter arrived, we returned to Geneva. The sweet girl welcomed me with warm affection, yet tears filled her eyes when she saw my wasted body and feverish cheeks. I saw a change in her too. She was thinner and had lost much of the heavenly vitality that had once charmed me. But her gentleness and compassionate looks made her a more fitting companion for someone as ruined and miserable as I was.

The peace I now enjoyed didn't last. Memory brought madness with it. When I thought of what had happened, real insanity possessed me. Sometimes I was wild with rage. Sometimes I was low and numb with despair. I neither spoke nor looked at anyone, but sat motionless, overwhelmed by the sheer mass of miseries crushing me.

Elizabeth alone could draw me from these fits. Her gentle voice would calm me when I was consumed by passion and reawaken my humanity when I sank into numbness. She wept with me and for me. When my reason returned, she would try to inspire resignation. Ah! Resignation is well enough for the innocent. But for the guilty, there is no peace. The agonies of remorse poison whatever comfort might be found in grief.
Soon after my arrival, my father spoke of my immediate marriage to Elizabeth. I said nothing.
"Do you have some other attachment?"
"None on earth. I love Elizabeth and look forward to our marriage with joy. Let the day be set. On that day I will dedicate myself, in life or death, to the happiness of my cousin."

"My dear Victor, don't speak that way. Heavy misfortunes have fallen on us. But let us cling closer to those who remain and give to the living the love we bore for those we've lost. Our circle will be small but bound tightly by affection and shared sorrow. And in time, when grief has softened, new and dear ones will be born to replace those so cruelly taken from us."

Such were my father's words. But the memory of the threat kept returning. You can hardly wonder that, given the creature's track record of bloody deeds, I almost considered him invincible. When he had pronounced the words "I shall be with you on your wedding night," I felt the threatened fate was inescapable. But death was no evil to me, as long as it was balanced by the loss of Elizabeth. So with a contented and even cheerful face, I agreed with my father that — if Elizabeth consented — the ceremony should take place in ten days. By doing so, I imagined I was sealing my fate.

Great God! If for one instant I had guessed the hellish intention of my fiendish enemy, I would have banished myself from my homeland forever and wandered the earth as a friendless outcast rather than consent to this wretched marriage. But as if possessed by magic powers, the monster had blinded me to his real plan. When I thought I was preparing only for my own death, I was actually hastening the death of a far more precious victim.

As the wedding date approached, whether from cowardice or some prophetic instinct, I felt my heart sink. But I hid my feelings behind a cheerful facade that brought smiles to my father's face, though it barely fooled Elizabeth's watchful eye. She looked forward to our marriage with quiet contentment, tinged with a small fear — imprinted by past misfortunes — that what now seemed certain happiness might dissolve like a dream, leaving nothing behind but deep, everlasting regret.

Preparations were made. Congratulatory visits were received. Everyone wore a smiling face. I locked up my anxiety as best I could and entered with apparent enthusiasm into my father's plans — though they might serve only as decorations for my tragedy. Through my father's efforts, part of Elizabeth's inheritance had been restored by the Austrian government. A small estate on the shores of Lake Como belonged to her. We agreed that immediately after the wedding, we would travel to Villa Lavenza and spend our first happy days beside that beautiful lake.

Meanwhile, I took every precaution to defend myself in case the creature attacked me openly. I carried pistols and a dagger at all times and was constantly on guard against trickery. These measures gave me some peace of mind. Indeed, as the date approached, the threat began to seem more like a delusion, unworthy of disturbing my peace. The happiness I expected from my marriage seemed more certain every day, and I heard it constantly discussed as an event nothing could prevent.

Elizabeth seemed happy. My outward calm helped soothe her mind. But on the day that was to fulfill my hopes and seal my destiny, she was melancholy. A foreboding of evil hung over her — perhaps she was also thinking of the dreadful secret I'd promised to reveal the next day. My father was overjoyed, and amid the bustle of preparations, he attributed his niece's sadness to nothing more than a bride's natural shyness.

After the ceremony, a large party gathered at my father's house. But we'd agreed that Elizabeth and I would travel by boat that night to Evian and continue our journey the next day. The day was beautiful. The wind was favorable. Everyone smiled on our wedding voyage.

Those were the last moments of my life during which I felt happiness. We moved swiftly across the lake. The sun was hot, but we were sheltered by a kind of canopy while we enjoyed the beauty of the scene. On one side we saw Mont Saleve, the pleasant banks of Montalegre, and in the distance, towering above all, beautiful Mont Blanc and its assembly of snowy peaks. On the other side we saw the mighty Jura, its dark face opposing any ambition that would leave its native country — an almost impassable barrier to any invader.

I took Elizabeth's hand. "You're sad, my love. Ah, if you knew what I've suffered and what I may still endure, you would try to let me enjoy the quiet and freedom from despair that this one day at least allows me."

"Be happy, my dear Victor," Elizabeth replied. "There's nothing to worry about, I hope. If a lively joy isn't visible on my face, my heart is content. Something whispers to me not to depend too much on the happiness that lies ahead, but I won't listen to such a dark voice. Look how fast we're moving, and how the clouds that sometimes hide and sometimes rise above Mont Blanc make this scene even more beautiful. Look too at the countless fish swimming in the clear water, where we can see every pebble on the bottom. What a perfect day! How happy and peaceful everything looks!"
Elizabeth tried to steer our thoughts away from anything sad. But her mood kept shifting. Joy would shine in her eyes for a moment, then give way to abstraction and daydreaming.

The sun sank lower. We passed the River Drance and saw its path through the gorges of the higher hills and the valleys of the lower ones. The Alps pressed closer to the lake. We approached the amphitheater of mountains that forms its eastern boundary. The spire of Evian gleamed through the surrounding woods, with mountain rising above mountain beyond it.

The wind, which had carried us along with wonderful speed, dropped to a light breeze at sunset. The soft air barely ruffled the water and caused a pleasant rustling among the trees as we approached the shore. It brought us the most delightful scent of flowers and hay. The sun sank below the horizon as we landed. As I touched the shore, I felt those cares and fears revive that would soon seize me and hold me forever.

chapters.title: Chapter 23
paragraphs: It was eight o'clock when we landed. We walked briefly along the shore, enjoying the fading light, then retired to the inn. We looked out at the lovely scene of water, woods, and mountains, growing dark yet still showing their black outlines.

The wind, which had died in the south, now rose violently from the west. The moon had reached its peak and was beginning to descend. Clouds swept across it faster than the flight of a hawk, dimming its rays. The lake reflected the turbulent sky, made even more restless by waves that were starting to build. A heavy rain suddenly descended.

I'd been calm during the day, but as soon as darkness hid the shapes of things, a thousand fears filled my mind. I was anxious and watchful. My right hand gripped a pistol hidden inside my coat. Every sound terrified me. But I resolved to sell my life dearly and not shrink from the fight until either my own life or my enemy's was ended.
Elizabeth watched my agitation in frightened silence. Then something in my glance communicated my terror to her. Trembling, she asked, "What's troubling you, my dear Victor? What are you afraid of?"
"Oh! Peace, peace, my love," I replied. "After tonight, all will be safe. But tonight is dreadful — truly dreadful."

I spent an hour in this state, then suddenly realized how terrifying the combat would be for my wife. I begged her to go to bed, planning not to join her until I'd learned something about my enemy's whereabouts.

She left me. I continued pacing the halls, inspecting every corner where the creature might hide. But I found no trace of him. I was beginning to think some lucky chance had prevented him from carrying out his threat — when I suddenly heard a shrill, terrible scream. It came from the room where Elizabeth had gone. As I heard it, the whole truth rushed into my mind. My arms dropped. Every muscle froze. I could feel blood trickling through my veins and tingling in my fingertips. This state lasted only an instant. The scream was repeated. I ran to the room.

Great God! Why didn't I die at that moment? Why am I here to describe the destruction of the best hope and purest creature on earth? She was there — lifeless and still — thrown across the bed, her head hanging down, her pale, twisted features half covered by her hair. Everywhere I look, I see the same image: her bloodless arms and limp body flung by the murderer onto the bridal bed. Could I see this and live? Alas! Life is stubborn. It clings tightest where it's most unwanted. For just a moment I lost consciousness and fell to the ground.

When I revived, I found myself surrounded by the inn's staff. Their faces showed breathless terror, but their horror seemed like a shadow, a mockery, compared to what I felt. I escaped from them to the room where Elizabeth's body lay — my love, my wife, so recently alive, so dear, so worthy. She'd been moved from the position I first saw her in. Now, as she lay with her head resting on her arm and a handkerchief across her face and neck, I might have thought her asleep. I rushed to her and embraced her passionately. But the deathly cold and stiffness of her limbs told me that what I held in my arms was no longer the Elizabeth I had loved and cherished. The murderer's fingermarks were on her neck. Her breath had stopped.

While I still hung over her in agony, I happened to look up. The windows had been darkened before. With a sense of horror I can't describe, I saw by the pale yellow moonlight flooding the room that the shutters had been thrown open. At the window stood a figure of the most hideous, loathsome kind. A grin was on the monster's face. He seemed to sneer as, with his fiendish finger, he pointed at my wife's corpse. I rushed to the window and drew a pistol from my coat. I fired. But he dodged me, leaped from the windowsill, and running with the speed of lightning, plunged into the lake.

The gunshot brought a crowd into the room. I pointed to the spot where he'd disappeared. We followed in boats. Nets were cast. But it was hopeless. After searching for several hours, we returned. Most of my companions believed the figure had been a product of my imagination.

I tried to go with the search parties, walking a short distance from the house. But my head spun. My steps were like a drunk man's. I finally collapsed in a state of complete exhaustion. A film covered my eyes. My skin burned with fever. In this condition I was carried back and put to bed, barely aware of what had happened. My eyes wandered around the room as if searching for something lost.

After a while I got up and, as if by instinct, crawled to the room where my beloved's body lay. Women were weeping around it. I hung over the body and joined my tears to theirs. No clear thought formed in my mind — just confused reflections on my misfortunes and their cause. I was bewildered, lost in a cloud of horror and wonder. The deaths of William, Justine, Clerval, and now my wife — even at that moment I didn't know whether my remaining family was safe from the creature's malice. My father might even now be writhing in his grasp. Ernest might be dead at his feet. This thought made me shudder and jolted me into action. I resolved to return to Geneva with all possible speed.

No horses could be found. I would have to cross the lake, but the wind was against us and rain poured in torrents. Still, it was barely morning. I could reasonably hope to arrive by nightfall. I hired rowers and took an oar myself — I had always found relief from mental anguish in physical effort. But the overwhelming grief I now felt made me incapable of any real exertion. I dropped the oar. Leaning my head on my hands, I gave way to every dark thought. If I looked up, I saw scenes that were familiar from my happier days — scenes I'd admired just yesterday in Elizabeth's company. Nothing is so painful as a great and sudden change. The sun might shine or clouds might gather, but nothing could look to me as it had the day before. A monster had snatched from me every hope of future happiness. No human being had ever been so miserable. This event stands alone in the history of human suffering.

But why should I dwell on what followed? Mine has been a tale of horrors. I've reached their peak. What I must now relate can only be tedious to you. Know that, one by one, my friends were torn from me. I was left utterly alone. My own strength is gone. I must tell what remains in a few words.

I reached Geneva. My father and Ernest were still alive. But my father collapsed under the news I brought. I see him now — that excellent, noble old man! His eyes wandered vacantly. They had lost their light — Elizabeth, his more than daughter, whom he loved with all the fierce devotion a man feels in the twilight of life, when few attachments remain and he clings all the more tightly to those that do. Cursed be the monster that brought misery to his gray hairs and doomed him to waste away in wretchedness! He couldn't bear the horrors accumulating around him. The springs of his life suddenly gave way. He couldn't rise from his bed. Within a few days, he died in my arms.

What became of me after that? I don't know. I lost all sensation. Chains and darkness were the only things I was aware of. Sometimes I dreamed of wandering through flowery meadows with the friends of my youth. But I always woke to find myself in a dungeon. Depression followed. Gradually I gained a clear understanding of my situation and was released from prison — for they had declared me mad, and for many months a solitary cell had been my home.

Freedom would have been a worthless gift if I hadn't also awakened to revenge. As memories of past horrors pressed on me, I began to think about their cause — the monster I had created, the wretched demon I had sent into the world to destroy me. A maddening rage consumed me whenever I thought of him. I prayed desperately for the chance to get my hands on him and unleash a great and final vengeance.

My hatred didn't confine itself to useless wishes for long. About a month after my release, I went to a criminal judge in the town. I told him I had an accusation to make — that I knew who had destroyed my family — and asked him to use his full authority to apprehend the murderer.
The magistrate listened with attention and kindness. "Be assured, sir," he said, "I will spare no effort to discover the villain."

"Thank you," I replied. "Listen, then, to the statement I have to make. It's a story so strange that I'd expect you not to believe it — if there weren't something in truth which, however incredible, compels conviction. The story is too coherent to be mistaken for a dream, and I have no reason to lie." My manner was controlled but impressive. I had formed in my heart a resolution to pursue my destroyer to the death. This purpose quieted my anguish and briefly reconciled me to life. I then told my story briefly but firmly, marking the dates accurately and never breaking into outrage or exclamation.

The magistrate seemed completely incredulous at first. But as I continued, he became more attentive and interested. I saw him sometimes shudder with horror. At other times, a lively surprise — not quite disbelief — appeared on his face.

When I'd finished, I said, "This is the being I accuse. I call upon you to use your full power to capture and punish him. It is your duty as a magistrate, and I trust your human feelings won't revolt at carrying it out."

This request caused a considerable change in the magistrate's expression. He'd been listening with the half-belief people give to tales of ghosts and the supernatural. But when called upon to take official action, his skepticism returned in full. He answered mildly, "I would gladly help you pursue this creature. But the being you describe seems to have powers that would defeat all my efforts. Who can chase an animal that crosses glaciers and hides in caves where no man would dare go? Besides, months have passed since his crimes. No one can guess where he's gone or where he might be now."

"I'm sure he's hovering near the spot where I live. If he has taken refuge in the Alps, he can be hunted like a mountain goat and killed like a beast of prey. But I can see what you're thinking. You don't believe my story and don't intend to pursue my enemy with the punishment he deserves."

As I spoke, rage flashed in my eyes. The magistrate was intimidated. "You're mistaken," he said. "I will do everything I can. If it's possible to catch the monster, I assure you he'll be punished according to his crimes. But from what you've described of his abilities, I fear it will prove impossible. And while every proper step is taken, you should prepare yourself for disappointment."

"That's unacceptable. But anything I say will be useless. My revenge means nothing to you. Yet while I admit it's a vice, I confess it's the consuming, sole passion of my soul. My rage is unspeakable when I think that the murderer I let loose still exists. You refuse my just demand. I have only one option. I devote myself — in life or in death — to his destruction."

I trembled with extreme agitation as I said this. There was a frenzy in my manner, and something of the fierce dignity that martyrs of old are said to have possessed. But to a Geneva magistrate, whose mind was occupied by far different concerns than devotion and heroism, this intensity of feeling looked very much like madness. He tried to soothe me the way a nurse calms a child and treated my story as the product of delirium.
"Man," I cried, "how ignorant you are in your pride of wisdom! Stop. You don't know what you're saying."
I stormed from the house, angry and frustrated, and went away to plan some other course of action.

chapters.title: Chapter 24
paragraphs: My situation was one in which all voluntary thought was swallowed up and lost. I was driven by fury. Revenge alone gave me strength and composure. It shaped my feelings and allowed me to be calculating and calm during periods when I would otherwise have collapsed into madness or death.

My first decision was to leave Geneva forever. My country, once dear to me when I was happy and loved, had become hateful in my misery. I took a sum of money and a few jewels that had belonged to my mother, and departed.

And now my wanderings began — wanderings that will end only with my life. I've crossed a vast portion of the earth and endured all the hardships that travelers in deserts and savage lands are forced to face. How I've survived, I hardly know. Many times I stretched my exhausted limbs on the sandy ground and prayed for death. But revenge kept me alive. I dared not die and leave my enemy still existing.

When I left Geneva, my first task was to find some clue that would lead me to my fiendish enemy. But my plan was uncertain, and I wandered for hours around the edges of the city, unsure which way to go. As night approached, I found myself at the entrance to the cemetery where William, Elizabeth, and my father were buried. I entered and approached their graves. Everything was silent except for the leaves stirred by the wind. The night was nearly dark. The scene would have been solemn and moving even to an uninvolved observer. The spirits of the dead seemed to hover around me, casting a shadow that was felt but not seen.

The deep grief this scene first stirred quickly gave way to rage and despair. They were dead, and I was alive. Their murderer also lived. To destroy him, I had to drag out my weary existence. I knelt on the grass, kissed the earth, and cried with trembling lips: "By the sacred ground on which I kneel, by the spirits that wander near me, by the deep and eternal grief I feel — I swear! And by you, O Night, and the powers that rule the darkness — I swear to pursue the monster who caused this misery until he or I die in mortal combat. For this purpose I will preserve my life. To carry out this revenge, I will endure the sun's light and walk the green earth, which would otherwise vanish from my sight forever. And I call upon you, spirits of the dead, and upon you, wandering agents of vengeance, to help and guide me in my task. Let the cursed, hellish monster drink deep of agony. Let him feel the despair that now torments me."
I had begun my oath with solemnity and awe — almost believing the shades of my murdered loved ones heard and approved. But frenzy took hold as I finished, and rage choked my words.

I was answered through the night's stillness by a loud, fiendish laugh. It echoed long and heavily. The mountains sent it back. I felt as if all hell surrounded me with mockery and laughter. Surely at that moment I would have gone mad and destroyed myself — but my vow had been heard, and I was saved for vengeance. The laughter died away. Then a familiar, despised voice, apparently right at my ear, whispered: "I am satisfied, miserable wretch! You have chosen to live, and I am satisfied."
I lunged toward the sound, but the devil escaped my grasp. Suddenly the broad disk of the moon rose and shone full upon his ghastly, distorted figure as he fled with more than human speed.

I chased him. For many months this has been my task. Guided by faint clues, I followed the course of the Rhone, but in vain. The blue Mediterranean appeared. By a strange coincidence, I saw the creature enter a ship bound for the Black Sea at night and hide himself aboard. I booked passage on the same vessel. But he escaped — I don't know how.

Across the wilds of Central Asia and Russia, though he still eluded me, I never stopped following. Sometimes the terrified peasants told me they'd seen him pass. Sometimes he himself — fearing that if I lost all trace of him I'd despair and die — left marks to guide me. The snows fell thick, and I saw the print of his enormous foot on the white plain. To you, just beginning life, for whom hardship is new and suffering unknown — how can you understand what I've felt and still feel? Cold, hunger, and exhaustion were the least of my pains. I was cursed by some devil and carried my eternal hell with me. Yet still, a spirit of good followed and directed my steps. When I complained most bitterly, it would suddenly rescue me from seemingly impossible difficulties. Sometimes, when nature overcame me with hunger, a meal would appear in the wilderness that restored my strength. The food was coarse — what local peasants ate — but I have no doubt it was placed there by the spirits I'd called upon for help. Often, when everything was dry and the sky cloudless and I was parched with thirst, a small cloud would appear, shed a few reviving drops, and vanish.

When I could, I followed rivers. But the creature generally avoided them, since populations clustered there. In emptier regions, I survived on wild animals I encountered. I had money and gained the friendship of villagers by sharing it. Or I brought some of the meat I'd killed, offering most of it to those who gave me fire and cooking utensils.

My life, as I lived it, was truly hateful. Only in sleep could I find joy. Oh, blessed sleep! In my deepest misery, I would fall into rest, and my dreams transported me to rapture. The guardian spirits had provided these moments — or rather hours — of happiness so I could keep up my strength for this pilgrimage. Without that rest, I would have collapsed. During the day, hope of the coming night sustained me. In sleep I saw my friends, my wife, my beloved country. Again I saw my father's kind face, heard Elizabeth's silver voice, and watched Clerval enjoying health and youth. Often, worn out by a grueling march, I convinced myself I was only dreaming until night came and I would find reality again in the arms of my dearest friends.
