What desperate tenderness I felt for them! How I clung to their dear forms when they sometimes visited even my waking hours, persuading myself they were still alive! In those moments, the vengeance burning within me would die. I pursued the creature's destruction more as a task assigned by heaven — the mechanical impulse of some force beyond my understanding — than as the burning desire of my soul.

What the creature I chased was feeling, I can't know. Sometimes he left messages carved into tree bark or cut into stone to guide me and fuel my fury. One inscription read: "My reign is not yet over" — "you live, and my power is complete. Follow me. I seek the everlasting ice of the north, where you will feel the misery of cold and frost to which I am immune. You will find near this place, if you follow quickly enough, a dead rabbit. Eat and be refreshed. Come, my enemy. We have yet to wrestle for our lives, but many hard and miserable hours must you endure before that time comes."

Mocking devil! Again I vowed vengeance. Again I swore to pursue him to torture and death. Never will I give up my search until he or I die. And then — with what joy shall I join Elizabeth and my departed friends, who even now prepare the reward for my long suffering and horrible pilgrimage!

As I continued northward, the snows grew thicker and the cold became almost unbearable. The peasants were shut in their huts. Only the hardiest ventured out to hunt the starving animals that had been driven from their hiding places. The rivers were frozen. No fish could be found. I was cut off from my main source of food.

The creature's triumph grew with my difficulties. One inscription read: "Prepare! Your suffering has only begun. Wrap yourself in furs and bring food, for we shall soon begin a journey where your suffering will satisfy my eternal hatred."

My courage and persistence were actually strengthened by these taunting words. I resolved not to falter. Calling on heaven for strength, I continued with undiminished determination across immense deserts until the ocean appeared at a distance, forming the uttermost boundary of the horizon. Oh! How different it was from the blue seas of the south! Covered with ice, it was distinguishable from land only by its superior wildness and ruggedness. The ancient Greeks wept for joy when they saw the Mediterranean from the hills of Asia, hailing the boundary of their suffering. I did not weep. But I knelt down and, with a full heart, thanked my guiding spirit for bringing me safely to the place where I hoped — despite my enemy's taunts — to confront and defeat him.

Some weeks earlier I'd acquired a sledge and dogs. I crossed the snows at incredible speed. I don't know whether the creature had the same advantage, but I found that where before I'd been falling behind, I was now gaining on him. When I first saw the ocean, he was only one day's journey ahead. I hoped to catch him before he reached the coast. With renewed courage I pressed on. In two days I arrived at a wretched coastal hamlet and inquired about the creature. I received accurate information. A gigantic monster, they said, had arrived the night before, armed with a gun and many pistols. He had terrified the inhabitants of a solitary cottage into fleeing. He'd seized their winter food supply, loaded it onto a sledge, harnessed a large pack of trained dogs, and — to the terrified villagers' relief — departed that same night across the frozen sea in a direction that led to no land. They guessed he would soon be destroyed by breaking ice or frozen to death.

Hearing this, I suffered a temporary collapse of despair. He'd escaped me. I would have to begin a devastating, nearly endless journey across the frozen ocean — through cold that few inhabitants could long endure and that I, born in a warm, mild climate, could not hope to survive. Yet at the thought that the creature might live and triumph, my rage and desire for vengeance returned like a mighty tide, overwhelming every other feeling. After a brief rest — during which the spirits of the dead seemed to hover around me, urging me onward to revenge — I prepared for my journey.
I exchanged my land sledge for one built for the rough terrain of the frozen ocean. Purchasing a generous supply of food, I left the land behind.

I can't guess how many days have passed since then. But I've endured suffering that nothing but the eternal fire of righteous vengeance burning in my heart could have sustained. Immense, jagged mountains of ice often blocked my way. I frequently heard the thunder of the sea shifting beneath me, threatening destruction. But the frost would return and make the ocean paths safe again.

Judging by the food I'd consumed, I'd guess about three weeks had passed. The constant deferral of hope, collapsing back on the heart, often wrung bitter drops of despair from my eyes. I had nearly succumbed to this misery. Once, after my poor dogs had struggled with incredible effort to the top of an icy ridge and one of them collapsed and died from exhaustion, I looked out over the vast expanse ahead with anguish. Then suddenly my eye caught a dark speck on the dusky plain. I strained to see what it was — and uttered a wild cry of joy when I recognized a sledge and the distorted shape of a well-known figure within. Oh! What a burning rush of hope flooded my heart! Warm tears filled my eyes. I quickly wiped them away to keep the creature in sight, but the burning drops blurred my vision. Giving in to the emotions overwhelming me, I wept aloud.

But this was no time for delay. I freed the dogs from their dead companion, gave them a generous portion of food, and after an hour's rest — absolutely necessary yet bitterly frustrating — I resumed my pursuit. The sledge was still visible. I never lost sight of it except when an ice ridge briefly blocked my view. I was clearly gaining ground. After nearly two days' travel, I saw my enemy no more than a mile away. My heart leaped.

But now, just when I seemed about to seize my prey, my hopes were suddenly and utterly extinguished. I lost all trace of him — more completely than ever before. A deep rumble sounded beneath the ice. The thunder of its movement as the water swelled and churned grew more ominous every second. I pressed on, but it was useless. The wind rose. The sea roared. With a tremendous, earth-shattering crack, the ice split apart. The destruction was swift. Within minutes, a churning sea rolled between me and my enemy. I was left drifting on a shrinking piece of ice, facing a hideous death.

Many terrible hours passed this way. Several of my dogs died. I myself was about to succumb when I saw your vessel riding at anchor, offering hope of rescue and life. I'd had no idea ships ventured this far north. I was stunned by the sight. I quickly broke apart my sledge to make oars, and with infinite effort managed to steer my ice raft toward your ship. If you'd been heading south, I would still have trusted myself to the sea rather than abandon my purpose. But you were heading north. You took me aboard when my strength was spent. I would soon have died — a death I still dread, for my task remains unfinished.

Oh! When will my guiding spirit finally lead me to the creature and allow me the rest I so desperately need? Must I die while he still lives? If I do — swear to me, Walton, that he shall not escape. Swear you'll seek him out and carry out my vengeance with his death. And dare I ask you to undertake my pilgrimage, to endure the hardships I've endured? No. I'm not that selfish. Yet when I'm dead, if he should appear — if the forces of vengeance bring him to you — swear that he shall not live. Swear he shall not triumph over my accumulated suffering and survive to add to his list of dark crimes. He is eloquent and persuasive. His words once had power even over my heart. But don't trust him. His soul is as hellish as his form — full of treachery and devilish malice. Don't listen to him. Call on the names of William, Justine, Clerval, Elizabeth, my father, and the wretched Victor. Then thrust your sword into his heart. I will hover near and guide the blade.
Walton, _in continuation._
August 26th, 17—.

You've read this strange and terrifying story, Margaret. Doesn't your blood run cold with horror, as mine does even now? Sometimes, seized by sudden agony, he couldn't continue. Other times his voice — broken but piercing — forced out words drenched in anguish. His fine eyes would blaze with outrage, then sink into sorrowful despair, then go dark with infinite wretchedness. Sometimes he controlled his expression and tone, relating the most horrible events with eerie calm. Then, like a volcano erupting, his face would twist into the wildest rage as he screamed curses at his tormentor.

His story is coherent and told with every appearance of simple truth. Yet I admit that the letters of Felix and Safie, which he showed me, and the sight of the monster from our ship convinced me more than his testimony alone, however earnest and consistent. Such a creature truly exists! I can't doubt it, yet I'm lost in astonishment. Sometimes I tried to get Frankenstein to tell me the details of how he created the being. But on this point he was immovable.

"Are you mad, my friend?" he said. "Where does your reckless curiosity lead? Would you also create a demonic enemy for yourself and the world? Peace, peace! Learn from my suffering and don't seek to increase your own."

Frankenstein discovered I'd been taking notes on his story. He asked to see them and then corrected and expanded them himself in many places — mainly bringing to life the conversations he'd had with his enemy. "Since you've preserved my narrative," he said, "I wouldn't want a corrupted version to go down to posterity."

A week has passed while I've listened to the strangest tale ever told. My thoughts and feelings have been consumed by interest in my guest — an interest created by his story and by his own noble, gentle manner. I wish I could comfort him. But can I counsel someone so infinitely miserable, so completely without hope, to live? Oh, no! The only joy he can know now will be when his shattered spirit finds peace in death. Yet he has one comfort, born of solitude and delirium: he believes that when he holds conversation with his friends in dreams, drawing consolation from their communion for his misery or fuel for his vengeance, they are not figments of his imagination but the actual beings themselves, visiting him from some remote world. This faith gives his visions a solemnity that makes them almost as powerful and interesting to me as truth.

Our conversations aren't always limited to his own history and misfortunes. On every subject of general knowledge, he shows extraordinary learning and a sharp, penetrating intelligence. His eloquence is powerful and moving. I can't listen to him describe a touching scene or appeal to the emotions of pity or love without shedding tears. What a magnificent person he must have been in his days of prosperity, when even now, in ruin, he is so noble and godlike! He seems to feel his own worth and the greatness of his fall.

"When I was younger," he said, "I believed myself destined for some great enterprise. My feelings were deep, but I had a coolness of judgment that suited me for brilliant achievements. This sense of my own worth sustained me when others would have been crushed, because I considered it wrong to throw away in useless grief talents that might benefit my fellow creatures. When I thought about what I'd accomplished — nothing less than creating a thinking, feeling being — I couldn't rank myself among ordinary dreamers. But this thought, which once lifted me, now only drives me deeper into despair. All my hopes and ambitions are nothing. Like the archangel who aspired to omnipotence, I am chained in an eternal hell. My imagination was vivid, yet my powers of analysis were intense. By combining these qualities, I conceived the idea and carried out the creation of a man. Even now I can't think without passion of my excitement while the work was still unfinished. I walked through heaven in my thoughts — now glorying in my powers, now burning with visions of what they would achieve. From childhood I was driven by high hopes and towering ambition. But how far I've fallen! Oh, my friend, if you had known me as I once was, you wouldn't recognize me in this state of degradation. Depression rarely visited me then. A great destiny seemed to carry me forward — until I fell, never to rise again."

Must I lose this admirable being? I've longed for a friend. I've searched for someone who would understand and love me. Here, on these empty seas, I've found such a person — but I fear I've gained him only to understand his value and lose him. I've tried to reconcile him to life, but he rejects the idea.

"Thank you, Walton," he said, "for your kind intentions toward such a miserable wretch. But when you speak of new connections and fresh affections, do you think anyone can replace those who are gone? Can any man be to me what Clerval was, or any woman another Elizabeth? Even where affection isn't based on particular excellence, childhood companions always have a certain power over our hearts that later friends can rarely match. They know our earliest nature, which — however it may be modified — is never erased. They can judge our actions with more certainty about our true motives. A brother or sister can never suspect the other of fraud unless early signs gave warning. But another friend, however close, may harbor suspicions despite himself. I enjoyed friends who were dear to me not just through habit but through their own merit. Wherever I am, Elizabeth's soothing voice and Clerval's conversation will be whispered in my ear forever. They are dead, and only one feeling could persuade me to preserve my life in such solitude. If I were engaged in some great undertaking of wide benefit to my fellow creatures, I could live to complete it. But that is not my destiny. I must pursue and destroy the being to whom I gave existence. Then my purpose on earth will be fulfilled, and I may die."
My beloved Sister,
September 2nd.

I write to you surrounded by danger, not knowing if I'll ever see dear England again or the dearer friends who live there. Mountains of ice surround us on all sides, leaving no escape and threatening at every moment to crush our vessel. The brave men I persuaded to join me look to me for help, but I have none to give. There is something terrifying in our situation, yet my courage and hope don't desert me. It's terrible, though, to realize that all these lives are endangered because of me. If we're lost, my reckless ambitions are to blame.

And what, Margaret, will you feel? You won't hear of my death. You'll wait anxiously for my return. Years will pass. Despair will visit you, yet hope will still torture you. Oh! My beloved sister, the thought of your expectations gradually dying is, in prospect, more terrible to me than my own death. But you have a husband and lovely children. You may be happy. Heaven bless you and make you so!

My unfortunate guest looks at me with the tenderest compassion. He tries to fill me with hope and speaks as if life were something he valued. He reminds me how often the same disasters have struck other navigators who attempted this sea. Despite myself, he fills me with cheerful expectations. Even the sailors feel the power of his eloquence. When he speaks, they no longer despair. He rouses their energy. While they hear his voice, they believe these vast mountains of ice are molehills that will vanish before the will of man. These feelings are temporary. Each day of delayed hope fills them with greater fear. I almost dread a mutiny caused by this despair.
September 5th.
A scene of extraordinary interest has just taken place. Though these papers may never reach you, I can't help recording it.

We're still surrounded by ice mountains, still in imminent danger of being crushed. The cold is extreme. Many of my unfortunate crew have already found their grave in this desolate place. Frankenstein has grown weaker every day. A feverish light still flickers in his eyes, but he's exhausted. When briefly roused to action, he quickly sinks back into apparent lifelessness.

I mentioned in my last letter my fear of a mutiny. This morning, while I was watching my friend's pale face — his eyes half closed, his limbs hanging limp — I was interrupted by half a dozen sailors who demanded entry to the cabin. They entered, and their leader addressed me. He said that he and his companions had been chosen by the rest of the crew to present a demand that, in justice, I could not refuse. We were trapped in ice and would probably never escape. But they feared that if the ice did break up and a passage opened, I would be reckless enough to continue the voyage and lead them into fresh dangers after they'd barely survived these. They demanded my solemn promise that if the ship was freed, I would immediately steer south.

This troubled me. I hadn't given up hope or even considered turning back if freed. I hesitated before answering. Then Frankenstein, who had been silent at first and seemed barely conscious, roused himself. His eyes sparkled. His cheeks flushed with momentary energy. Turning toward the men, he said,

"What do you mean? What are you demanding of your captain? Are you so easily turned from your purpose? Didn't you call this a glorious expedition? And why was it glorious? Not because the way was smooth and calm as a southern sea, but because it was full of dangers and terror — because at every turn your courage was to be tested and your bravery proven — because danger and death surrounded you, and you were to face them and overcome them. That's what made it glorious. That's what made it honorable. You were to be hailed as benefactors of your species, your names revered as belonging to brave men who faced death for honor and the benefit of humanity. And now, at the first real test of your courage — or if you prefer, the first mighty, terrifying trial — you shrink away. You're content to be remembered as men who weren't strong enough to endure a little cold and danger. Poor souls — they were chilly, so they went home to their warm firesides. That hardly required coming this far and dragging your captain to the shame of defeat just to prove you're cowards. Oh! Be men, or be more than men. Hold firm to your purpose. Stand like rock. This ice is not as strong as your hearts might be. It's changeable and cannot resist you, if you say it shall not. Don't return to your families with the mark of disgrace on your brows. Return as heroes who have fought and conquered — who don't know what it means to turn their backs on the enemy."

He spoke with a voice perfectly tuned to the different emotions of his speech, his eye full of noble purpose and heroism. Can you wonder the men were moved? They looked at one another, unable to respond. I spoke then and told them to go away and think about what had been said. I wouldn't lead them further north if they truly wanted to turn back. But I hoped that, on reflection, their courage would return.
They left. I turned to my friend. But he had collapsed into exhaustion and was barely clinging to life.

How this will end, I don't know. But I'd rather die than return in shame with my purpose unfulfilled. Yet I fear that will be my fate. The men, with no sustaining vision of glory and honor, will never willingly continue to endure these hardships.
September 7th.

The decision is made. I've agreed to turn back if we're not destroyed first. So my hopes are shattered by cowardice and indecision. I come back ignorant and disappointed. It would take more philosophy than I possess to bear this injustice with patience.
September 12th.

It is over. I'm returning to England. I've lost my hopes of discovery and glory. I've lost my friend. But I'll try to describe these bitter events to you, dear sister. And as I'm carried back toward England and toward you, I will not despair.

On September 9th, the ice began to move. Roarings like thunder were heard in the distance as the ice islands split and cracked in every direction. We were in the most extreme danger. But since we could only wait passively, my chief concern was my unfortunate guest, whose illness had worsened so badly that he was entirely confined to bed. The ice cracked behind us and was driven northward with great force. A breeze sprang from the west. On the 11th, the passage south became completely clear. When the sailors saw this — their return home apparently guaranteed — a shout of wild joy burst from them, long and loud. Frankenstein, who was dozing, woke and asked the cause. "They're cheering," I said, "because they'll soon return to England."
"Do you really mean to go back?"
"Alas, yes. I can't resist their demands. I can't lead them unwillingly to danger. I must return."

"Do as you wish. But I will not. You may abandon your purpose. But mine was given to me by heaven, and I dare not give it up. I'm weak, but surely the spirits that fuel my vengeance will grant me enough strength." Saying this, he tried to spring from the bed. But the effort was too great. He fell back and fainted.

It was a long time before he was revived. I often thought his life had ended entirely. At last he opened his eyes. He breathed with difficulty and couldn't speak. The ship's surgeon gave him a calming drug and told us to leave him undisturbed. He also told me that my friend certainly had only hours to live.

His death sentence was pronounced. I could only grieve and be patient. I sat by his bed, watching him. His eyes were closed. I thought he was sleeping. But then he called me in a faint voice. He asked me to come near and said, "Alas! The strength I counted on is gone. I feel that I shall soon die, while he — my enemy and persecutor — may still live. Don't think, Walton, that in my final moments I feel the burning hatred and desperate desire for revenge I once expressed. But I do feel justified in wanting his death. During these last days I've been examining my past conduct. I don't find it blameworthy. In a fit of passionate madness I created a rational being. I was bound to ensure his happiness and well-being as far as I could. That was my duty. But there was another duty that outweighed it. My obligations to the members of my own species had a greater claim, because they encompassed a greater amount of happiness or misery. With this in mind, I refused — and was right to refuse — to create a companion for the creature. He showed unparalleled cruelty and selfishness. He destroyed my friends. He killed beings who possessed the most exquisite capacity for happiness and wisdom. I don't know where his thirst for vengeance may end. Wretched himself, he must be prevented from making others wretched too. He ought to die. His destruction was my task, but I have failed. When I first asked you — selfishly and wrongly — to carry on my work, I admit my motives were base. But I renew that request now, motivated only by reason and virtue.

"Yet I can't ask you to give up your country and friends for this task. And now that you're returning to England, your chances of finding him are slim. But I leave the weighing of these factors, and the balancing of what you consider your duties, to you. My judgment is already clouded by the approach of death. I dare not ask you to do what I think is right, for I may still be misled by passion.

"That he should live to cause more harm disturbs me. But in other respects, this hour — when I expect my release at any moment — is the only happy one I've known in several years. The forms of my beloved dead appear before me, and I hurry to join them. Farewell, Walton! Seek happiness in peace and avoid ambition — even the seemingly innocent ambition of making your mark through science and discovery. Yet why do I say this? I was destroyed by such hopes, yet another may succeed."

His voice grew fainter as he spoke. At last, exhausted, he fell silent. About half an hour later he tried to speak again but couldn't. He pressed my hand weakly. His eyes closed forever. A gentle smile passed across his lips — and he was gone.

Margaret, what can I say about the loss of this extraordinary spirit? How can I convey the depth of my grief? My tears flow. My mind is shrouded in a cloud of sorrow. But I'm heading toward England, and there I may find some consolation.

I'm interrupted. What do these sounds mean? It's midnight. The breeze blows gently. The watch on deck barely stirs. Again — a sound like a human voice, but hoarser. It comes from the cabin where Frankenstein's body still lies. I must go and investigate. Good night, my sister.
Great God! What a scene has just taken place! I'm still dizzy from it. I'm not sure I have the power to describe it. Yet my tale would be incomplete without this final, extraordinary event.

I entered the cabin where my unfortunate friend's body lay. Over him hung a form I can't find words to describe — gigantic in size, yet grotesque and horribly misshapen. As the creature hung over the coffin, his face was hidden behind long, tangled hair. But one enormous hand was extended — its color and rough texture like that of a mummy. When he heard me approach, he stopped his cries of grief and horror and sprang toward the window. I had never seen a face so hideously, so loathsomely ugly. I shut my eyes involuntarily and tried to remember my duty regarding this destroyer. I called on him to stop.

He paused, looking at me with wonder. Then, turning again toward the lifeless body of his creator, he seemed to forget my presence. Every feature and gesture was driven by the wildest, most uncontrollable passion.

"That is also my victim!" he cried. "With his murder my crimes are complete. The miserable story of my existence reaches its end! Oh, Frankenstein! Generous, self-sacrificing soul! What good does it do to ask your forgiveness now? I, who irreversibly destroyed you by destroying all you loved. Alas! He's cold. He cannot answer me."

His voice seemed to choke. My first impulse — to obey my dying friend's request and destroy his enemy — was now suspended by a mixture of curiosity and compassion. I approached this terrifying being. I dared not look at his face again — there was something so frightening and otherworldly in his ugliness. I tried to speak, but words died on my lips. The creature continued uttering wild, incoherent self-accusations. At length, during a pause in the storm of his passion, I found the strength to address him.
"Your repentance is worthless now," I said. "If you had listened to your conscience and heeded remorse before driving your vengeance to this extreme, Frankenstein would still be alive."

"And do you imagine," said the creature, "that I was deaf to agony and remorse? He" — pointing to the corpse — "he did not suffer in the final act. Oh! Not one ten-thousandth of the anguish that was mine during every drawn-out moment of its execution. A horrible selfishness drove me forward while my heart was poisoned with remorse. Do you think Clerval's groans were music to my ears? My heart was made to be filled with love and sympathy. When it was wrenched by misery into hatred and violence, it didn't endure the change without torture beyond anything you can imagine.

"After murdering Clerval, I returned to Switzerland, heartbroken and defeated. I pitied Frankenstein. My pity reached the level of horror. I loathed myself. But when I discovered that he — the author of my existence and my unspeakable torment — dared to hope for happiness, that while piling misery and despair on me he sought his own joy in feelings and pleasures from which I was forever excluded — then helpless envy and bitter outrage filled me with an insatiable thirst for revenge. I remembered my threat and resolved to carry it out. I knew I was preparing terrible suffering for myself, but I was the slave, not the master, of an impulse I hated yet couldn't resist. Yet when she died! No — then I was not miserable. I had shut down all feeling. I had crushed all anguish. I reveled in the depths of my despair. Evil became my good. Having gone this far, I had no choice but to embrace the element I'd chosen. The completion of my demonic plan became an all-consuming passion. And now it's finished. There lies my last victim!"

At first I was touched by his expressions of misery. But when I recalled what Frankenstein had said about his powers of persuasion, and when I looked again at my friend's lifeless body, indignation flared within me. "Wretch!" I said. "It's fitting that you should come here to whine over the destruction you've caused. You throw a torch into a pile of buildings. When they've burned down, you sit among the ruins and weep. Hypocritical monster! If the man you mourn were still alive, you would still be hunting him — he would still be your prey. It's not pity you feel. You're only sorry because the victim of your evil is beyond your reach."

"Oh, that isn't how it is — not at all," the creature interrupted. "Yet I know that's the impression my actions must give. I don't seek sympathy in my misery. I expect none. When I first sought it, it was the love of virtue and the fullness of happiness and affection overflowing from my whole being that I wished to share. But now that virtue has become a shadow, and happiness and love have turned to bitter, loathing despair — why should anyone sympathize with me? I'm content to suffer alone for as long as my suffering lasts. When I die, I'm satisfied that my memory should be loaded with hatred and disgrace. I once dreamed of virtue, fame, and joy. I once falsely hoped to find beings who would look past my outward form and love me for the good qualities I was capable of showing. I was raised on high thoughts of honor and devotion. But crime has degraded me below the lowest animal. No guilt, no evil, no misery can compare to mine. When I review the terrible catalog of my sins, I can't believe I am the same creature whose mind was once filled with sublime visions of beauty and goodness. But it is so. The fallen angel has become a malicious devil. Yet even that enemy of God had friends and companions in his exile. I am alone.

"You, who call Frankenstein your friend, seem to know of my crimes and his misfortunes. But in the account he gave you, he couldn't sum up the hours and months of misery I endured in helpless agony. While I was destroying his happiness, I wasn't satisfying my own desires. They were always burning and insatiable. I still craved love and companionship, and I was still rejected. Was there no injustice in this? Am I the only criminal, when all of humanity sinned against me? Why don't you condemn Felix, who drove his friend from his door with contempt? Why don't you curse the peasant who tried to kill the man who saved his child? No — these are considered virtuous, blameless beings! I, the miserable and abandoned, am a freak of nature — to be kicked, spurned, and trampled. Even now my blood boils at the memory of this injustice.

"But it's true that I am a wretch. I have murdered the lovely and the helpless. I strangled the innocent in their sleep. I crushed the throat of one who never harmed me or any living thing. I dedicated my creator — the finest specimen of all that is worthy of love and admiration among men — to misery. I pursued him even to his irreversible ruin. There he lies, white and cold in death. You hate me. But your hatred cannot equal the hatred I feel for myself. I look at the hands that committed these deeds. I think of the heart where these horrors were conceived. I long for the moment when these hands will no longer be before my eyes, when that imagination will haunt my thoughts no more.

"Don't fear that I'll cause more harm. My work is nearly done. Neither your death nor anyone else's is needed to complete the story of my being and achieve what must be done. Only my own death is required. Don't think I'll be slow to make this sacrifice. I'll leave your vessel on the ice raft that brought me here. I'll seek the northernmost point of the globe. I'll gather my funeral pyre and burn this miserable body to ashes, so that its remains can't guide some curious, reckless wretch to create another being like me. I shall die. I'll no longer feel the agonies that now consume me or be prey to feelings unsatisfied yet unquenchable. He who called me into being is dead. When I too am gone, the very memory of us both will quickly vanish. I'll no longer see the sun or stars or feel the wind on my cheeks. Light, feeling, and awareness will pass away. In that nothingness I must find my peace. Some years ago, when the world first opened before me — when I felt the warmth of summer and heard the rustling of leaves and the singing of birds, and these were everything to me — I would have wept to die. Now it's my only consolation. Polluted by crimes and torn by the bitterest remorse, where can I find rest but in death?

"Farewell! I leave you. In you I leave the last human being these eyes will ever see. Farewell, Frankenstein! If you were still alive and still desired revenge against me, it would be better satisfied by my life than by my destruction. But that wasn't your wish. You sought my death so I couldn't cause greater suffering. And if somehow, in some way unknown to me, you haven't entirely ceased to think and feel, you wouldn't wish a vengeance greater than what I already feel. Ruined as you were, my agony was still greater than yours, for the bitter sting of remorse will never stop burning in my wounds until death closes them forever.

"But soon," he cried with sad, solemn intensity, "I shall die, and what I now feel will be felt no more. Soon these burning torments will be extinguished. I shall climb my funeral pyre in triumph and exult in the agony of the consuming flames. The light of that fire will fade away. My ashes will be swept into the sea by the winds. My spirit will sleep in peace — or if it thinks, it will surely not think like this. Farewell."
He sprang from the cabin window onto the ice raft floating beside the ship. He was soon carried away by the waves and lost in darkness and distance.
